abstract: In this paper we develop a Bayes criterion which includes the Rissanen complexity, for inferring regular grammar models. We develop two methods for regular grammar Bayesian inference. The fIrst method is based on treating the regular grammar as a I-dimensional Markov source, and the second is based on the combinatoric characteristics of the regular grammar itself. We apply the resulting Bayes criteria to a particular example in order to show the efficiency of each method.
originalAbstract: In this paper we develop a Bayes criterion which includes the Rissanen complexity, for inferring regular grammar models. We develop two methods for regular grammar Bayesian inference. The fIrst method is based on treating the regular grammar as a I-dimensional Markov source, and the second is based on the combinatoric characteristics of the regular grammar itself. We apply the resulting Bayes criteria to a particular example in order to show the efficiency of each method.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Bayesian criterion for inferring regular grammar models. A regular grammar describes structured sequences through a restricted system of production rules. The proposed criterion includes Rissanen complexity, bringing the complexity of the model into the inference process alongside the evidence used to choose among candidate explanations.

Two methods implement this approach. The first treats the grammar as a one-dimensional Markov source, viewing sequence generation through a probabilistic source model. The second works from the combinatorial characteristics of the grammar itself. These are two ways to formulate the inference problem, using different descriptions of the structure being learned.

The authors apply the resulting criteria to a particular example to illustrate the efficiency of each method. The stated contribution is thus a pair of Bayesian inference procedures and an example demonstrating their use. The complexity term matters because model selection must account for how elaborate a proposed grammar is, as well as how it explains the observed sequences.
summary.tldr: Two Bayesian methods infer regular grammars using a selection criterion that incorporates model complexity.

title: Bayesian Inference of Regular Grammar and Markov Source Models

abstract: The development of learning algorithms is generally based upon the min(cid:173) imization of an energy function. It is a fundamental requirement to com(cid:173) pute the gradient of this energy function with respect to the various pa(cid:173) rameters of the neural architecture, e.g., synaptic weights, neural gain,etc. In principle, this requires solving a system of nonlinear equations for each parameter of the model, which is computationally very expensive. A new methodology for neural learning of time-dependent nonlinear mappings is presented. It exploits the concept of adjoint operators to enable a fast global computation of the network's response to perturbations in all the systems parameters. The importance of the time boundary conditions of the adjoint functions is discussed. An algorithm is presented in which the adjoint sensitivity equations are solved simultaneously (Le., forward in time) along with the nonlinear dynamics of the neural networks. This methodology makes real-time applications and hardware implementation of temporal learning feasible.

paragraphs: Training a network often requires knowing how an objective changes when each model parameter changes. For networks learning nonlinear relationships over time, computing these sensitivities separately can be expensive: the abstract describes an approach that would require solving a nonlinear system for every parameter, including connection weights and neural gains.

The paper introduces a methodology based on adjoint operators to compute the network's response to parameter perturbations collectively. The purpose is to obtain the information needed for learning without treating every parameter as an independent nonlinear calculation. This makes sensitivity computation a central part of the temporal learning algorithm.

A distinctive feature is that the adjoint sensitivity equations are solved forward in time alongside the network's own nonlinear dynamics. The paper also discusses how conditions imposed at time boundaries affect the adjoint functions. The authors argue that this combination makes real-time temporal learning and hardware implementation feasible, connecting a mathematical reformulation of gradients to practical ways of running a learning system.
summary.tldr: Adjoint equations compute temporal network sensitivities collectively and forward in time, supporting real-time learning implementations.

title: Adjoint-Functions and Temporal Learning Algorithms in Neural Networks

abstract: A new computational model that addresses the formation of both topog- raphy and ocular dominance is presented. This is motivated by exper- imental evidence that these phenomena may be subserved by the same mechanisms. An important aspect of this model is that ocular domi- nance segregation can occur when input activity is both distributed, and positively correlated between the eyes. This allows investigation of the dependence of the pattern of ocular dominance stripes on the degree of correlation between the eyes: it is found that increasing correlation leads to narrower stripes. Experiments are suggested to test whether such be- haviour occurs in the natural system.

This is motivated by exper- imental evidence that these phenomena may be subserved by the same mechanisms. An important aspect of this model is that ocular domi- nance segregation can occur when input activity is both distributed, and positively correlated between the eyes. This allows investigation of the dependence of the pattern of ocular dominance stripes on the degree of correlation between the eyes: it is found that increasing correlation leads to narrower stripes. Experiments are suggested to test whether such be- haviour occurs in the natural system.

paragraphs: This paper presents a computational model for the development of topography and ocular dominance. Topography concerns spatial organization, while ocular dominance concerns the segregation of responses associated with the two eyes. The model is motivated by experimental evidence that the same mechanisms may contribute to both forms of organization.

A key property is that eye-specific segregation can emerge even when input activity is distributed and positively correlated between the eyes. Positive correlation means the two eyes' activity tends to vary together. The model therefore makes it possible to study segregation under conditions where the inputs from the eyes share activity patterns.

The authors vary the degree of correlation and find that stronger correlation produces narrower ocular-dominance stripes. This creates a specific relationship between an input property and the spatial pattern formed by the model. They suggest experiments to test whether the natural system behaves similarly. The stripe-width result is thus a computational prediction linked to a proposed biological test.
summary.tldr: A model forms ocular-dominance stripes despite positively correlated eye inputs and predicts narrower stripes as correlation increases.

title: Topography and Ocular Dominance with Positive Correlations

abstract: We address the problem of optical flow reconstruction and in par(cid:173) ticular the problem of resolving ambiguities near edges. They oc(cid:173) cur due to (i) the aperture problem and (ii) the occlusion problem, where pixels on both sides of an intensity edge are assigned the same velocity estimates (and confidence). However, these measurements are correct for just one side of the edge (the non occluded one). Our approach is to introduce an uncertamty field with respect to the estimates and confidence measures. We note that the confi(cid:173) dence measures are large at intensity edges and larger at the con(cid:173) vex sides of the edges, i.e. inside corners, than at the concave side. We resolve the ambiguities through local interactions via coupled Markov random fields (MRF) . The result is the detection of motion for regions of images with large global convexity.

paragraphs: This paper tackles ambiguous motion estimates near image edges during optical flow reconstruction. It identifies two sources: the aperture problem and occlusion. In the occlusion case, pixels on both sides of an intensity boundary can receive the same velocity estimate and confidence even though the measurement is correct only on the nonoccluded side.

The proposed method introduces an uncertainty field associated with both motion estimates and their confidence measures. This makes uncertainty part of the reconstruction rather than relying on confidence alone. The authors observe that confidence is high at intensity edges and higher on their convex sides, described as inside corners, than on their concave sides.

Coupled Markov random fields resolve the ambiguities through local interactions. This provides a way for neighboring evidence, uncertainty, and motion estimates to influence one another. The stated outcome is detection of motion in image regions with strong global convexity. The contribution connects local edge ambiguity with a coordinated representation that can support motion detection across larger regions.
summary.tldr: Coupled Markov random fields use explicit uncertainty to resolve edge-related motion ambiguities and detect motion in globally convex regions.

title: Resolving motion ambiguities

abstract: The spatial distribution and time course of electrical signals in neurons have important theoretical and practical consequences. Because it is difficult to infer how neuronal form affects electrical signaling, we have developed a quantitative yet intuitive approach to the analysis of electrotonus. This approach transforms the architecture of the cell from anatomical to electrotonic space, using the logarithm of voltage attenuation as the distance metric. We describe the theory behind this approach and illustrate its use.
originalAbstract: The spatial distribution and time course of electrical signals in neurons have important theoretical and practical consequences. Because it is difficult to infer how neuronal form affects electrical signaling, we have developed a quantitative yet intuitive approach to the analysis of electrotonus. This approach transforms the architecture of the cell from anatomical to electrotonic space, using the logarithm of voltage attenuation as the distance metric. We describe the theory behind this approach and illustrate its use.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of understanding electrical signaling from a neuron’s anatomical shape. The spatial distribution and timing of voltages matter for neuronal function, but a picture of the cell’s branches does not directly express how signals attenuate. The authors develop a transformation intended to make that relationship quantitative and intuitive.

The method maps the cell’s architecture from anatomical space into electrotonic space. Its distance measure is based on the logarithm of voltage attenuation. Consequently, distances in the transformed representation describe electrical weakening rather than simply physical separation. The representation changes what it means for two locations in the neuron to be electrically close or distant.

The authors explain the theory underlying the transformation and illustrate its use. Its contribution is an analytical view of neuronal structure organized around signal propagation. By making attenuation part of the geometry, the method offers a way to reason about the functional consequences of form using a representation directly tied to electrical behavior.
summary.tldr: The electrotonic transformation redraws neuronal structure using voltage attenuation as distance to clarify the connection between anatomy and signaling.

title: The Electrotonic Transformation: a Tool for Relating Neuronal Form to Function
Direct Multi-Step Time Series Prediction Using TD(λ)

abstract: The Self-Organizing Map (SOM) algorithm has been extensively studied and has been applied with considerable success to a wide variety of problems. However, the algorithm is derived from heuris(cid:173) tic ideas and this leads to a number of significant limitations. In this paper, we consider the problem of modelling the probabil(cid:173) ity density of data in a space of several dimensions in terms of a smaller number of latent, or hidden, variables. We introduce a novel form of latent variable model, which we call the GTM algo(cid:173) rithm (for Generative Topographic Mapping), which allows general non-linear transformations from latent space to data space, and which is trained using the EM (expectation-maximization) algo(cid:173) rithm. Our approach overcomes the limitations of the SOM, while introducing no significant disadvantages. We demonstrate the per(cid:173) formance of the GTM algorithm on simulated data from flow diag(cid:173) nostics for a multi-phase oil pipeline.

paragraphs: Generative Topographic Mapping, or GTM, models data with many dimensions using a smaller set of hidden variables. The motivation comes from self-organizing maps, which have been useful across many problems but are based on heuristic ideas. The authors seek a probabilistic model that addresses limitations arising from that foundation.

GTM defines a latent-variable model with nonlinear transformations from the smaller hidden space into the observed data space. This allows the relationship between the compact representation and the data to be curved or otherwise nonlinear. Training uses expectation-maximization, connecting the construction of the representation to the task of modeling the data's probability density.

The paper reports that this approach overcomes limitations of self-organizing maps without significant disadvantages. It demonstrates GTM on simulated data for flow diagnostics in a multiphase oil pipeline. The central contribution is a probability-based way to connect lower-dimensional hidden variables with richer observations, while retaining the ability to represent nonlinear structure.
summary.tldr: GTM uses a nonlinear latent-variable probability model trained by expectation-maximization as an alternative to heuristic self-organizing maps.

title: GTM: A Principled Alternative to the Self-Organizing Map

abstract: The softassign quadratic assignment algorithm has recently emerged as an effective strategy for a variety of optimization prob(cid:173) lems in pattern recognition and combinatorial optimization. While the effectiveness of the algorithm was demonstrated in thousands of simulations, there was no known proof of convergence. Here, we provide a proof of convergence for the most general form of the algorithm.
originalAbstract: The softassign quadratic assignment algorithm has recently emerged as an effective strategy for a variety of optimization prob(cid:173) lems in pattern recognition and combinatorial optimization. While the effectiveness of the algorithm was demonstrated in thousands of simulations, there was no known proof of convergence. Here, we provide a proof of convergence for the most general form of the algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper provides a mathematical foundation for the softassign quadratic assignment algorithm, an optimization method used in pattern recognition and combinatorial problems. Its central question concerns convergence: whether the algorithm's repeated updates approach a limiting result. That question is distinct from whether the method produces useful answers in individual applications.

The motivation is a gap between practical evidence and theoretical understanding. The algorithm had already appeared effective across thousands of simulations, but those observations did not constitute a convergence proof. Successful runs can establish that a method works in many tested situations; a proof establishes a property through mathematical reasoning about the algorithm.

The stated contribution is a convergence proof covering the algorithm's most general form. This gives its observed effectiveness a firmer theoretical basis without restricting the contribution to one application or simulation setting. The result should be read specifically as a convergence guarantee: the abstract does not identify convergence with finding the globally best assignment. Its significance is establishing a previously unproved property of an already useful optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper proves convergence for the most general form of the softassign quadratic assignment algorithm.

title: A Convergence Proof for the Softassign Quadratic Assignment Algorithm

abstract: We compare the ability of three exemplar-based memory models, each using three different face stimulus representations, to account for the probability a human subject responded "old" in an old/new facial mem(cid:173) ory experiment. The models are 1) the Generalized Context Model, 2) SimSample, a probabilistic sampling model, and 3) MMOM, a novel model related to kernel density estimation that explicitly encodes stim(cid:173) ulus distinctiveness. The representations are 1) positions of stimuli in MDS "face space," 2) projections of test faces onto the "eigenfaces" of the study set, and 3) a representation based on response to a grid of Gabor filter jets. Of the 9 model/representation combinations, only the distinc(cid:173) tiveness model in MDS space predicts the observed "morph familiarity inversion" effect, in which the subjects' false alarm rate for morphs be(cid:173) tween similar faces is higher than their hit rate for many of the studied faces. This evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that human mem(cid:173) ory for faces is a kernel density estimation task, with the caveat that dis(cid:173) tinctive faces require larger kernels than do typical faces.

paragraphs: The paper studies how people decide whether they have seen a face before. It compares three memory models across three ways of representing faces, producing nine combinations. The target is the probability that a person calls a test face familiar, including cases where familiarity judgments are mistaken.

The models include the Generalized Context Model, a probabilistic sampling model called SimSample, and MMOM, which explicitly represents distinctiveness. The face descriptions use positions in a multidimensional similarity space, projections onto eigenfaces, or responses from Gabor filters. This design examines both the memory computation and the representation on which it operates.

Only MMOM in the multidimensional similarity space predicts the reported familiarity inversion: blends of similar faces can attract more false recognition than many studied faces attract correct recognition. The result supports an account resembling kernel density estimation, where stored faces contribute regions of familiarity. However, the supported account gives distinctive faces broader kernels than typical faces, making distinctiveness essential to explaining the observed judgments.
summary.tldr: A face-memory model that adjusts familiarity kernels for distinctiveness explains why some blended faces seem more familiar than studied faces.

title: Facial Memory Is Kernel Density Estimation (Almost)

abstract: Olshausen & Field demonstrated that a learning algorithm that attempts to generate a sparse code for natural scenes develops a complete family of localised, oriented, bandpass receptive fields, similar to those of 'simple cells' in VI. This paper describes an algorithm which finds a sparse code for sequences of images that preserves information about the input. This algorithm when trained on natural video sequences develops bases representing the movement in particular directions with particular speeds, similar to the receptive fields of the movement-sensitive cells observed in cortical visual areas. Furthermore, to previous approaches to learning direction selectivity, the timing of neuronal activity encodes the phase of the movement, so the precise timing of spikes is crucially important to the information encoding.
originalAbstract: Olshausen & Field demonstrated that a learning algorithm that attempts to generate a sparse code for natural scenes develops a complete family of localised, oriented, bandpass receptive fields, similar to those of 'simple cells' in VI. This paper describes an algorithm which finds a sparse code for sequences of images that preserves information about the input. This algorithm when trained on natural video sequences develops bases representing the movement in particular directions with particular speeds, similar to the receptive fields of the movement-sensitive cells observed in cortical visual areas. Furthermore, to previous approaches to learning direction selectivity, the timing of neuronal activity encodes the phase of the movement, so the precise timing of spikes is crucially important to the information encoding.

paragraphs: The paper extends sparse coding from individual natural images to sequences of images. Sparse coding seeks a representation in which relatively few components are active while information about the input is preserved. Earlier work on still scenes produced features resembling certain visual neurons; this study asks what properties emerge when the input includes movement over time.

The proposed algorithm learns from natural video sequences. Its learned basis elements represent motion in particular directions and at particular speeds, resembling the receptive fields of movement-sensitive cells in visual cortical areas. This connects an information-preserving learning objective with motion-selective representations, showing that such properties can emerge through learning from moving imagery.

Timing also carries information in the resulting representation. The timing of neuronal activity encodes the phase of movement, so precise spike timing is important to what the model represents. The contribution therefore concerns both which motion patterns learned units respond to and when they respond. The stated resemblance to biological cells supports a modeling connection without establishing that the brain uses this exact algorithm.
summary.tldr: Learning an information-preserving sparse code from natural video produces motion-selective features whose activity timing encodes movement phase.

title: Emergence of Movement Sensitive Neurons' Properties by Learning a Sparse Code for Natural Moving Images

paragraphs: The paper uses products of experts to learn generative models of handwritten digits. These models combine probabilistic experts and discover stochastic binary features that represent nonlinear image structure. A separate model is learned for each digit class, allowing a test image to be assessed through the scores assigned by the different class models.

Recognition improves by organizing each class's models into a hierarchy. Each level has one hidden layer, and the next level learns from the hidden-unit activities produced by the previously trained level. Every level supplies its own unnormalized log-probability score. With three levels for each of ten digits, an image generates thirty scores describing its compatibility with the learned models.

A supervised logistic classification network, trained on separate data, combines those scores into a digit prediction. The resulting system is reported as comparable with contemporary leading discriminative methods on MNIST. The finding supports the usefulness of the learned high-dimensional generative representations, with recognition achieved by combining their class-specific, multilevel scores in a final supervised classifier.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical, class-specific products of experts provide scores that a supervised classifier combines for competitive handwritten-digit recognition.

title: Recognizing Hand-written Digits Using Hierarchical Products of Experts

abstract: Saliency mechanisms play an important role when visual recognition must be performed in cluttered scenes. We propose a computational defi- nition of saliency that deviates from existing models by equating saliency to discrimination. In particular, the salient attributes of a given visual class are defined as the features that enable best discrimination between that class and all other classes of recognition interest. It is shown that this definition leads to saliency algorithms of low complexity, that are scalable to large recognition problems, and is compatible with existing models of early biological vision. Experimental results demonstrating success in the context of challenging recognition problems are also pre- sented.

We propose a computational defi- nition of saliency that deviates from existing models by equating saliency to discrimination. In particular, the salient attributes of a given visual class are defined as the features that enable best discrimination between that class and all other classes of recognition interest. It is shown that this definition leads to saliency algorithms of low complexity, that are scalable to large recognition problems, and is compatible with existing models of early biological vision. Experimental results demonstrating success in the context of challenging recognition problems are also pre- sented.

paragraphs: Recognizing objects in clutter requires deciding which visual information is useful. This paper defines saliency through discrimination: a feature is salient for a visual class when it helps distinguish that class from the other classes relevant to the recognition task. Saliency is thus tied to what the system needs to recognize and distinguish.

This definition makes the competing classes part of the selection criterion. A feature's usefulness depends on whether it separates the target from those alternatives, giving saliency a direct role in recognition. The authors show that their formulation leads to algorithms with low computational complexity that can scale to large recognition problems, while remaining compatible with existing models of early biological vision.

Experiments demonstrate success on challenging recognition tasks. These results support using discriminative usefulness to guide attention to visual attributes in cluttered scenes. The contribution connects three concerns within one formulation: identifying informative features, keeping the computation manageable, and maintaining compatibility with biological accounts of early visual processing. Compatibility is the stated relationship, rather than proof that biological vision implements this exact mechanism.
summary.tldr: The paper defines visual saliency as class-discriminative usefulness and derives efficient recognition algorithms from that definition.

title: Discriminant Saliency for Visual Recognition from Cluttered Scenes

abstract: We show how to learn a Mahanalobis distance metric for k -nearest neighbor (kNN) classification by semidefinite programming. The metric is trained with the goal that the k -nearest neighbors always belong to the same class while examples from different classes are separated by a large margin. On seven data sets of varying size and difficulty, we find that metrics trained in this way lead to significant improvements in kNN classification--for example, achieving a test error rate of 1.3% on the MNIST handwritten digits. As in support vector machines (SVMs), the learning problem reduces to a convex optimization based on the hinge loss. Unlike learning in SVMs, however, our framework requires no modification or extension for problems in multiway (as opposed to binary) classification.
originalAbstract: We show how to learn a Mahanalobis distance metric for k -nearest neighbor (kNN) classification by semidefinite programming. The metric is trained with the goal that the k -nearest neighbors always belong to the same class while examples from different classes are separated by a large margin. On seven data sets of varying size and difficulty, we find that metrics trained in this way lead to significant improvements in kNN classification--for example, achieving a test error rate of 1.3% on the MNIST handwritten digits. As in support vector machines (SVMs), the learning problem reduces to a convex optimization based on the hinge loss. Unlike learning in SVMs, however, our framework requires no modification or extension for problems in multiway (as opposed to binary) classification.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification depends on which training examples count as close to a new example. This paper learns that notion of closeness from labeled data using a Mahalanobis distance metric. The training objective encourages an example's nearest neighbors to share its class and pushes examples from other classes away by a large margin.

The authors formulate metric learning as a semidefinite program. Like support vector machine training, the resulting problem is convex and uses hinge loss. The learned object is a distance measure for nearest-neighbor classification, and the framework directly accommodates multiple classes without the modifications or extensions associated with moving from binary to multiway SVM classification.

Across seven datasets of different sizes and difficulty, the learned metrics produce significant improvements in nearest-neighbor classification. The reported MNIST test error is 1.3%. These findings support learning the geometry used by the classifier rather than relying on a fixed distance. Having same-class nearest neighbors is the training goal; the empirical results describe how successfully the resulting metrics support classification on the evaluated data.
summary.tldr: Learning a large-margin distance metric improves nearest-neighbor classification across seven datasets, including a reported 1.3% MNIST test error.

title: Distance Metric Learning for Large Margin Nearest Neighbor Classification

abstract: We present a computational model of human eye movements in an ob- ject class detection task. The model combines state-of-the-art computer vision object class detection methods (SIFT features trained using Ad- aBoost) with a biologically plausible model of human eye movement to produce a sequence of simulated ﬁxations, culminating with the acqui- sition of a target. We validated the model by comparing its behavior to the behavior of human observers performing the identical object class detection task (looking for a teddy bear among visually complex non- target objects). We found considerable agreement between the model and human data in multiple eye movement measures, including number of ﬁxations, cumulative probability of ﬁxating the target, and scanpath distance.
originalAbstract: We present a computational model of human eye movements in an ob- ject class detection task. The model combines state-of-the-art computer vision object class detection methods (SIFT features trained using Ad- aBoost) with a biologically plausible model of human eye movement to produce a sequence of simulated ﬁxations, culminating with the acqui- sition of a target. We validated the model by comparing its behavior to the behavior of human observers performing the identical object class detection task (looking for a teddy bear among visually complex non- target objects). We found considerable agreement between the model and human data in multiple eye movement measures, including number of ﬁxations, cumulative probability of ﬁxating the target, and scanpath distance.

paragraphs: This paper models how people move their eyes while searching for an object belonging to a particular category. The task involves locating a teddy bear among visually complicated objects. The model aims to reproduce the sequence of fixations leading to the target, connecting object recognition with the behavior used to find it.

The approach combines a computer vision detector with a biologically plausible model of eye movements. The detector uses SIFT features trained with AdaBoost, while the eye movement component generates simulated fixations. Together, these components provide a way to study how information useful for recognizing a target can guide a sequence of looks through a scene.

The authors compare the model with human observers performing the same search task. They report considerable agreement in the number of fixations, the cumulative probability of looking at the target, and scanpath distance. Agreement across these measures supports the model as an account of several aspects of search behavior in the studied task.
summary.tldr: A model combining object detection and eye movement mechanisms reproduces several measures of human visual search behavior.

title: A Computational Model of Eye Movements during Object Class Detection

abstract: Bob offers a face-detection web service where clients can submit their images for analysis. Alice would very much like to use the service, but is reluctant to reveal the content of her images to Bob. Bob, for his part, is reluctant to release his face detector, as he spent a lot of time, energy and money constructing it. Secure Multi- Party computations use cryptographic tools to solve this problem without leaking any information. Unfortunately, these methods are slow to compute and we intro- duce a couple of machine learning techniques that allow the parties to solve the problem while leaking a controlled amount of information. The ﬁrst method is an information-bottleneck variant of AdaBoost that lets Bob ﬁnd a subset of features that are enough for classifying an image patch, but not enough to actually recon- struct it. The second machine learning technique is active learning that allows Alice to construct an online classiﬁer, based on a small number of calls to Bob’s face detector. She can then use her online classiﬁer as a fast rejector before using a cryptographically secure classiﬁer on the remaining image patches.

paragraphs: The paper considers a face-detection service where the client wants to protect an image and the provider wants to protect its detector. Cryptographic secure multiparty computation can address both concerns without information leakage, but its computational cost motivates a different tradeoff. The authors introduce two machine-learning techniques that permit a controlled amount of information to be revealed.

The first is an information-bottleneck version of AdaBoost. It helps the provider select features that contain enough information to classify an image patch but not enough to reconstruct that patch. The aim is to preserve what detection needs while restricting the image content available through the selected representation.

The second technique uses active learning so the client can build an online classifier through a small number of queries to the provider. This local classifier quickly rejects patches before the remaining patches undergo cryptographically secure classification. The two techniques target different sources of cost: the information used for classification and the number of patches requiring the secure procedure.
summary.tldr: Feature selection and an actively learned local rejector reduce face-detection costs while allowing controlled information leakage.

title: Efficient Methods for Privacy Preserving Face Detection

abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can be applied to study the functional connectivity of the neural elements which form complex network at a whole brain level. Most analyses of functional resting state networks (RSN) have been based on the analysis of correlation between the temporal dynamics of various regions of the brain. While these models can identify coherently behaving groups in terms of correlation they give little insight into how these groups interact. In this paper we take a different view on the analysis of functional resting state networks. Starting from the definition of resting state as functional coherent groups we search for functional units of the brain that communicate with other parts of the brain in a coherent manner as measured by mutual information. We use the infinite relational model (IRM) to quantify functional coherent groups of resting state networks and demonstrate how the extracted component interactions can be used to discriminate between functional resting state activity in multiple sclerosis and normal subjects.

Correlation-based analyses identify such coherent groups, but provide less insight into interactions among them. This paper shifts attention toward groups defined by coherent relationships with other parts of the brain, making the pattern of interactions central to the analysis.

The approach measures relationships using mutual information and applies an infinite relational model to identify functionally coherent units. The organizing idea is that regions can be grouped according to how they communicate with the wider network. This produces components together with a description of their interactions, rather than focusing only on similarity within a component.

The authors demonstrate that these extracted interactions can discriminate between resting-state activity in people with multiple sclerosis and normal subjects. The finding gives the interaction-based representation a concrete use in comparing the studied groups. It supports analyzing how functional units relate to one another as an informative aspect of whole-brain resting-state organization.
summary.tldr: An infinite relational model groups brain regions by their interactions and uses those interactions to distinguish studied resting-state subject groups.

title: Infinite Relational Modeling of Functional Connectivity in Resting State fMRI

abstract: We study a setting in which Poisson processes generate sequences of decision-making events. The optimization goal is allowed to depend on the rate of decision outcomes; the rate may depend on a potentially long backlog of events and decisions. We model the problem as a Poisson process with a throttling policy that enforces a data-dependent rate limit and reduce the learning problem to a convex optimization problem that can be solved efficiently. This problem setting matches applications in which damage caused by an attacker grows as a function of the rate of unsuppressed hostile events. We report on experiments on abuse detection for an email service.

paragraphs: Some decision problems depend on how rapidly outcomes occur, as well as on the outcomes themselves. This paper studies events generated by Poisson processes, allowing the optimization objective to depend on the rate of decision outcomes. That rate can reflect a potentially long history of earlier events and choices.

The authors model intervention through a throttling policy that imposes a data-dependent rate limit on the process. This connects the current decision to the accumulated sequence of activity. They reduce learning the policy to a convex optimization problem that can be solved efficiently, providing a practical route to optimization despite the role of historical events.

The setting is motivated by abuse prevention, where an attacker's damage can grow with the rate of hostile events that remain unsuppressed. The paper reports experiments on abuse detection for an email service. Its main contribution is a framework for learning rate-sensitive decisions, bringing the timing and accumulation of harmful activity directly into the optimization problem.
summary.tldr: Learning data-dependent rate limits for Poisson event streams reduces to efficient convex optimization, with an application to email abuse detection.

title: Throttling Poisson Processes

abstract: This paper proposes a novel boosting algorithm called VadaBoost which is motivated by recent empirical Bernstein bounds. VadaBoost iteratively minimizes a cost function that balances the sample mean and the sample variance of the exponential loss. Each step of the proposed algorithm minimizes the cost efficiently by providing weighted data to a weak learner rather than requiring a brute force evaluation of all possible weak learners. Thus, the proposed algorithm solves a key limitation of previous empirical Bernstein boosting methods which required brute force enumeration of all possible weak learners. Experimental results confirm that the new algorithm achieves the performance improvements of EBBoost yet goes beyond decision stumps to handle any weak learner. Significant performance gains are obtained over AdaBoost for arbitrary weak learners including decision trees (CART).

This paper proposes VadaBoost, an algorithm motivated by empirical Bernstein bounds that balances the sample mean and sample variance of exponential loss. Its objective therefore considers both the average loss and how much that loss varies across the training sample.

The main computational contribution is how each boosting step is performed. VadaBoost supplies weighted data to a weak learner to minimize its cost efficiently. Earlier empirical Bernstein boosting methods required evaluating every possible weak learner by brute force. Removing that enumeration requirement lets the variance-sensitive objective work with a much broader choice of weak learner.

Experiments show that VadaBoost retains the performance improvements associated with EBBoost while extending beyond decision stumps to handle arbitrary weak learners. The reported comparisons include significant gains over AdaBoost with weak learners such as CART decision trees. The contribution is therefore both an objective that penalizes loss variability and an efficient training procedure that makes that objective usable with richer learners.
summary.tldr: VadaBoost efficiently balances mean and variance of exponential loss, extending empirical-Bernstein boosting to arbitrary weak learners with reported performance gains.

title: Variance Penalizing AdaBoost

abstract: In this paper, we give a new generalization error bound of Multiple Kernel Learning (MKL) for a general class of regularizations. Our main target in this paper is dense type regularizations including ℓp-MKL that imposes ℓp-mixed-norm regularization instead of ℓ1-mixed-norm regularization. According to the recent numerical experiments, the sparse regularization does not necessarily show a good performance compared with dense type regularizations. Motivated by this fact, this paper gives a general theoretical tool to derive fast learning rates that is applicable to arbitrary monotone norm-type regularizations in a unifying manner. As a by-product of our general result, we show a fast learning rate of ℓp-MKL that is tightest among existing bounds. We also show that our general learning rate achieves the minimax lower bound. Finally, we show that, when the complexities of candidate reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces are inhomogeneous, dense type regularization shows better learning rate compared with sparse ℓ1 regularization.

paragraphs: The paper develops generalization guarantees for multiple kernel learning across a broad class of regularizers. Its main emphasis is on dense regularization, including Lp mixed norms, motivated by observations that sparse L1 regularization does not always perform as well. The theoretical question is how regularization choices affect the rate at which prediction error improves with more data.

Applying it to Lp multiple kernel learning yields a rate they describe as the tightest among existing bounds. They also show that their general learning rate achieves a minimax lower bound, connecting the guarantee to a fundamental worst-case benchmark.

A further result distinguishes settings where the candidate kernel spaces have different complexities. In this inhomogeneous case, dense regularization has a better learning rate than sparse L1 regularization. This supplies a theoretical reason why retaining broader kernel contributions can be beneficial when the component spaces differ in complexity, rather than treating sparsity as uniformly preferable.
summary.tldr: A unified learning-rate analysis supports dense multiple kernel regularization, including better rates than sparse regularization for kernels with differing complexities.

title: Unifying Framework for Fast Learning Rate of Non-Sparse Multiple Kernel Learning

abstract: Graphical model selection refers to the problem of estimating the unknown graph structure given observations at the nodes in the model. We consider a challenging instance of this problem when some of the nodes are latent or hidden. We characterize conditions for tractable graph estimation and develop efficient methods with provable guarantees. We consider the class of Ising models Markov on locally tree-like graphs, which are in the regime of correlation decay. We propose an efficient method for graph estimation, and establish its structural consistency when the number of samples $n$ scales as $n = \Omega(\theta_{\min}^{-\delta \eta(\eta+1)-2}\log p)$, where $\theta_{\min}$ is the minimum edge potential, $\delta$ is the depth (i.e., distance from a hidden node to the nearest observed nodes), and $\eta$ is a parameter which depends on the minimum and maximum node and edge potentials in the Ising model. The proposed method is practical to implement and provides flexibility to control the number of latent variables and the cycle lengths in the output graph. We also present necessary conditions for graph estimation by any method and show that our method nearly matches the lower bound on sample requirements.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to reconstruct a graph of statistical relationships when some of its nodes are hidden. Hidden nodes make the task harder because the observed variables provide only indirect evidence about parts of the structure. The authors focus on Ising models whose graphs are locally tree-like and whose correlations decay, establishing conditions under which efficient reconstruction is possible.

Their method has a structural consistency guarantee under a stated sample-size scaling. The requirement grows logarithmically with the number of variables, while also depending on the weakest edge potential, the distance between hidden nodes and nearby observed nodes, and a parameter determined by node and edge potentials. Thus, the guarantee explicitly reflects how difficult the hidden structure is to detect.

The algorithm is described as practical to implement and allows control over the number of latent variables and the lengths of cycles in its output. The authors also derive necessary sample requirements for any reconstruction method. Their method nearly matches that lower bound, indicating that its data requirements are close to the established fundamental limit within the studied setting.
summary.tldr: An efficient method recovers hidden-node Ising graph structures under locally tree-like, correlation-decay conditions with nearly lower-bound sample requirements.

title: Latent Graphical Model Selection: Efficient Methods for Locally Tree-like Graphs

abstract: We consider an abstract class of optimization problems that are parameterized concavely in a single parameter, and show that the solution path along the parameter can always be approximated with accuracy $\varepsilon >0$ by a set of size $O(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$. A lower bound of size $\Omega (1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ shows that the upper bound is tight up to a constant factor. We also devise an algorithm that calls a step-size oracle and computes an approximate path of size $O(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$. Finally, we provide an implementation of the oracle for soft-margin support vector machines, and a parameterized semi-definite program for matrix completion.

Finally, we provide an implementation of the oracle for soft-margin support vector machines, and a parameterized semi-definite program for matrix completion.

paragraphs: This paper considers optimization problems that change with a single parameter. Instead of seeking a solution at just one parameter value, it studies how to represent the solution path as that parameter varies. The defining condition is that the optimization problem depends concavely on the parameter, which specifies the class covered by the results.

For any positive accuracy target epsilon, the authors show that a set of size proportional to one over the square root of epsilon can approximate the path. They also prove a matching lower bound up to a constant factor. This means the dependence on accuracy cannot generally be improved across the studied class merely by finding a different approximation strategy.

The paper supplies an algorithm that achieves this path size by consulting a step-size oracle. It also implements that oracle for soft-margin support vector machines and a parameterized semidefinite program for matrix completion. These constructions connect the abstract approximation result to concrete optimization problems with adjustable parameters.
summary.tldr: For concavely parameterized optimization problems, the paper proves tight bounds on approximate solution-path size and gives an oracle-based construction.

title: Approximating Concavely Parameterized Optimization Problems

abstract: Distributed machine learning has typically been approached from a data parallel perspective, where big data are partitioned to multiple workers and an algorithm is executed concurrently over different data subsets under various synchronization schemes to ensure speed-up and/or correctness. A sibling problem that has received relatively less attention is how to ensure efficient and correct model parallel execution of ML algorithms, where parameters of an ML program are partitioned to different workers and undergone concurrent iterative updates. We argue that model and data parallelisms impose rather different challenges for system design, algorithmic adjustment, and theoretical analysis. In this paper, we develop a system for model-parallelism, STRADS, that provides a programming abstraction for scheduling parameter updates by discovering and leveraging changing structural properties of ML programs. STRADS enables a flexible tradeoff between scheduling efficiency and fidelity to intrinsic dependencies within the models, and improves memory efficiency of distributed ML. We demonstrate the efficacy of model-parallel algorithms implemented on STRADS versus popular implementations for topic modeling, matrix factorization, and Lasso.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can split training examples among workers or split the model's parameters among them. This paper focuses on the second approach, model parallelism, in which workers concurrently update different parameters. The authors argue that dependencies among these updates create distinct challenges for systems, algorithms, and correctness analysis.

They introduce STRADS, a system with a programming abstraction for scheduling parameter updates. Its scheduling uses structural properties of the learning program that can change during execution. The abstraction lets implementations balance scheduling efficiency against how faithfully they respect the model's intrinsic dependencies, while also improving memory efficiency in distributed learning.

The paper demonstrates model-parallel algorithms on topic modeling, matrix factorization, and Lasso, comparing STRADS implementations with popular alternatives. These demonstrations support the system's usefulness across several learning problems. The main contribution is to make parameter-update scheduling an explicit part of distributed execution, so decisions about concurrent work can respond to the structure of the model being trained rather than relying only on a division of the input data.
summary.tldr: STRADS schedules distributed parameter updates using changing model structure to balance efficiency, dependencies, and memory use.

title: On Model Parallelization and Scheduling Strategies for Distributed Machine Learning

abstract: Diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (DWI) and fiber tractography are the only methods to measure the structure of the white matter in the living human brain. The diffusion signal has been modelled as the combined contribution from many individual fascicles of nerve fibers passing through each location in the white matter. Typically, this is done via basis pursuit, but estimation of the exact directions is limited due to discretization. The difficulties inherent in modeling DWI data are shared by many other problems involving fitting non-parametric mixture models. Ekanadaham et al. proposed an approach, continuous basis pursuit, to overcome discretization error in the 1-dimensional case (e.g., spike-sorting). Here, we propose a more general algorithm that fits mixture models of any dimensionality without discretization. Our algorithm uses the principles of L2-boost, together with refitting of the weights and pruning of the parameters. The addition of these steps to L2-boost both accelerates the algorithm and assures its accuracy. We refer to the resulting algorithm as elastic basis pursuit, or EBP, since it expands and contracts the active set of kernels as needed. We show that in contrast to existing approaches to fitting mixtures, our boosting framework (1) enables the selection of the optimal bias-variance tradeoff along the solution path, and (2) scales with high-dimensional problems. In simulations of DWI, we find that EBP yields better parameter estimates than a non-negative least squares (NNLS) approach, or the standard model used in DWI, the tensor model, which serves as the basis for diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). We demonstrate the utility of the method in DWI data acquired in parts of the brain containing crossings of multiple fascicles of nerve fibers.

Methods that restrict possible bundle directions to a discrete set introduce discretization error. The authors develop a method for fitting mixtures of any dimensionality without this discretization.

summary.tldr: Elastic basis pursuit fits continuous high-dimensional mixtures through boosting, refitting, and pruning, with improved fiber-direction estimates in diffusion-imaging simulations.

title: Deconvolution of High Dimensional Mixtures via Boosting, with Application to Diffusion-Weighted MRI of Human Brain

abstract: Sparse high dimensional graphical model selection is a popular topic in contemporary machine learning. To this end, various useful approaches have been proposed in the context of $\ell_1$ penalized estimation in the Gaussian framework. Though many of these approaches are demonstrably scalable and have leveraged recent advances in convex optimization, they still depend on the Gaussian functional form. To address this gap, a convex pseudo-likelihood based partial correlation graph estimation method (CONCORD) has been recently proposed. This method uses cyclic coordinate-wise minimization of a regression based pseudo-likelihood, and has been shown to have robust model selection properties in comparison with the Gaussian approach. In direct contrast to the parallel work in the Gaussian setting however, this new convex pseudo-likelihood framework has not leveraged the extensive array of methods that have been proposed in the machine learning literature for convex optimization. In this paper, we address this crucial gap by proposing two proximal gradient methods (CONCORD-ISTA and CONCORD-FISTA) for performing $\ell_1$-regularized inverse covariance matrix estimation in the pseudo-likelihood framework. We present timing comparisons with coordinate-wise minimization and demonstrate that our approach yields tremendous pay offs for $\ell_1$-penalized partial correlation graph estimation outside the Gaussian setting, thus yielding the fastest and most scalable approach for such problems. We undertake a theoretical analysis of our approach and rigorously demonstrate convergence, and also derive rates thereof.

The authors introduce CONCORD-ISTA and CONCORD-FISTA, two proximal-gradient algorithms for the corresponding l1-regularized inverse-covariance estimation problem. These methods bring established convex-optimization machinery into the pseudo-likelihood framework, where the statistical formulation can operate beyond the Gaussian functional form.

Timing comparisons with cyclic coordinate-wise minimization show substantial computational gains, and the paper proves convergence and convergence rates. The abstract characterizes the resulting approach as highly scalable but supplies no particular runtime or dataset size. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and theoretical: faster optimization for this estimator, accompanied by guarantees that the optimization procedure converges.
summary.tldr: Proximal-gradient optimization accelerates sparse graphical-model estimation with CONCORD.

title: Optimization Methods for Sparse Pseudo-Likelihood Graphical Model Selection

abstract: In user-facing applications, displaying calibrated confidence measures---probabilities that correspond to true frequency---can be as important as obtaining high accuracy. We are interested in calibration for structured prediction problems such as speech recognition, optical character recognition, and medical diagnosis. Structured prediction presents new challenges for calibration: the output space is large, and users may issue many types of probability queries (e.g., marginals) on the structured output. We extend the notion of calibration so as to handle various subtleties pertaining to the structured setting, and then provide a simple recalibration method that trains a binary classifier to predict probabilities of interest. We explore a range of features appropriate for structured recalibration, and demonstrate their efficacy on three real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether confidence estimates in structured prediction match how often the associated events actually occur. This property, calibration, matters when users interpret a probability as a measure of reliability. The authors focus on settings such as speech recognition, optical character recognition, and medical diagnosis, where the predicted output has multiple related parts.

Structured outputs make calibration more complicated because there can be many possible outcomes and many different probability questions. A user might ask about only one part of a prediction rather than the entire output. The paper extends the definition of calibration to accommodate these subtleties, so the target is meaningful confidence for the queries users may actually issue.

The proposed recalibration method trains a binary classifier to estimate the probabilities of interest. The authors investigate features suited to this task and demonstrate their effectiveness on three real-world datasets. The contribution therefore combines a definition tailored to structured prediction with a simple learning procedure for adjusting confidence estimates, addressing a concern distinct from prediction accuracy alone.
summary.tldr: The paper extends calibration to structured outputs and uses a binary classifier to recalibrate probabilities for different user queries.

title: Calibrated Structured Prediction

abstract: We consider the estimation of sparse graphical models that characterize the dependency structure of high-dimensional tensor-valued data. To facilitate the estimation of the precision matrix corresponding to each way of the tensor, we assume the data follow a tensor normal distribution whose covariance has a Kronecker product structure. The penalized maximum likelihood estimation of this model involves minimizing a non-convex objective function. In spite of the non-convexity of this estimation problem, we prove that an alternating minimization algorithm, which iteratively estimates each sparse precision matrix while fixing the others, attains an estimator with the optimal statistical rate of convergence as well as consistent graph recovery. Notably, such an estimator achieves estimation consistency with only one tensor sample, which is unobserved in previous work. Our theoretical results are backed by thorough numerical studies.

It assumes a tensor normal distribution whose covariance separates into a Kronecker product. That structure allows the model to describe dependencies through a distinct precision matrix for each tensor direction, with sparsity identifying a relatively small set of connections.

Estimating these matrices by penalized maximum likelihood leads to a non-convex optimization problem. The authors analyze an alternating method that updates one sparse precision matrix while holding the others fixed. Despite the non-convex objective, they prove that the resulting estimator achieves the optimal statistical convergence rate and consistent recovery of the dependency graph.

A particularly notable result is estimation consistency using only one tensor sample under the analyzed model. One tensor observation still has internal multidimensional structure, which is central to the setting of this claim. Numerical studies support the theoretical results. The contribution links a practical alternating optimization strategy to strong statistical guarantees for this structured graphical model.
summary.tldr: Under a tensor normal model with Kronecker covariance, alternating estimation achieves optimal statistical rates and consistent graph recovery.

title: Non-convex Statistical Optimization for Sparse Tensor Graphical Model

abstract: We consider the problem of statistical computations with persistence diagrams, a summary representation of topological features in data. These diagrams encode persistent homology, a widely used invariant in topological data analysis. While several avenues towards a statistical treatment of the diagrams have been explored recently, we follow an alternative route that is motivated by the success of methods based on the embedding of probability measures into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. In fact, a positive definite kernel on persistence diagrams has recently been proposed, connecting persistent homology to popular kernel-based learning techniques such as support vector machines. However, important properties of that kernel which would enable a principled use in the context of probability measure embeddings remain to be explored. Our contribution is to close this gap by proving universality of a variant of the original kernel, and to demonstrate its effective use in two-sample hypothesis testing on synthetic as well as real-world data.

It follows an approach inspired by embedding probability distributions into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, where kernel-based methods provide a common mathematical setting for comparing distributions.

The authors identify a remaining theoretical gap: properties needed to use that connection for probability-distribution embeddings had not been established. The paper demonstrates the resulting approach through two-sample hypothesis testing on synthetic and real-world data. Such testing asks whether two collections are consistent with the same underlying distribution. The contribution therefore moves beyond using topological summaries as inputs to prediction: it supports statistical comparison of populations represented by persistence diagrams and demonstrates that use empirically.
summary.tldr: A universality proof for a persistence-diagram kernel supports principled distribution embeddings and effective two-sample testing.

title: Statistical Topological Data Analysis - A Kernel Perspective

abstract: The facility location problem is widely used for summarizing large datasets and has additional applications in sensor placement, image retrieval, and clustering. One difficulty of this problem is that submodular optimization algorithms require the calculation of pairwise benefits for all items in the dataset. This is infeasible for large problems, so recent work proposed to only calculate nearest neighbor benefits. One limitation is that several strong assumptions were invoked to obtain provable approximation guarantees. In this paper we establish that these extra assumptions are not necessary—solving the sparsified problem will be almost optimal under the standard assumptions of the problem. We then analyze a different method of sparsification that is a better model for methods such as Locality Sensitive Hashing to accelerate the nearest neighbor computations and extend the use of the problem to a broader family of similarities. We validate our approach by demonstrating that it rapidly generates interpretable summaries.

The authors show that those extra assumptions are unnecessary: solving the sparsified problem can be almost optimal under the problem’s standard assumptions. Together, the results address both the quality retained after sparsification and the practical work needed to obtain the sparse relationships.
summary.tldr: Sparse facility-location problems can yield almost-optimal summaries under standard assumptions, with further analysis supporting faster neighbor computations.

title: Leveraging Sparsity for Efficient Submodular Data Summarization

abstract: How to cluster event sequences generated via different point processes is an interesting and important problem in statistical machine learning. To solve this problem, we propose and discuss an effective model-based clustering method based on a novel Dirichlet mixture model of a special but significant type of point processes --- Hawkes process. The proposed model generates the event sequences with different clusters from the Hawkes processes with different parameters, and uses a Dirichlet process as the prior distribution of the clusters. We prove the identifiability of our mixture model and propose an effective variational Bayesian inference algorithm to learn our model. An adaptive inner iteration allocation strategy is designed to accelerate the convergence of our algorithm. Moreover, we investigate the sample complexity and the computational complexity of our learning algorithm in depth. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world data show that the clustering method based on our model can learn structural triggering patterns hidden in asynchronous event sequences robustly and achieve superior performance on clustering purity and consistency compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: Event sequences can differ in how events trigger later events, even when their timing is irregular. This paper groups sequences by modeling those underlying dynamics. Its mixture model assigns different clusters different Hawkes process parameters, so membership reflects a shared pattern of event generation rather than just a superficial resemblance between sequences.

The model uses a Dirichlet process prior over clusters and learns its parameters through variational Bayesian inference. The authors prove identifiability, providing a theoretical basis for distinguishing the mixture's components. They also introduce an adaptive strategy for allocating inner iterations, intended to accelerate convergence, and analyze both the data requirements and computational demands of learning.

Experiments on synthetic and real data indicate that the method can robustly uncover triggering structure in asynchronous sequences. It also achieves better clustering purity and consistency than the compared methods. These findings support the value of grouping sequences through a model of their generating processes, with theoretical analysis accompanying the practical learning procedure.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet mixture of Hawkes processes clusters event sequences by their underlying triggering patterns.

title: A Dirichlet Mixture Model of Hawkes Processes for Event Sequence Clustering

abstract: Robotic motion-planning problems, such as a UAV flying fast in a partially-known environment or a robot arm moving around cluttered objects, require finding collision-free paths quickly. Typically, this is solved by constructing a graph, where vertices represent robot configurations and edges represent potentially valid movements of the robot between theses configurations. The main computational bottlenecks are expensive edge evaluations to check for collisions. State of the art planning methods do not reason about the optimal sequence of edges to evaluate in order to find a collision free path quickly. In this paper, we do so by drawing a novel equivalence between motion planning and the Bayesian active learning paradigm of decision region determination (DRD). Unfortunately, a straight application of ex- isting methods requires computation exponential in the number of edges in a graph. We present BISECT, an efficient and near-optimal algorithm to solve the DRD problem when edges are independent Bernoulli random variables. By leveraging this property, we are able to significantly reduce computational complexity from exponential to linear in the number of edges. We show that BISECT outperforms several state of the art algorithms on a spectrum of planning problems for mobile robots, manipulators, and real flight data collected from a full scale helicopter. Open-source code and details can be found here: https://github.com/sanjibac/matlab learning collision_checking

paragraphs: Robot motion planning often represents configurations as graph vertices and possible movements as edges. Checking whether an edge is collision-free can be expensive, making the order of checks a major computational decision. This paper focuses on selecting those checks so that a valid path can be found quickly.

The authors connect motion planning to decision region determination, a Bayesian active-learning problem. Directly applying existing methods would require computation exponential in the graph's number of edges. Their BISECT algorithm exploits an explicit assumption: edge validity is modeled by independent Bernoulli random variables. Under this structure, they obtain an efficient, near-optimal algorithm and reduce the stated computational complexity to linear in the number of edges.

Evaluations include mobile robots, manipulators, and real flight data from a full-scale helicopter. BISECT outperforms several leading planning algorithms in these comparisons. The work shows how reasoning about which collision check to perform next can improve planning efficiency, with the independence model providing the key computational simplification behind the proposed method.
summary.tldr: BISECT selects collision checks efficiently through a near-optimal active-learning formulation that assumes independent edge validity.

title: Near-Optimal Edge Evaluation in Explicit Generalized Binomial Graphs

abstract: Learning in models with discrete latent variables is challenging due to high variance gradient estimators. Generally, approaches have relied on control variates to reduce the variance of the REINFORCE estimator. Recent work \citep{jang2016categorical, maddison2016concrete} has taken a different approach, introducing a continuous relaxation of discrete variables to produce low-variance, but biased, gradient estimates. In this work, we combine the two approaches through a novel control variate that produces low-variance, \emph{unbiased} gradient estimates. Then, we introduce a modification to the continuous relaxation and show that the tightness of the relaxation can be adapted online, removing it as a hyperparameter. We show state-of-the-art variance reduction on several benchmark generative modeling tasks, generally leading to faster convergence to a better final log-likelihood.

paragraphs: Training models with discrete latent variables is difficult when gradient estimates fluctuate strongly between samples. Existing approaches address this either by reducing the variance of REINFORCE with control variates or by replacing discrete variables with continuous relaxations. The latter can produce less noisy gradients but introduce bias into the estimate.

REBAR combines these ideas through a new control variate that uses a continuous relaxation while preserving an unbiased gradient estimate. The relaxation thus contributes to variance reduction without imposing the bias associated with using relaxed gradients directly. The authors also modify the relaxation so that its tightness can be adapted during training, removing that choice as a fixed hyperparameter.

On several benchmark generative modeling tasks, the method achieves state-of-the-art variance reduction in the reported comparisons. This generally translates into faster convergence and a better final log-likelihood, rather than being claimed for every case. The findings connect an estimator's statistical properties to practical improvements in learning models whose hidden variables are discrete.
summary.tldr: REBAR uses continuous relaxations within a control variate to reduce discrete-variable gradient variance without bias, generally improving training outcomes.

title: REBAR: Low-variance, unbiased gradient estimates for discrete latent variable models

abstract: The lasso and elastic net linear regression models impose a double-exponential prior distribution on the model parameters to achieve regression shrinkage and variable selection, allowing the inference of robust models from large data sets. However, there has been limited success in deriving estimates for the full posterior distribution of regression coefficients in these models, due to a need to evaluate analytically intractable partition function integrals. Here, the Fourier transform is used to express these integrals as complex-valued oscillatory integrals over "regression frequencies". This results in an analytic expansion and stationary phase approximation for the partition functions of the Bayesian lasso and elastic net, where the non-differentiability of the double-exponential prior has so far eluded such an approach. Use of this approximation leads to highly accurate numerical estimates for the expectation values and marginal posterior distributions of the regression coefficients, and allows for Bayesian inference of much higher dimensional models than previously possible.

paragraphs: Lasso and elastic net regression use shrinkage to support variable selection and robust modeling. In their Bayesian treatment, understanding the full posterior distribution of regression coefficients requires difficult integrals called partition functions. These integrals have limited efforts to estimate more than a single fitted set of coefficients.

The paper uses a Fourier transform to rewrite the partition functions as complex-valued oscillatory integrals over regression frequencies. This reformulation makes an analytic expansion and a stationary phase approximation possible. The transformation is central because the double-exponential prior is not differentiable everywhere, a feature that had previously obstructed this kind of approximation.

Using the resulting approximation, the authors report highly accurate numerical estimates of coefficient expectations and marginal posterior distributions. They also report that the approach enables Bayesian inference for much higher-dimensional models than previously possible. The contribution expands access to posterior information about individual coefficients by making the necessary computation more tractable, while retaining an approximation as the basis of the numerical estimates.
summary.tldr: A Fourier-based reformulation enables accurate posterior approximations for Bayesian lasso and elastic net regression in higher dimensions.

title: Analytic solution and stationary phase approximation for the Bayesian lasso and elastic net

abstract: We describe a simple, low-level approach for embedding probabilistic programming in a deep learning ecosystem. In particular, we distill probabilistic programming down to a single abstraction—the random variable. Our lightweight implementation in TensorFlow enables numerous applications: a model-parallel variational auto-encoder (VAE) with 2nd-generation tensor processing units (TPUv2s); a data-parallel autoregressive model (Image Transformer) with TPUv2s; and multi-GPU No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS). For both a state-of-the-art VAE on 64x64 ImageNet and Image Transformer on 256x256 CelebA-HQ, our approach achieves an optimal linear speedup from 1 to 256 TPUv2 chips. With NUTS, we see a 100x speedup on GPUs over Stan and 37x over PyMC3.

It organizes the interface around a single abstraction, the random variable, and implements the approach in TensorFlow. The aim is to make probabilistic models and inference work with the distributed computation and accelerators available in that environment.

These examples span neural generative modeling and sampling-based inference. These results show substantial acceleration for the demonstrated applications while retaining a simple probabilistic programming abstraction.
summary.tldr: A random-variable-based TensorFlow implementation supports distributed probabilistic programming with strong accelerator speedups in demonstrated applications.

title: Simple, Distributed, and Accelerated Probabilistic Programming

abstract: Image matting is an ill-posed problem. It requires a user input trimap or some strokes to obtain an alpha matte of the foreground object. A fine user input is essential to obtain a good result, which is either time consuming or suitable for experienced users who know where to place the strokes. In this paper, we explore the intrinsic relationship between the user input and the matting algorithm to address the problem of where and when the user should provide the input. Our aim is to discover the most informative sequence of regions for user input in order to produce a good alpha matte with minimum labeling efforts. To this end, we propose an active matting method with recurrent reinforcement learning. The proposed framework involves human in the loop by sequentially detecting informative regions for trivial human judgement. Comparing to traditional matting algorithms, the proposed framework requires much less efforts, and can produce satisfactory results with just 10 regions. Through extensive experiments, we show that the proposed model reduces user efforts significantly and achieves comparable performance to dense trimaps in a user-friendly manner. We further show that the learned informative knowledge can be generalized across different matting algorithms.
