paragraphs: Image matting estimates how much each pixel belongs to a foreground object. Because the image alone does not uniquely determine that separation, matting methods often need a user-provided trimap or strokes. Good guidance can require substantial effort, especially when users do not know which regions most need clarification.

Active Matting learns where and when to request that guidance. A recurrent reinforcement learning method selects a sequence of informative image regions, and a person supplies simple judgments about them. The selection process explicitly considers the relationship between user input and the matting algorithm. Its objective is to obtain a good foreground matte with as little labeling effort as possible.

The experiments report significantly reduced user effort and performance comparable to using dense trimaps. The framework can produce satisfactory results with just ten queried regions in the reported evaluation. The authors also show that learned knowledge about informative regions transfers across different matting algorithms. This suggests that choosing useful questions can improve the interaction itself, rather than requiring users to master each algorithm's input requirements.
summary.tldr: Active Matting learns which image regions to ask users about, reducing the effort needed for foreground extraction.

title: Active Matting

abstract: This paper introduces hyperspherical prototype networks, which unify classification and regression with prototypes on hyperspherical output spaces. For classification, a common approach is to define prototypes as the mean output vector over training examples per class. Here, we propose to use hyperspheres as output spaces, with class prototypes defined a priori with large margin separation. We position prototypes through data-independent optimization, with an extension to incorporate priors from class semantics. By doing so, we do not require any prototype updating, we can handle any training size, and the output dimensionality is no longer constrained to the number of classes. Furthermore, we generalize to regression, by optimizing outputs as an interpolation between two prototypes on the hypersphere. Since both tasks are now defined by the same loss function, they can be jointly trained for multi-task problems. Experimentally, we show the benefit of hyperspherical prototype networks for classification, regression, and their combination over other prototype methods, softmax cross-entropy, and mean squared error approaches.

paragraphs: Prototype methods represent prediction targets using reference vectors. This paper places those vectors on a hypersphere and uses that shared output geometry for both classification and regression. For classification, class prototypes are positioned in advance with large separation, instead of being calculated as averages of training examples.

The prototype placement comes from data-independent optimization, with an extension that incorporates prior information about class semantics. Because the prototypes are fixed, they need no updating during training. The construction accommodates any training-set size and releases the output dimensionality from a requirement to equal the number of classes, giving the representation a different relationship to the prediction task.

For regression, the network’s output is optimized as an interpolation between two prototypes on the sphere. Classification and regression consequently share a loss function and can be trained jointly in multitask problems. Experiments report benefits across classification, regression, and their combination compared with other prototype methods, softmax cross-entropy, and mean-squared-error approaches. The central contribution is a common geometric formulation for these prediction settings.
summary.tldr: Fixed prototypes on a hypersphere give classification and regression a shared geometry and loss function for joint training.

title: Hyperspherical Prototype Networks

abstract: Low-rank metric learning aims to learn better discrimination of data subject to low-rank constraints. It keeps the intrinsic low-rank structure of datasets and reduces the time cost and memory usage in metric learning. However, it is still a challenge for current methods to handle datasets with both high dimensions and large numbers of samples. To address this issue, we present a novel fast low-rank metric learning (FLRML) method. FLRML casts the low-rank metric learning problem into an unconstrained optimization on the Stiefel manifold, which can be efficiently solved by searching along the descent curves of the manifold. FLRML significantly reduces the complexity and memory usage in optimization, which makes the method scalable to both high dimensions and large numbers of samples. Furthermore, we introduce a mini-batch version of FLRML to make the method scalable to larger datasets which are hard to be loaded and decomposed in limited memory. The outperforming experimental results show that our method is with high accuracy and much faster than the state-of-the-art methods under several benchmarks with large numbers of high-dimensional data. Code has been made available at https://github.com/highan911/FLRML.

paragraphs: Low-rank metric learning learns how to distinguish data while preserving a compact underlying structure. This can reduce computation and memory, but existing methods still struggle when datasets combine many samples with many dimensions. The paper introduces FLRML to address these two scaling demands together, rather than treating either one in isolation.

FLRML reformulates the learning problem as an unconstrained optimization on the Stiefel manifold. Optimization proceeds along descent curves within that space, using the manifold formulation to handle the structure of the problem. The authors report that this substantially lowers optimization complexity and memory requirements, making the method applicable to datasets that are large in both sample count and dimensionality.

A mini-batch version extends the approach to datasets that cannot readily be loaded and decomposed within available memory. Benchmark experiments report high accuracy and substantially faster execution than state-of-the-art methods on large, high-dimensional data. The contribution is therefore both an optimization reformulation and a way to carry that formulation into a more memory-efficient training procedure.
summary.tldr: FLRML uses manifold optimization and a mini-batch extension to make low-rank metric learning faster and more memory efficient.

title: Fast Low-rank Metric Learning for Large-scale and High-dimensional Data

abstract: We present Placeto, a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to efficiently find device placements for distributed neural network training. Unlike prior approaches that only find a device placement for a specific computation graph, Placeto can learn generalizable device placement policies that can be applied to any graph. We propose two key ideas in our approach: (1) we represent the policy as performing iterative placement improvements, rather than outputting a placement in one shot; (2) we use graph embeddings to capture relevant information about the structure of the computation graph, without relying on node labels for indexing. These ideas allow Placeto to train efficiently and generalize to unseen graphs. Our experiments show that Placeto requires up to 6.1x fewer training steps to find placements that are on par with or better than the best placements found by prior approaches. Moreover, Placeto is able to learn a generalizable placement policy for any given family of graphs that can be used without any re-training to predict optimized placements for unseen graphs from the same family. This eliminates the huge overhead incurred by the prior RL approaches whose lack of generalizability necessitates re-training from scratch every time a new graph is to be placed.
originalAbstract: We present Placeto, a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to efficiently find device placements for distributed neural network training. Unlike prior approaches that only find a device placement for a specific computation graph, Placeto can learn generalizable device placement policies that can be applied to any graph. We propose two key ideas in our approach: (1) we represent the policy as performing iterative placement improvements, rather than outputting a placement in one shot; (2) we use graph embeddings to capture relevant information about the structure of the computation graph, without relying on node labels for indexing. These ideas allow Placeto to train efficiently and generalize to unseen graphs. Our experiments show that Placeto requires up to 6.1x fewer training steps to find placements that are on par with or better than the best placements found by prior approaches. Moreover, Placeto is able to learn a generalizable placement policy for any given family of graphs that can be used without any re-training to predict optimized placements for unseen graphs from the same family. This eliminates the huge overhead incurred by the prior RL approaches whose lack of generalizability necessitates re-training from scratch every time a new graph is to be placed.

paragraphs: Distributed neural network training requires assigning computations to devices. Learning a good assignment separately for every computation graph can create substantial overhead. Placeto addresses this problem by learning a placement policy that can transfer to new graphs, making the learned decision process reusable.

The policy improves a placement iteratively instead of producing an entire assignment in one step. It also uses graph embeddings to represent relevant computation structure without depending on node labels for indexing. These design choices let the policy work with graph structure in a way intended to support efficient training and application to unseen graphs.

Experiments show that Placeto needs up to 6.1 times fewer training steps to find placements matching or improving upon the best placements found by prior approaches. The authors also demonstrate transfer without retraining to unseen graphs from the same family used to learn the policy. That family-specific result is the practical generalization claim: repeated placement problems within a family can avoid training a new policy from scratch.
summary.tldr: Placeto learns iterative device-placement policies that transfer without retraining to unseen computation graphs from the same family.

title: Learning Generalizable Device Placement Algorithms for Distributed Machine Learning

abstract: The medoid of a set of n points is the point in the set that minimizes the sum of distances to other points. It can be determined exactly in O(n^2) time by computing the distances between all pairs of points. Previous works show that one can significantly reduce the number of distance computations needed by adaptively querying distances. The resulting randomized algorithm is obtained by a direct conversion of the computation problem to a multi-armed bandit statistical inference problem. In this work, we show that we can better exploit the structure of the underlying computation problem by modifying the traditional bandit sampling strategy and using it in conjunction with a suitably chosen multi-armed bandit algorithm. Four to five orders of magnitude gains over exact computation are obtained on real data, in terms of both number of distance computations needed and wall clock time. Theoretical results are obtained to quantify such gains in terms of data parameters. Our code is publicly available online at https://github.com/TavorB/Correlated-Sequential-Halving.

paragraphs: A medoid is the member of a dataset with the smallest total distance to all other members. Computing every pairwise distance identifies it exactly but requires quadratic work in the number of points. Earlier randomized approaches reduce this burden by adaptively selecting distances to query through a multi-armed bandit formulation.

This paper goes beyond a direct conversion to a standard bandit problem. It modifies the sampling strategy to exploit the structure of medoid computation and combines that strategy with a suitably chosen bandit algorithm. The key idea is that the original computational problem contains structure that a generic sampling rule need not fully use.

On real data, the authors report gains of four to five orders of magnitude over exact computation in both distance evaluations and elapsed time. They also provide theoretical results expressing gains in terms of data parameters. The empirical speedups are therefore findings on the evaluated data, while the analysis describes how the benefits depend on properties of the underlying problem.
summary.tldr: A structure-aware bandit sampling strategy greatly accelerates medoid identification on evaluated real datasets.

title: Ultra Fast Medoid Identification via Correlated Sequential Halving

abstract: In this paper, we study private sparsification of graphs. In particular, we give an algorithm that given an input graph, returns a sparse graph which approximates the spectrum of the input graph while ensuring differential privacy. This allows one to solve many graph problems privately yet efficiently and accurately. This is exemplified with application of the proposed meta-algorithm to graph algorithms for privately answering cut-queries, as well as practical algorithms for computing {\scshape MAX-CUT} and {\scshape SPARSEST-CUT} with better accuracy than previously known. We also give the first efficient private algorithm to learn Laplacian eigenmap on a graph.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to produce a sparse representation of a graph while ensuring differential privacy. The output graph approximates the spectrum of the original graph, retaining a mathematical description of its structure in a form with fewer edges. The goal is to make useful graph computations both private and computationally efficient.

The sparsification algorithm serves as a general method that can support several downstream graph problems. Its value comes from combining privacy with structural approximation: the sparse graph is intended to preserve information useful for later computations while satisfying the privacy requirement. The paper demonstrates this role through methods for privately answering cut queries and practical algorithms for MAX-CUT and SPARSEST-CUT.

For the cut optimization applications, the authors report better accuracy than previously known private approaches. They also provide what they describe as the first efficient private algorithm for learning a Laplacian eigenmap on a graph. These applications show that the contribution extends beyond producing a smaller graph to enabling a range of private structural analyses.
summary.tldr: Private spectral graph sparsification enables efficient graph analysis, including improved private cut algorithms and an efficient private Laplacian eigenmap algorithm.

title: On Differentially Private Graph Sparsification and Applications

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNN) come in many flavors, but should always be either invariant (permutation of the nodes of the input graph does not affect the output) or \emph{equivariant} (permutation of the input permutes the output). In this paper, we consider a specific class of invariant and equivariant networks, for which we prove new universality theorems. More precisely, we consider networks with a single hidden layer, obtained by summing channels formed by applying an equivariant linear operator, a pointwise non-linearity, and either an invariant or equivariant linear output layer. Recently, Maron et al. (2019) showed that by allowing higher-order tensorization inside the network, universal invariant GNNs can be obtained. As a first contribution, we propose an alternative proof of this result, which relies on the Stone-Weierstrass theorem for algebra of real-valued functions. Our main contribution is then an extension of this result to the \emph{equivariant} case, which appears in many practical applications but has been less studied from a theoretical point of view. The proof relies on a new generalized Stone-Weierstrass theorem for algebra of equivariant functions, which is of independent interest. Additionally, unlike many previous works that consider a fixed number of nodes, our results show that a GNN defined by a single set of parameters can approximate uniformly well a function defined on graphs of varying size.

paragraphs: Renumbering a graph's nodes should either leave a network's output unchanged or reorder its output in the corresponding way. These properties are called invariance and equivariance. This paper studies the approximation power of a specific network family that respects these symmetries, asking which graph functions such networks can represent.

The networks have one hidden layer and sum channels built from an equivariant linear operation, a pointwise nonlinearity, and an invariant or equivariant output operation. Building on universality results that allow higher-order tensors inside networks, the authors provide a different proof for the invariant case. They then extend universality to equivariant outputs using a generalized Stone-Weierstrass theorem for equivariant functions.

A further result allows one set of network parameters to approximate a function uniformly well across graphs of varying sizes, rather than restricting attention to a fixed node count. The work establishes expressive capacity for the specified architecture family, including the less-studied equivariant setting. Its central findings are approximation theorems, explaining what these symmetry-respecting networks can represent rather than reporting a training-performance comparison.
summary.tldr: New universality theorems establish approximation power for invariant and equivariant graph networks, including shared parameters across varying graph sizes.

title: Universal Invariant and Equivariant Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Deep residual networks (ResNets) have demonstrated better generalization performance than deep feedforward networks (FFNets). However, the theory behind such a phenomenon is still largely unknown. This paper studies this fundamental problem in deep learning from a so-called ``neural tangent kernel'' perspective. Specifically, we first show that under proper conditions, as the width goes to infinity, training deep ResNets can be viewed as learning reproducing kernel functions with some kernel function. We then compare the kernel of deep ResNets with that of deep FFNets and discover that the class of functions induced by the kernel of FFNets is asymptotically not learnable, as the depth goes to infinity. In contrast, the class of functions induced by the kernel of ResNets does not exhibit such degeneracy. Our discovery partially justifies the advantages of deep ResNets over deep FFNets in generalization abilities. Numerical results are provided to support our claim.

This paper examines the difference through neural tangent kernels. The approach studies a limiting mathematical description of network learning, making it possible to compare the function classes associated with the two architectures.

The authors first show that, under appropriate conditions and as width tends to infinity, training a deep residual network can be viewed as learning functions in a reproducing kernel space. They then compare this kernel with the corresponding kernel for feedforward networks as depth increases.

In the infinite-depth limit, the function class induced by the feedforward kernel becomes unlearnable in the sense studied, while the residual-network kernel avoids that degeneracy. Numerical results support the theoretical claim. This supplies a partial explanation for the generalization advantage of residual networks: their limiting kernel retains learning properties lost by the feedforward counterpart. The conclusion is specifically grounded in the stated conditions and limiting analysis.
summary.tldr: An infinite-width kernel analysis finds that residual networks avoid a depth-related degeneracy affecting feedforward networks, partially explaining their generalization advantage.

title: Why Do Deep Residual Networks Generalize Better than Deep Feedforward Networks? --- A Neural Tangent Kernel Perspective

abstract: This paper studies the problem of learning the correlation structure of a set of intervention functions defined on the directed acyclic graph (DAG) of a causal model. This is useful when we are interested in jointly learning the causal effects of interventions on different subsets of variables in a DAG, which is common in field such as healthcare or operations research. We propose the first multi-task causal Gaussian process (GP) model, which we call DAG-GP, that allows for information sharing across continuous interventions and across experiments on different variables. DAG-GP accommodates different assumptions in terms of data availability and captures the correlation between functions lying in input spaces of different dimensionality via a well-defined integral operator. We give theoretical results detailing when and how the DAG-GP model can be formulated depending on the DAG. We test both the quality of its predictions and its calibrated uncertainties. Compared to single-task models, DAG-GP achieves the best fitting performance in a variety of real and synthetic settings. In addition, it helps to select optimal interventions faster than competing approaches when used within sequential decision making frameworks, like active learning or Bayesian optimization.

paragraphs: Different interventions in a causal system can be related even when they change different sets of variables. This paper studies how to learn those relationships jointly using the system’s directed acyclic graph. Its DAG-GP model shares information across continuous intervention choices and across experiments that intervene on different variables, rather than learning each intervention function independently.

A central challenge is that intervention functions can have input spaces of different dimensions. DAG-GP captures their correlations through a well-defined integral operator. The model accommodates different assumptions about which data are available, and the theoretical results describe when and how it can be formulated for a given causal graph. Thus, the graph helps determine the structure of information sharing.

The authors evaluate predictions and uncertainty calibration in real and synthetic settings. DAG-GP achieves the best fitting performance relative to the single-task models compared. When incorporated into sequential decision frameworks such as active learning or Bayesian optimization, it also helps select optimal interventions faster than competing approaches, connecting shared causal learning with more efficient experimental choices.
summary.tldr: DAG-GP shares information among related causal interventions to improve predictions and speed intervention selection in the evaluated settings.

title: Multi-task Causal Learning with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Our understanding of learning input-output relationships with neural nets has improved rapidly in recent years, but little is known about the convergence of the underlying representations, even in the simple case of linear autoencoders (LAEs). We show that when trained with proper regularization, LAEs can directly learn the optimal representation -- ordered, axis-aligned principal components. We analyze two such regularization schemes: non-uniform L2 regularization and a deterministic variant of nested dropout [Rippel et al, ICML' 2014]. Though both regularization schemes converge to the optimal representation, we show that this convergence is slow due to ill-conditioning that worsens with increasing latent dimension. We show that the inefficiency of learning the optimal representation is not inevitable -- we present a simple modification to the gradient descent update that greatly speeds up convergence empirically.

paragraphs: Understanding a neural network's input-output behavior does not fully explain the representation it learns internally. This paper studies that distinction in linear autoencoders. It asks whether training can recover a particular optimal representation: principal components arranged in order and aligned with the axes of the latent representation.

The authors show that appropriate regularization can produce this outcome. They analyze non-uniform L2 regularization and a deterministic version of nested dropout, establishing convergence to the desired representation for both. However, they also show that convergence is slow because of ill-conditioning, and that this problem becomes worse as the latent dimension increases.

The paper then proposes a simple change to the gradient descent update that substantially accelerates convergence in experiments. The findings separate two questions: whether the desired representation is eventually learned and how efficiently training reaches it. Regularization addresses the first, while the modified update empirically improves the second, showing that slow recovery need not be an unavoidable feature of learning principal components.
summary.tldr: Properly regularized linear autoencoders recover ordered principal components, and a modified gradient update empirically speeds their slow convergence.

title: Regularized linear autoencoders recover the principal components, eventually

abstract: Recently, there have been significant interests in studying the so-called "double-descent" of the generalization error of linear regression models under the overparameterized and overfitting regime, with the hope that such analysis may provide the first step towards understanding why overparameterized deep neural networks (DNN) still generalize well. However, to date most of these studies focused on the min L2-norm solution that overfits the data. In contrast, in this paper we study the overfitting solution that minimizes the L1-norm, which is known as Basis Pursuit (BP) in the compressed sensing literature. Under a sparse true linear regression model with p i.i.d. Gaussian features, we show that for a large range of p up to a limit that grows exponentially with the number of samples n, with high probability the model error of BP is upper bounded by a value that decreases with p. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first analytical result in the literature establishing the double-descent of overfitting BP for finite n and p. Further, our results reveal significant differences between the double-descent of BP and min L2-norm solutions. Specifically, the double-descent upper-bound of BP is independent of the signal strength, and for high SNR and sparse models the descent-floor of BP can be much lower and wider than that of min L2-norm solutions.

paragraphs: This paper examines why fitting training data exactly need not lead to poor prediction in an overparameterized linear model. It studies Basis Pursuit, which selects an exact-fitting solution with minimum L1 norm. That choice differs from the minimum L2 norm solutions emphasized in much of the earlier double-descent analysis.

The theoretical setting assumes a sparse true linear regression model and independent, identically distributed Gaussian features. Over a large range of feature counts, extending to a limit that grows exponentially with the sample count, the authors prove a high-probability upper bound on model error that decreases as features are added. The decreasing quantity is the bound; the result does not assert that every realized error decreases at every step.

The authors describe this as the first finite-sample, finite-feature analytical double-descent result for overfitting Basis Pursuit. Its bound is independent of signal strength. For sparse models with high signal-to-noise ratio, its descent floor can also be substantially lower and wider than that of minimum L2 norm solutions, revealing a meaningful difference between the two fitting rules.
summary.tldr: Under sparse Gaussian regression assumptions, Basis Pursuit has a decreasing error upper bound across a broad but bounded overparameterized regime.

title: Overfitting Can Be Harmless for Basis Pursuit, But Only to a Degree

abstract: We propose a novel unsupervised learning approach to 3D shape correspondence that builds a multiscale matching pipeline into a deep neural network. This approach is based on smooth shells, the current state-of-the-art axiomatic correspondence method, which requires an a priori stochastic search over the space of initial poses. Our goal is to replace this costly preprocessing step by directly learning good initializations from the input surfaces. To that end, we systematically derive a fully differentiable, hierarchical matching pipeline from entropy regularized optimal transport. This allows us to combine it with a local feature extractor based on smooth, truncated spectral convolution filters. Finally, we show that the proposed unsupervised method significantly improves over the state-of-the-art on multiple datasets, even in comparison to the most recent supervised methods. Moreover, we demonstrate compelling generalization results by applying our learned filters to examples that significantly deviate from the training set.

paragraphs: Deep Shells tackles correspondence between three-dimensional shapes: determining which locations on one surface match locations on another. It builds on smooth shells, a correspondence method that requires a stochastic search over initial poses before matching. The paper aims to replace that expensive preprocessing with initializations learned directly from the input surfaces.

The authors derive a hierarchical, fully differentiable matching procedure using entropy-regularized optimal transport. Its multiscale structure becomes part of a neural network, allowing matching and learned features to work together. A local feature extractor uses smooth, truncated spectral convolution filters. Because the matching pipeline is differentiable, it can be combined with this feature extractor within the proposed unsupervised learning approach.

The reported experiments show significant improvements over existing methods on multiple datasets, including comparisons with recent supervised approaches. The authors also apply the learned filters to shapes that differ substantially from the training examples and report strong generalization. These findings support learning the initialization and matching features as a way to improve correspondence without supervised training.
summary.tldr: Deep Shells learns unsupervised 3D shape matching through a differentiable optimal-transport pipeline that replaces costly initialization search.

title: Deep Shells: Unsupervised Shape Correspondence with Optimal Transport

abstract: The continual learning problem involves training models with limited capacity to perform well on a set of an unknown number of sequentially arriving tasks. While meta-learning shows great potential for reducing interference between old and new tasks, the current training procedures tend to be either slow or offline, and sensitive to many hyper-parameters. In this work, we propose Look-ahead MAML (La-MAML), a fast optimisation-based meta-learning algorithm for online-continual learning, aided by a small episodic memory. By incorporating the modulation of per-parameter learning rates in our meta-learning update, our approach also allows us to draw connections to and exploit prior work on hypergradients and meta-descent. This provides a more flexible and efficient way to mitigate catastrophic forgetting compared to conventional prior-based methods. La-MAML achieves performance superior to other replay-based, prior-based and meta-learning based approaches for continual learning on real-world visual classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model with limited capacity to learn tasks that arrive sequentially, without knowing how many will appear. Learning a new task can interfere with earlier ones, producing catastrophic forgetting. Meta-learning offers a way to reduce that interference, but existing training procedures can be slow, require offline processing, or depend sensitively on many hyperparameters.

Look-ahead MAML, or La-MAML, is an optimization-based meta-learning algorithm designed for online continual learning. It uses a small episodic memory and incorporates adjustments to individual parameter learning rates into the meta-learning update. This gives the learning process flexibility over how strongly different parameters change as new tasks arrive.

The learning-rate mechanism connects the method to hypergradients and meta-descent, providing a basis for more flexible and efficient forgetting mitigation than conventional prior-based approaches. On real-world visual classification benchmarks, La-MAML outperforms the compared replay-based, prior-based, and meta-learning methods. The reported findings support adapting the update process itself as a practical component of learning continually from a stream of tasks.
summary.tldr: La-MAML combines a small memory with meta-learned per-parameter learning rates to reduce forgetting during online continual learning.

title: Look-ahead Meta Learning for Continual Learning

abstract: The optimization problems associated with training generative adversarial neural networks can be largely reduced to certain {\em non-monotone} variational inequality problems (VIPs), whereas existing convergence results are mostly based on monotone or strongly monotone assumptions. In this paper, we propose {\em optimistic dual extrapolation (OptDE)}, a method that only performs {\em one} gradient evaluation per iteration. We show that OptDE is provably convergent to {\em a strong solution} under different coherent non-monotone assumptions. In particular, when a {\em weak solution} exists, the convergence rate of our method is $O(1/{\epsilon^{2}})$, which matches the best existing result of the methods with two gradient evaluations. Further, when a {\em $\sigma$-weak solution} exists, the convergence guarantee is improved to the linear rate $O(\log\frac{1}{\epsilon})$. Along the way--as a byproduct of our inquiries into non-monotone variational inequalities--we provide the near-optimal $O\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\log \frac{1}{\epsilon}\big)$ convergence guarantee in terms of restricted strong merit function for monotone variational inequalities. We also show how our results can be naturally generalized to the stochastic setting, and obtain corresponding new convergence results. Taken together, our results contribute to the broad landscape of variational inequality--both non-monotone and monotone alike--by providing a novel and more practical algorithm with the state-of-the-art convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a framework for problems including much of the optimization involved in training generative adversarial networks. Existing convergence analyses often assume monotonicity, a structural property that these problems may lack. This paper proposes optimistic dual extrapolation, OptDE, to obtain guarantees under specified coherent non-monotone conditions.

OptDE uses one gradient evaluation per iteration. When a weak solution exists, the authors prove convergence to a strong solution with O(1/epsilon²) complexity, matching the best existing rate for methods using two gradient evaluations. Under the stronger condition that a sigma-weak solution exists, the guarantee improves to O(log(1/epsilon)). These improvements depend on the stated solution assumptions.

For monotone problems, the paper also establishes a near-optimal O((1/epsilon) log(1/epsilon)) guarantee measured by a restricted strong merit function. It extends the analysis to stochastic settings and derives corresponding convergence results. The contribution combines lower gradient-evaluation demands per iteration with guarantees spanning several problem structures; it does not make the non-monotone assumptions unnecessary.
summary.tldr: OptDE uses one gradient evaluation per iteration while achieving strong convergence guarantees under specified coherent non-monotone and monotone conditions.

title: Optimistic Dual Extrapolation for Coherent Non-monotone Variational Inequalities

abstract: We revisit the fundamental problem of prediction with expert advice, in a setting where the environment is benign and generates losses stochastically, but the feedback observed by the learner is subject to a moderate adversarial corruption. We prove that a variant of the classical Multiplicative Weights algorithm with decreasing step sizes achieves constant regret in this setting and performs optimally in a wide range of environments, regardless of the magnitude of the injected corruption. Our results reveal a surprising disparity between the often comparable Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) and Online Mirror Descent (OMD) frameworks: we show that for experts in the corrupted stochastic regime, the regret performance of OMD is in fact strictly inferior to that of FTRL.
originalAbstract: We revisit the fundamental problem of prediction with expert advice, in a setting where the environment is benign and generates losses stochastically, but the feedback observed by the learner is subject to a moderate adversarial corruption. We prove that a variant of the classical Multiplicative Weights algorithm with decreasing step sizes achieves constant regret in this setting and performs optimally in a wide range of environments, regardless of the magnitude of the injected corruption. Our results reveal a surprising disparity between the often comparable Follow the Regularized Leader (FTRL) and Online Mirror Descent (OMD) frameworks: we show that for experts in the corrupted stochastic regime, the regret performance of OMD is in fact strictly inferior to that of FTRL.

paragraphs: Prediction with expert advice asks a learner to make decisions using several competing advisers and their observed losses. This paper considers a mixed setting: the underlying environment generates losses stochastically, but an adversary can moderately corrupt the feedback the learner receives. The challenge is to retain the benefits of a benign environment despite manipulated observations.

The authors analyze a variant of Multiplicative Weights whose step sizes decrease over time. They prove constant regret in this setting and optimal performance across a wide range of environments, regardless of the injected corruption’s magnitude. Constant regret concerns how regret grows with the time horizon; the statement should not be read as saying corruption has no effect on performance.

For experts under corrupted stochastic feedback, the authors show strictly inferior regret performance for Online Mirror Descent. The finding makes the choice of update framework consequential even when the underlying, uncorrupted losses are stochastic.
summary.tldr: Decreasing-step Multiplicative Weights achieves constant regret under corrupted stochastic feedback, while the analysis separates FTRL from the worse-performing OMD framework.

title: Prediction with Corrupted Expert Advice

abstract: Quantum logic inspired embedding (aka Quantum Embedding (QE)) of a Knowledge-Base (KB) was proposed recently by Garg:2019. It is claimed that the QE preserves the logical structure of the input KB given in the form of unary and binary predicates hierarchy. Such structure preservation allows one to perform Boolean logic style deductive reasoning directly over these embedding vectors. The original QE idea, however, is limited to the transductive (not inductive) setting. Moreover, the original QE scheme runs quite slow on real applications involving millions of entities. This paper alleviates both of these key limitations. We start by reformulating the original QE problem to allow for the induction. On the way, we also underscore some interesting analytic and geometric properties of the solution and leverage them to design a faster training scheme. As an application, we show that one can achieve state-of-the-art performance on the well-known NLP task of fine-grained entity type classification by using the inductive QE approach. Our training runs 9-times faster than the original QE scheme on this task.

title: Inductive Quantum Embedding

abstract: Biological brains are inherently limited in their capacity to process and store information, but are nevertheless capable of solving complex tasks with apparent ease. Intelligent behavior is related to these limitations, since resource constraints drive the need to generalize and assign importance differentially to features in the environment or memories of past experiences. Recently, there have been parallel efforts in reinforcement learning and neuroscience to understand strategies adopted by artificial and biological agents to circumvent limitations in information storage. However, the two threads have been largely separate. In this article, we propose a dynamical framework to maximize expected reward under constraints of limited resources, which we implement with a cost function that penalizes precise representations of action-values in memory, each of which may vary in its precision. We derive from first principles an algorithm, Dynamic Resource Allocator (DRA), which we apply to two standard tasks in reinforcement learning and a model-based planning task, and find that it allocates more resources to items in memory that have a higher impact on cumulative rewards. Moreover, DRA learns faster when starting with a higher resource budget than what it eventually allocates for performing well on tasks, which may explain why frontal cortical areas in biological brains appear more engaged in early stages of learning before settling to lower asymptotic levels of activity. Our work provides a normative solution to the problem of learning how to allocate costly resources to a collection of uncertain memories in a manner that is capable of adapting to changes in the environment.

More broadly, the framework supplies an adaptive solution for distributing costly resources among uncertain memories as the environment changes.
summary.tldr: DRA learns how to distribute limited memory precision toward action-values that matter most for cumulative reward.

title: Dynamic allocation of limited memory resources in reinforcement learning

abstract: The objective in statistical Optimal Transport (OT) is to consistently estimate the optimal transport plan/map solely using samples from the given source and target marginal distributions. This work takes the novel approach of posing statistical OT as that of learning the transport plan's kernel mean embedding from sample based estimates of marginal embeddings. The proposed estimator controls overfitting by employing maximum mean discrepancy based regularization, which is complementary to $\phi$-divergence (entropy) based regularization popularly employed in existing estimators. A key result is that, under very mild conditions, $\epsilon$-optimal recovery of the transport plan as well as the Barycentric-projection based transport map is possible with a sample complexity that is completely dimension-free. Moreover, the implicit smoothing in the kernel mean embeddings enables out-of-sample estimation. An appropriate representer theorem is proved leading to a kernelized convex formulation for the estimator, which can then be potentially used to perform OT even in non-standard domains. Empirical results illustrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Statistical optimal transport seeks a transport plan or map using samples from source and target distributions. This paper recasts the task as learning the transport plan's kernel mean embedding from estimates of the marginal embeddings. That representation makes distributional information in the samples central to how the transport estimator is constructed.

The estimator controls overfitting with regularization based on maximum mean discrepancy. This complements the divergence-based regularization commonly used in other estimators. Under very mild conditions, the authors show that recovering an approximately optimal transport plan and a map obtained by barycentric projection is possible with sample complexity independent of dimension.

The smoothing inherent in kernel mean embeddings also permits estimation for points outside the observed sample. A representer theorem leads to a kernelized convex formulation, which could potentially extend optimal transport to nonstandard domains. Empirical results illustrate the approach's effectiveness. Its contribution combines a statistical recovery guarantee with a computational formulation, while the proposed reach into unusual domains remains a possibility stated by the authors.
summary.tldr: Learning kernel embeddings yields an optimal-transport estimator with dimension-free sample complexity under mild conditions and support for out-of-sample estimation.

title: Statistical Optimal Transport posed as Learning Kernel Embedding

abstract: We study the asymmetric low-rank factorization problem:\[\min_{\mathbf{U} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}, \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^\top -\mathbf{\Sigma}\|_F^2\]where $\mathbf{\Sigma}$ is a given matrix of size $m \times n$ and rank $d$. This is a canonical problem that admits two difficulties in optimization: 1) non-convexity and 2) non-smoothness (due to unbalancedness of $\mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{V}$). This is also a prototype for more complex problems such as asymmetric matrix sensing and matrix completion. Despite being non-convex and non-smooth, it has been observed empirically that the randomly initialized gradient descent algorithm can solve this problem in polynomial time. Existing theories to explain this phenomenon all require artificial modifications of the algorithm, such as adding noise in each iteration and adding a balancing regularizer to balance the $\mathbf{U}$ and $\mathbf{V}$.This paper presents the first proof that shows randomly initialized gradient descent converges to a global minimum of the asymmetric low-rank factorization problem with a polynomial rate. For the proof, we develop 1) a new symmetrization technique to capture the magnitudes of the symmetry and asymmetry, and 2) a quantitative perturbation analysis to approximate matrix derivatives. We believe both are useful for other related non-convex problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a given rank-d matrix as the product of two factors, each with d columns. The objective measures the squared reconstruction error. Although this problem has a simple form, optimizing the factors is nonconvex, and unequal magnitudes between them complicate the analysis. It also serves as a prototype for matrix sensing and matrix completion.

Empirically, randomly initialized gradient descent has been observed to solve this factorization problem in polynomial time. Previous theoretical explanations required modifying the algorithm, for example by injecting noise during optimization or adding a regularizer to balance the two factors. The authors provide the first proof of polynomial-rate convergence to a global minimum for randomly initialized gradient descent on the stated asymmetric factorization problem.

The proof introduces a symmetrization technique that tracks both symmetry and asymmetry, alongside quantitative perturbation analysis for approximating matrix derivatives. These tools explain the behavior of the unmodified algorithm in this setting. The authors also suggest that the techniques may be useful for related nonconvex problems, presenting that broader applicability as a possibility.
summary.tldr: The paper proves polynomial-rate global convergence of randomly initialized gradient descent for the stated asymmetric low-rank matrix factorization problem.

title: Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Asymmetric Low-Rank Matrix Factorization

abstract: Inferring 3D locations and shapes of multiple objects from a single 2D image is a long-standing objective of computer vision. Most of the existing works either predict one of these 3D properties or focus on solving both for a single object. One fundamental challenge lies in how to learn an effective representation of the image that is well-suited for 3D detection and reconstruction. In this work, we propose to learn a regular grid of 3D voxel features from the input image which is aligned with 3D scene space via a 3D feature lifting operator. Based on the 3D voxel features, our novel CenterNet-3D detection head formulates the 3D detection as keypoint detection in the 3D space. Moreover, we devise an efficient coarse-to-fine reconstruction module, including coarse-level voxelization and a novel local PCA-SDF shape representation, which enables fine detail reconstruction and two orders of magnitude faster inference than prior methods. With complementary supervision from both 3D detection and reconstruction, one enables the 3D voxel features to be geometry and context preserving, benefiting both tasks. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through 3D detection and reconstruction on single-object and multiple-object scenarios.

paragraphs: Recovering both the locations and shapes of multiple objects from one image requires a representation useful for two different 3D tasks. This paper learns a regular grid of voxel features aligned with scene space. A feature-lifting operator maps information from the input image into that shared three-dimensional representation.

The CenterNet-3D detection head treats object detection as finding keypoints in 3D space. A separate coarse-to-fine module reconstructs shapes using coarse voxelization and a local PCA-SDF representation. Both tasks supervise the shared voxel features, encouraging them to preserve geometry and context. Their complementary training signals therefore benefit the representation used by each task.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness in both single-object and multiple-object settings. They report fine-detail reconstruction with inference two orders of magnitude faster than prior methods. The approach's significance is the combination of scene-aligned features, 3D detection, and efficient shape reconstruction within one system, allowing location and shape estimation to reinforce each other through shared learning.
summary.tldr: Shared 3D voxel features support joint object detection and detailed shape reconstruction from a single image, with substantially faster reported reconstruction inference.

title: Voxel-based 3D Detection and Reconstruction of Multiple Objects from a Single Image

abstract: We study the problem of off-policy evaluation from batched contextual bandit data with multidimensional actions, often termed slates. The problem is common to recommender systems and user-interface optimization, and it is particularly challenging because of the combinatorially-sized action space. Swaminathan et al. (2017) have proposed the pseudoinverse (PI) estimator under the assumption that the conditional mean rewards are additive in actions. Using control variates, we consider a large class of unbiased estimators that includes as specific cases the PI estimator and (asymptotically) its self-normalized variant. By optimizing over this class, we obtain new estimators with risk improvement guarantees over both the PI and the self-normalized PI estimators. Experiments with real-world recommender data as well as synthetic data validate these improvements in practice.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the performance of a policy using previously collected contextual bandit data when each action contains several coordinated choices. Such actions are called slates and occur in recommendation systems and interface optimization. Evaluation becomes difficult because the number of possible combinations can grow extremely large.

An existing pseudoinverse estimator addresses this setting under an assumption that conditional average rewards are additive across actions. The authors use control variates to construct a broader family of unbiased estimators. This family contains the pseudoinverse estimator and, asymptotically, its self-normalized version, bringing these approaches into a common framework.

Optimizing within that family produces new estimators with guarantees of improved estimation risk over both existing versions. The point is to use the freedom within an unbiased estimator family to make evaluation more accurate, while retaining its statistical foundation. Experiments on synthetic data and real recommendation data support the improvements in practice. The additive-reward assumption is central context for the pseudoinverse approach on which this work builds.
summary.tldr: Control variates yield slate-policy evaluators with guaranteed risk improvements over pseudoinverse estimators, supported by synthetic and recommendation-data experiments.

title: Control Variates for Slate Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: In data analysis problems where we are not able to rely on distributional assumptions, what types of inference guarantees can still be obtained? Many popular methods, such as holdout methods, cross-validation methods, and conformal prediction, are able to provide distribution-free guarantees for predictive inference, but the problem of providing inference for the underlying regression function (for example, inference on the conditional mean $\mathbb{E}[Y|X]$) is more challenging. In the setting where the features $X$ are continuously distributed, recent work has established that any confidence interval for $\mathbb{E}[Y|X]$ must have non-vanishing width, even as sample size tends to infinity. At the other extreme, if $X$ takes only a small number of possible values, then inference on $\mathbb{E}[Y|X]$ is trivial to achieve. In this work, we study the problem in settings in between these two extremes. We find that there are several distinct regimes in between the finite setting and the continuous setting, where vanishing-width confidence intervals are achievable if and only if the effective support size of the distribution of $X$ is smaller than the square of the sample size.

paragraphs: Distribution-free prediction guarantees do not automatically provide confidence intervals for an underlying regression function. The distinction is between predicting an outcome and estimating a quantity such as the average outcome conditional on the features. This paper investigates when confidence intervals for that conditional mean can become increasingly precise without relying on distributional assumptions.

The abstract describes two contrasting endpoints. With continuously distributed features, previous results show that valid confidence intervals cannot have widths that vanish as the sample grows. When features take only a small number of values, inference is straightforward. The paper studies the intermediate settings, where the feature distribution is neither a small finite collection nor the continuous extreme.

The authors identify several regimes and characterize the possibility of shrinking intervals through effective support size. In the settings studied, vanishing width is achievable if and only if this size is smaller than the square of the sample size. This establishes a boundary for distribution-free regression inference: the relevant comparison involves how broadly feature values are distributed relative to the available data.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when distribution-free confidence intervals for regression can shrink, using effective feature-support size relative to squared sample size.

title: Distribution-free inference for regression: discrete, continuous, and in between

abstract: We study fair classification in the presence of an omniscient adversary that, given an $\eta$, is allowed to choose an arbitrary $\eta$-fraction of the training samples and arbitrarily perturb their protected attributes. The motivation comes from settings in which protected attributes can be incorrect due to strategic misreporting, malicious actors, or errors in imputation; and prior approaches that make stochastic or independence assumptions on errors may not satisfy their guarantees in this adversarial setting. Our main contribution is an optimization framework to learn fair classifiers in this adversarial setting that comes with provable guarantees on accuracy and fairness. Our framework works with multiple and non-binary protected attributes, is designed for the large class of linear-fractional fairness metrics, and can also handle perturbations besides protected attributes. We prove near-tightness of our framework's guarantees for natural hypothesis classes: no algorithm can have significantly better accuracy and any algorithm with better fairness must have lower accuracy. Empirically, we evaluate the classifiers produced by our framework for statistical rate on real-world and synthetic datasets for a family of adversaries.

paragraphs: Fair classification often relies on protected attributes recorded in training data, but these attributes may be incorrect. This paper studies an adversarial version of that problem: an omniscient adversary may select a specified fraction of training samples and change their protected attributes arbitrarily. This captures errors that need not follow stochastic or independence assumptions.

The authors develop an optimization framework with provable accuracy and fairness guarantees under this corruption model. It supports multiple protected attributes, attributes with more than two possible values, and a broad family of fairness criteria called linear-fractional metrics. The framework can also accommodate perturbations beyond protected attributes, extending its scope beyond the primary motivating setting.

For natural hypothesis classes, the paper proves that its guarantees are nearly tight. No algorithm can substantially improve accuracy, and improving fairness beyond the guarantee requires sacrificing accuracy. This makes the result an account of the achievable tradeoff as well as a learning method. Experiments evaluate statistical rate on real and synthetic datasets against a family of adversaries.
summary.tldr: A classification framework provides nearly tight accuracy and fairness guarantees when an adversary corrupts protected attributes.

title: Fair Classification with Adversarial Perturbations

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are known to suffer from performance degradation as the number of layers increases, which is usually attributed to over-smoothing. Despite the apparent consensus, we observe that there exists a discrepancy between the theoretical understanding of over-smoothing and the practical capabilities of GCNs. Specifically, we argue that over-smoothing does not necessarily happen in practice, a deeper model is provably expressive, can converge to global optimum with linear convergence rate, and achieve very high training accuracy as long as properly trained. Despite being capable of achieving high training accuracy, empirical results show that the deeper models generalize poorly on the testing stage and existing theoretical understanding of such behavior remains elusive. To achieve better understanding, we carefully analyze the generalization capability of GCNs, and show that the training strategies to achieve high training accuracy significantly deteriorate the generalization capability of GCNs. Motivated by these findings, we propose a decoupled structure for GCNs that detaches weight matrices from feature propagation to preserve the expressive power and ensure good generalization performance. We conduct empirical evaluations on various synthetic and real-world datasets to validate the correctness of our theory.

We conduct empirical evaluations on various synthetic and real-world datasets to validate the correctness of our theory.

paragraphs: Deep graph convolutional networks often perform worse as layers are added, a pattern commonly attributed to over-smoothing. This paper questions whether that explanation accounts for their practical behavior. The authors argue that over-smoothing need not occur in practice and that properly trained deeper models can remain expressive and achieve very high training accuracy.

Their theoretical analysis establishes global-optimum convergence at a linear rate in the setting studied. Yet strong training performance does not resolve the empirical problem: deeper models can still perform poorly on test data. The authors analyze generalization and find that training strategies used to obtain high training accuracy can substantially damage the ability to generalize.

Motivated by this distinction, they propose separating the weight matrices from feature propagation in the GCN architecture. The aim is to retain expressive power while obtaining good generalization. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theory. The paper's contribution is therefore both diagnostic and architectural: it identifies a generalization issue and uses that analysis to motivate a decoupled design.
summary.tldr: Deep GCNs can fit training data well yet generalize poorly, motivating an architecture that separates learned weights from feature propagation.

title: On Provable Benefits of Depth in Training Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: State-of-the-art approaches to reasoning and question answering over knowledge graphs (KGs) usually scale with the number of edges and can only be applied effectively on small instance-dependent subgraphs. In this paper, we address this issue by showing that multi-hop and more complex logical reasoning can be accomplished separately without losing expressive power. Motivated by this insight, we propose an approach to multi-hop reasoning that scales linearly with the number of relation types in the graph, which is usually significantly smaller than the number of edges or nodes. This produces a set of candidate solutions that can be provably refined to recover the solution to the original problem. Our experiments on knowledge-based question answering show that our approach solves the multi-hop MetaQA dataset, achieves a new state-of-the-art on the more challenging WebQuestionsSP, is orders of magnitude more scalable than competitive approaches, and can achieve compositional generalization out of the training distribution.

paragraphs: Answering questions over a knowledge graph can require following several relationships and applying more complex logical constraints. Many existing methods scale with the graph's edge count, restricting effective use to small, question-specific subgraphs. SQALER addresses this computational obstacle by separating multi-hop reasoning from the more complex logical reasoning stage.

The paper shows that this separation can preserve expressive power. Its multi-hop method scales linearly with the number of relation types, a quantity usually much smaller than the number of graph nodes or edges. It produces candidate answers that can then be refined, with a proof that the refinement recovers the original problem's solution.

Experiments show that the approach solves the multi-hop MetaQA dataset and establishes a new state of the art on WebQuestionsSP. The authors also report scalability improvements of orders of magnitude over competitive methods. Their results demonstrate that compositional generalization beyond the training distribution is possible. The central contribution is a reasoning decomposition that combines a smaller scaling variable with a principled route to final answers.
summary.tldr: SQALER separates multi-hop search from logical refinement to scale knowledge-graph question answering while preserving expressive power.

title: SQALER: Scaling Question Answering by Decoupling Multi-Hop and Logical Reasoning

abstract: For video recognition task, a global representation summarizing the whole contents of the video snippets plays an important role for the final performance. However, existing video architectures usually generate it by using a simple, global average pooling (GAP) method, which has limited ability to capture complex dynamics of videos. For image recognition task, there exist evidences showing that covariance pooling has stronger representation ability than GAP. Unfortunately, such plain covariance pooling used in image recognition is an orderless representative, which cannot model spatio-temporal structure inherent in videos. Therefore, this paper proposes a Temporal-attentive Covariance Pooling (TCP), inserted at the end of deep architectures, to produce powerful video representations. Specifically, our TCP first develops a temporal attention module to adaptively calibrate spatio-temporal features for the succeeding covariance pooling, approximatively producing attentive covariance representations. Then, a temporal covariance pooling performs temporal pooling of the attentive covariance representations to characterize both intra-frame correlations and inter-frame cross-correlations of the calibrated features. As such, the proposed TCP can capture complex temporal dynamics. Finally, a fast matrix power normalization is introduced to exploit geometry of covariance representations. Note that our TCP is model-agnostic and can be flexibly integrated into any video architectures, resulting in TCPNet for effective video recognition. The extensive experiments on six benchmarks (e.g., Kinetics, Something-Something V1 and Charades) using various video architectures show our TCPNet is clearly superior to its counterparts, while having strong generalization ability. The source code is publicly available.

paragraphs: Video recognition depends on summarizing a sequence into a useful representation. Simple global averaging can miss complex dynamics, while ordinary covariance pooling ignores the ordering needed to describe video structure. This paper introduces Temporal-attentive Covariance Pooling, or TCP, to summarize relationships within and across frames.

TCP first applies temporal attention to adjust spatial and temporal features before covariance pooling. It then pools attentive covariance representations to capture both correlations within frames and cross-correlations between frames. A fast matrix power normalization uses the geometry of the resulting covariance representation. Together, these operations aim to preserve richer temporal information in the final video summary.

The module is designed to fit at the end of different video architectures. Experiments across six benchmarks, including Kinetics, Something-Something V1, and Charades, show improvements over the corresponding architectures and report strong generalization. The findings support improving video recognition through the way features are aggregated, with attention and covariance jointly contributing to a representation of temporal dynamics.
summary.tldr: Temporal-attentive covariance pooling captures within-frame and between-frame relationships, improving video recognition across six evaluated benchmarks.

title: Temporal-attentive Covariance Pooling Networks for Video Recognition

abstract: Many tasks in deep learning involve optimizing over the inputs to a network to minimize or maximize some objective; examples include optimization over latent spaces in a generative model to match a target image, or adversarially perturbing an input to worsen classifier performance. Performing such optimization, however, is traditionally quite costly, as it involves a complete forward and backward pass through the network for each gradient step. In a separate line of work, a recent thread of research has developed the deep equilibrium (DEQ) model, a class of models that foregoes traditional network depth and instead computes the output of a network by finding the fixed point of a single nonlinear layer. In this paper, we show that there is a natural synergy between these two settings. Although, naively using DEQs for these optimization problems is expensive (owing to the time needed to compute a fixed point for each gradient step), we can leverage the fact that gradient-based optimization can itself be cast as a fixed point iteration to substantially improve the overall speed. That is, we simultaneously both solve for the DEQ fixed point and optimize over network inputs, all within a single "augmented" DEQ model that jointly encodes both the original network and the optimization process. Indeed, the procedure is fast enough that it allows us to efficiently train DEQ models for tasks traditionally relying on an "inner" optimization loop. We demonstrate this strategy on various tasks such as training generative models while optimizing over latent codes, training models for inverse problems like denoising and inpainting, adversarial training and gradient based meta-learning.

paragraphs: Some learning tasks optimize a network’s input, such as finding a latent code that produces a target image or an input perturbation that worsens classification. Ordinarily, each optimization step requires a full forward and backward computation. Deep equilibrium models introduce a related expense: their output is obtained by solving for a fixed point of a nonlinear layer.

The paper combines these two computations by observing that gradient-based input optimization can itself be expressed as a fixed-point iteration. An augmented equilibrium model encodes both the original network and the optimization process. It solves for the network state and improves the input together, avoiding the naive arrangement of repeatedly solving a separate equilibrium problem for each input update.

The resulting speed improvement is sufficient to make training practical for tasks with an inner optimization loop. Demonstrations include generative modeling with optimized latent codes, denoising and inpainting, adversarial training, and gradient-based meta-learning. The contribution is a shared computational formulation: inference and input optimization become one coupled equilibrium problem, enabling more efficient use of equilibrium networks across these tasks.
summary.tldr: An augmented equilibrium network jointly solves inference and input optimization, substantially speeding tasks that otherwise require repeated inner optimization.

title: Joint inference and input optimization in equilibrium networks

abstract: In this paper, we model the subspace of convolutional filters with a neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) to enable gradual changes in generated images. Decomposing convolutional filters over a set of filter atoms allows efficiently modeling and sampling from a subspace of high-dimensional filters. By further modeling filters atoms with a neural ODE, we show both empirically and theoretically that such introduced continuity can be propagated to the generated images, and thus achieves gradually evolved image generation. We support the proposed framework of image generation with continuous filter atoms using various experiments, including image-to-image translation and image generation conditioned on continuous labels. Without auxiliary network components and heavy supervision, the proposed continuous filter atoms allow us to easily manipulate the gradual change of generated images by controlling integration intervals of neural ordinary differential equation. This research sheds the light on using the subspace of network parameters to navigate the diverse appearance of image generation.

paragraphs: Generating a sequence of images with gradual changes requires a way to control how appearance evolves. This paper places that control in the generator's convolutional filters. It decomposes high-dimensional filters into a set of smaller building blocks, called filter atoms, making a subspace of possible filters easier to model and sample.

The authors use a neural ordinary differential equation to model the filter atoms continuously. Adjusting the equation's integration interval changes their evolution and thereby controls changes in the generated images. They provide both theoretical and empirical support that the introduced continuity can propagate from the filter representation to the image output.

Experiments include image-to-image translation and generation conditioned on continuous labels. The framework enables gradual image manipulation without auxiliary network components or heavy supervision. Its central contribution is a way to navigate generated appearance through a structured subspace of network parameters. The reported results support filter atoms as an efficient control representation and show how continuous parameter evolution can become visible as gradual changes in generated content.
summary.tldr: Continuous filter atoms modeled by a neural differential equation let a generator produce controllable, gradual changes in image appearance.

title: Image Generation using Continuous Filter Atoms

abstract: In this paper, we propose an end-to-end framework for instance segmentation. Based on the recently introduced DETR, our method, termed SOLQ, segments objects by learning unified queries. In SOLQ, each query represents one object and has multiple representations: class, location and mask. The object queries learned perform classification, box regression and mask encoding simultaneously in an unified vector form. During training phase, the mask vectors encoded are supervised by the compression coding of raw spatial masks. In inference time,mask vectors produced can be directly transformed to spatial masks by the inverse process of compression coding. Experimental results show that SOLQ can achieve state-of-the-art performance, surpassing most of existing approaches. Moreover, the joint learning of unified query representation can greatly improve the detection performance of DETR. We hope our SOLQ can serve as a strong baseline for the Transformer-based instance segmentation.

paragraphs: SOLQ is an end-to-end instance segmentation framework built on DETR. It represents each object with a learned query that jointly captures its class, location, and mask. The central design is a unified vector representation through which classification, bounding-box regression, and mask encoding are learned together.

To train the mask component, the method compresses raw spatial masks into codes and uses those codes to supervise the predicted mask vectors. At inference time, the inverse coding process converts each predicted vector directly into a spatial mask. This links the compact query representation to the pixel-level output needed for segmentation.

The authors report state-of-the-art segmentation performance, exceeding most existing approaches in their evaluation. They also find that jointly learning the unified query representation can substantially improve DETR’s detection performance. This means the combined representation contributes beyond the added mask output: its joint training also benefits object detection. The paper presents SOLQ as a strong potential baseline for Transformer-based instance segmentation.
summary.tldr: SOLQ jointly learns object class, box, and compressed mask representations through unified queries, improving segmentation and DETR detection.

title: SOLQ: Segmenting Objects by Learning Queries

abstract: Certified robustness is a desirable property for deep neural networks in safety-critical applications, and popular training algorithms can certify robustness of a neural network by computing a global bound on its Lipschitz constant. However, such a bound is often loose: it tends to over-regularize the neural network and degrade its natural accuracy. A tighter Lipschitz bound may provide a better tradeoff between natural and certified accuracy, but is generally hard to compute exactly due to non-convexity of the network. In this work, we propose an efficient and trainable \emph{local} Lipschitz upper bound by considering the interactions between activation functions (e.g. ReLU) and weight matrices. Specifically, when computing the induced norm of a weight matrix, we eliminate the corresponding rows and columns where the activation function is guaranteed to be a constant in the neighborhood of each given data point, which provides a provably tighter bound than the global Lipschitz constant of the neural network. Our method can be used as a plug-in module to tighten the Lipschitz bound in many certifiable training algorithms. Furthermore, we propose to clip activation functions (e.g., ReLU and MaxMin) with a learnable upper threshold and a sparsity loss to assist the network to achieve an even tighter local Lipschitz bound. Experimentally, we show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both clean and certified accuracy on MNIST, CIFAR-10 and TinyImageNet datasets with various network architectures.

paragraphs: Robustness certification can use a Lipschitz bound to control how much a network's output changes when its input changes. Global bounds can be loose, leading training to constrain the network too strongly and reduce clean-data accuracy. This paper develops an efficient, trainable local bound that accounts for behavior near each individual input.

The method examines interactions between activation functions and weight matrices. When an activation is guaranteed to remain constant within the relevant neighborhood, associated rows and columns are removed from the matrix-norm calculation. This produces a provably tighter local bound than the global bound used for comparison and can be incorporated into many certifiable training algorithms.

The authors additionally clip activations using a learnable upper threshold and introduce a sparsity loss to encourage tighter bounds. Across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and TinyImageNet experiments with multiple architectures, they report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods in both clean and certified accuracy. The findings show how accounting for local activation behavior can improve the practical tradeoff between ordinary prediction and provable robustness.
summary.tldr: Trainable local Lipschitz bounds exploit constant activations to tighten robustness certificates and improve clean and certified accuracy in experiments.

title: Training Certifiably Robust Neural Networks with Efficient Local Lipschitz Bounds

abstract: Deep Markov models (DMM) are generative models which are scalable and expressive generalization of Markov models for representation, learning, and inference problems. However, the fundamental stochastic stability guarantees of such models have not been thoroughly investigated. In this paper, we present a novel stability analysis method and provide sufficient conditions of DMM's stochastic stability. The proposed stability analysis is based on the contraction of probabilistic maps modeled by deep neural networks. We make connections between the spectral properties of neural network's weights and different types of used activation function on the stability and overall dynamic behavior of DMMs with Gaussian distributions. Based on the theory, we propose a few practical methods for designing constrained DMMs with guaranteed stability. We empirically substantiate our theoretical results via intuitive numerical experiments using the proposed stability constraints.
