paragraphs: Deep Markov models use neural networks to make Markov-style generative modeling more expressive. Their flexibility raises a basic question about dynamics: under what conditions is their stochastic behavior stable? This paper develops a stability analysis and gives sufficient conditions that guarantee stability for the models considered.

The analysis examines contraction in probabilistic maps represented by deep networks. It connects the spectral properties of network weight matrices and the choice of activation functions to stability and overall dynamics. The stated treatment concerns deep Markov models with Gaussian distributions, making the probabilistic setting part of the scope of the results.

Building on the theory, the authors propose practical ways to constrain model design so that stability is guaranteed. Numerical experiments using those constraints support the theoretical conclusions. The value of the work is the link between mathematical properties of neural-network components and controlled behavior of the resulting stochastic model. Because the conditions are sufficient, the results provide routes to stable designs without claiming that every stable model must satisfy those same constraints.
summary.tldr: Contraction-based analysis gives sufficient stability conditions and practical design constraints for Gaussian deep Markov models.

title: On the Stochastic Stability of Deep Markov Models

abstract: Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) raises keen attention to identifying sparse trainable subnetworks, or winning tickets, which can be trained in isolation to achieve similar or even better performance compared to the full models. Despite many efforts being made, the most effective method to identify such winning tickets is still Iterative Magnitude-based Pruning (IMP), which is computationally expensive and has to be run thoroughly for every different network. A natural question that comes in is: can we “transform” the winning ticket found in one network to another with a different architecture, yielding a winning ticket for the latter at the beginning, without re-doing the expensive IMP? Answering this question is not only practically relevant for efficient “once-for-all” winning ticket ﬁnding, but also theoretically appealing for uncovering inherently scalable sparse patterns in networks. We conduct extensive experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, and propose a variety of strategies to tweak the winning tickets found from different networks of the same model family (e.g., ResNets). Based on these results, we articulate the Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (E-LTH): by mindfully replicating (or dropping) and re-ordering layers for one network, its corresponding winning ticket could be stretched (or squeezed) into a subnetwork for another deeper (or shallower) network from the same family, whose performance is nearly the same competitive as the latter’s winning ticket directly found by IMP. We have also extensively compared E-LTH with pruning-at-initialization and dynamic sparse training methods, as well as discussed the generalizability of E-LTH to different model families, layer types, and across datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/ElasticLTH.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis concerns sparse subnetworks that can train successfully in isolation. Finding these winning tickets with iterative magnitude-based pruning is computationally expensive, especially when the process must be repeated for each architecture. This paper asks whether a ticket found in one network can be transformed for another.

The authors investigate strategies for adapting tickets between networks in the same model family, such as ResNets. Their Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis proposes that carefully replicating or dropping layers, and changing their order, can stretch or compress a ticket to suit a deeper or shallower network. The goal is performance nearly as competitive as a ticket discovered directly for the destination network.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet motivate the hypothesis. The paper also compares the approach with pruning-at-initialization and dynamic sparse training methods, and discusses transfer across model families, layer types, and datasets. The central finding supports reusing sparse structures within model families as a way to reduce repeated ticket-search costs.
summary.tldr: Winning sparse subnetworks can be adapted across depths within a model family, potentially avoiding repeated expensive pruning searches.

title: The Elastic Lottery Ticket Hypothesis

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic raises the problem of adapting face recognition systems to the new reality, where people may wear surgical masks to cover their noses and mouths. Traditional data sets (e.g., CelebA, CASIA-WebFace) used for training these systems were released before the pandemic, so they now seem unsuited due to the lack of examples of people wearing masks. We propose a method for enhancing data sets containing faces without masks by creating synthetic masks and overlaying them on faces in the original images. Our method relies on SparkAR Studio, a developer program made by Facebook that is used to create Instagram face filters. In our approach, we use 9 masks of different colors, shapes and fabrics. We employ our method to generate a number of 445,446 (90%) samples of masks for the CASIA-WebFace data set and 196,254 (96.8%) masks for the CelebA data set, releasing the mask images at https://github.com/securifai/masked_faces. We show that our method produces significantly more realistic training examples of masks overlaid on faces by asking volunteers to qualitatively compare it to other methods or data sets designed for the same task. We also demonstrate the usefulness of our method by evaluating state-of-the-art face recognition systems (FaceNet, VGG-face, ArcFace) trained on our enhanced data sets and showing that they outperform equivalent systems trained on original data sets (containing faces without masks) or competing data sets (containing masks generated by related methods), when the test benchmarks contain masked faces.

paragraphs: Face-recognition datasets collected before widespread mask wearing contain few masked faces. This paper augments existing images by placing synthetic masks onto faces using SparkAR Studio, with nine mask variants differing in color, shape, and fabric.

The method creates 445,446 masked samples, corresponding to 90% of CASIA-WebFace, and 196,254 samples, corresponding to 96.8% of CelebA. Volunteers compare the generated examples with competing approaches and judge the proposed overlays significantly more realistic.

FaceNet, VGG-face, and ArcFace models trained on the enhanced datasets perform better on masked-face test benchmarks than corresponding models trained on the original unmasked datasets or competing synthetic-mask datasets. The abstract does not provide recognition rates or demographic analyses. The contribution is a data-generation technique and released augmented data, with both perceptual realism assessments and downstream recognition evidence in the tested setting.
summary.tldr: Realistic synthetic masks expand face datasets and improve recognition on masked-face benchmarks.

title: A realistic approach to generate masked faces applied on two novel masked face recognition data sets

abstract: When making everyday decisions, people are guided by their conscience, an internal sense of right and wrong, to behave morally. By contrast, artificial agents may behave immorally when trained on environments that ignore moral concerns, such as violent video games. With the advent of generally capable agents that pretrain on many environments, mitigating inherited biases towards immoral behavior will become necessary. However, prior work on aligning agents with human values and morals focuses on small-scale settings lacking in semantic complexity. To enable research in larger, more realistic settings, we introduce Jiminy Cricket, an environment suite of 25 text-based adventure games with thousands of semantically rich, morally salient scenarios. Via dense annotations for every possible action, Jiminy Cricket environments robustly evaluate whether agents can act morally while maximizing reward. To improve moral behavior, we leverage language models with commonsense moral knowledge and develop strategies to mediate this knowledge into actions. In extensive experiments, we find that our artificial conscience approach can steer agents towards moral behavior without sacrificing performance.

paragraphs: Agents trained to maximize reward in environments that ignore moral concerns may learn harmful behavior. This paper creates a richer setting for investigating that problem through Jiminy Cricket, a suite of 25 text adventure games containing thousands of morally significant scenarios. The goal is to evaluate behavior in situations with substantial language and semantic complexity.

The environments include dense annotations for every possible action, enabling evaluation of moral behavior alongside reward-seeking performance. This provides a way to distinguish progress within a game from the moral character of the actions used to achieve it. The benchmark expands the scope beyond the small settings emphasized in earlier work.

The authors also develop an artificial conscience approach that uses commonsense moral knowledge from language models to influence agent actions. Their experiments find that this approach can steer agents toward more moral behavior without sacrificing performance. The result demonstrates compatibility between these objectives in the evaluated settings, while the suite provides a resource for further research on morally guided agents.
summary.tldr: Jiminy Cricket evaluates moral behavior in text adventures, where an artificial conscience can improve tested agents' conduct without reducing performance.

title: What Would Jiminy Cricket Do? Towards Agents That Behave Morally

abstract: Recently, neural implicit surfaces learning by volume rendering has become popular for multi-view reconstruction. However, one key challenge remains: existing approaches lack explicit multi-view geometry constraints, hence usually fail to generate geometry-consistent surface reconstruction. To address this challenge, we propose geometry-consistent neural implicit surfaces learning for multi-view reconstruction. We theoretically analyze that there exists a gap between the volume rendering integral and point-based signed distance function (SDF) modeling. To bridge this gap, we directly locate the zero-level set of SDF networks and explicitly perform multi-view geometry optimization by leveraging the sparse geometry from structure from motion (SFM) and photometric consistency in multi-view stereo. This makes our SDF optimization unbiased and allows the multi-view geometry constraints to focus on the true surface optimization. Extensive experiments show that our proposed method achieves high-quality surface reconstruction in both complex thin structures and large smooth regions, thus outperforming the state-of-the-arts by a large margin.

To address this challenge, we propose geometry-consistent neural implicit surfaces learning for multi-view reconstruction. We theoretically analyze that there exists a gap between the volume rendering integral and point-based signed distance function (SDF) modeling. To bridge this gap, we directly locate the zero-level set of SDF networks and explicitly perform multi-view geometry optimization by leveraging the sparse geometry from structure from motion (SFM) and photometric consistency in multi-view stereo. paragraphs: Geo-Neus addresses surface reconstruction from multiple images using a neural signed distance function. The paper identifies a problem with approaches trained through volume rendering: without explicit constraints linking geometry across views, they can fail to reconstruct a consistent surface. Its theoretical analysis identifies a gap between the volume-rendering integral and point-based signed distance modeling.

The proposed method directly locates the signed distance network's zero-level set, which defines the reconstructed surface. It then applies geometric optimization using sparse structure recovered through structure from motion and photometric consistency across views. This directs the multi-view constraints toward points on the actual modeled surface, connecting image evidence more explicitly to the geometry being optimized.

The authors state that this construction makes signed distance optimization unbiased and focuses the geometric constraints on true surface optimization. Experiments report high-quality reconstructions for both complex thin structures and large smooth regions, with a large improvement over state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution is therefore both an analysis of a modeling mismatch and a reconstruction method designed to bridge it.
summary.tldr: Geo-Neus improves multi-view reconstruction by applying explicit geometric constraints directly to the surface defined by a neural signed distance function.

title: Geo-Neus: Geometry-Consistent Neural Implicit Surfaces Learning for Multi-view Reconstruction

abstract: Information-theoretic Bayesian optimization techniques have become popular for optimizing expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions due to their non-myopic qualities. Entropy Search and Predictive Entropy Search both consider the entropy over the optimum in the input space, while the recent Max-value Entropy Search considers the entropy over the optimal value in the output space. We propose Joint Entropy Search (JES), a novel information-theoretic acquisition function that considers an entirely new quantity, namely the entropy over the joint optimal probability density over both input and output space. To incorporate this information, we consider the reduction in entropy from conditioning on fantasized optimal input/output pairs. The resulting approach primarily relies on standard GP machinery and removes complex approximations typically associated with information-theoretic methods. With minimal computational overhead, JES shows superior decision-making, and yields state-of-the-art performance for information-theoretic approaches across a wide suite of tasks. As a light-weight approach with superior results, JES provides a new go-to acquisition function for Bayesian optimization.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization chooses evaluations carefully when a black-box function is costly to evaluate. Information-theoretic methods guide that choice by asking what an evaluation could reveal about the optimum. Earlier approaches examine uncertainty either about the input where the optimum occurs or about the optimal output value.

Joint Entropy Search considers those two quantities together. Its acquisition function measures information about the joint distribution of the optimal input and output. To incorporate that information, it conditions on imagined optimal input-output pairs and considers the resulting reduction in entropy. This treats uncertainty about location and value as a connected decision-making target.

The implementation primarily uses standard Gaussian process machinery, avoiding complex approximations commonly associated with information-theoretic approaches. The authors report minimal computational overhead, improved decision-making, and state-of-the-art performance among information-theoretic methods across a broad collection of tasks. The contribution is a practical way to use a richer description of the unknown optimum when deciding where the next expensive evaluation should take place.
summary.tldr: Joint Entropy Search selects evaluations using uncertainty about both the optimal input and its value.

title: Joint Entropy Search For Maximally-Informed Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Consider the problem setting of Interaction-Grounded Learning (IGL), in which a learner's goal is to optimally interact with the environment with no explicit reward to ground its policies. The agent observes a context vector, takes an action, and receives a feedback vector, using this information to effectively optimize a policy with respect to a latent reward function. Prior analyzed approaches fail when the feedback vector contains the action, which significantly limits IGL’s success in many potential scenarios such as Brain-computer interface (BCI) or Human-computer interface (HCI) applications. We address this by creating an algorithm and analysis which allows IGL to work even when the feedback vector contains the action, encoded in any fashion. We provide theoretical guarantees and large-scale experiments based on supervised datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of the new approach.

paragraphs: Interaction-Grounded Learning studies how an agent can improve its behavior without receiving an explicit reward. The learner observes a context, chooses an action, and receives a feedback vector. Its objective is to use these interactions to optimize a policy with respect to a reward function that remains latent, rather than directly supplied.

A problem with previously analyzed approaches is that they fail when the feedback itself contains the action. This is a meaningful obstacle for potential brain-computer and human-computer interface applications, where feedback may include information about what the system did. The paper introduces an algorithm and analysis that accommodate action information in the feedback, regardless of how that action is encoded.

The authors support the approach with theoretical guarantees and large-scale experiments constructed from supervised datasets. These results demonstrate effectiveness in the studied setting while expanding the feedback structures that IGL can handle. The contribution concerns learning from action-inclusive feedback; the cited interface applications provide motivation rather than reported deployment evidence.
summary.tldr: The paper extends Interaction-Grounded Learning to feedback that contains the chosen action, with theoretical guarantees and dataset-based experiments.

title: Interaction-Grounded Learning with Action-Inclusive Feedback

abstract: This paper introduces a new interpretation of the Variational Autoencoder framework by taking a fully geometric point of view. We argue that vanilla VAE models unveil naturally a Riemannian structure in their latent space and that taking into consideration those geometrical aspects can lead to better interpolations and an improved generation procedure. This new proposed sampling method consists in sampling from the uniform distribution deriving intrinsically from the learned Riemannian latent space and we show that using this scheme can make a vanilla VAE competitive and even better than more advanced versions on several benchmark datasets. Since generative models are known to be sensitive to the number of training samples we also stress the method's robustness in the low data regime.

paragraphs: A variational autoencoder learns a latent space from which it can generate data. This paper asks what changes when that space is understood geometrically. The authors argue that an ordinary VAE naturally gives rise to a Riemannian structure, providing a learned geometry that can inform how latent representations are traversed and sampled.

The proposed generation procedure samples from a uniform distribution defined intrinsically by that geometry. Here, uniformity is tied to the learned Riemannian space itself. This changes how the model chooses latent locations for generation and makes the structure of the representation part of the sampling procedure. The authors also argue that accounting for this geometry can improve interpolation between representations.

On several benchmark datasets, the sampling scheme makes a vanilla VAE competitive with, and sometimes better than, more advanced variants. The paper additionally emphasizes robustness when training data are scarce. Together, these findings suggest that generation quality can benefit from how a learned latent space is used, alongside improvements to the generative model.
summary.tldr: Sampling according to a VAE’s learned latent geometry can improve generation and make a standard VAE competitive with more advanced variants.

title: A Geometric Perspective on Variational Autoencoders

abstract: Recent studies reveal that a well-trained deep reinforcement learning (RL) policy can be particularly vulnerable to adversarial perturbations on input observations. Therefore, it is crucial to train RL agents that are robust against any attacks with a bounded budget. Existing robust training methods in deep RL either treat correlated steps separately, ignoring the robustness of long-term rewards, or train the agents and RL-based attacker together, doubling the computational burden and sample complexity of the training process. In this work, we propose a strong and efficient robust training framework for RL, named Worst-case-aware Robust RL (WocaR-RL) that directly estimates and optimizes the worst-case reward of a policy under bounded l_p attacks without requiring extra samples for learning an attacker. Experiments on multiple environments show that WocaR-RL achieves state-of-the-art performance under various strong attacks, and obtains significantly higher training efficiency than prior state-of-the-art robust training methods. The code of this work is available at https://github.com/umd-huang-lab/WocaR-RL.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can perform well under ordinary observations yet be vulnerable when an adversary perturbs those observations. Robust training must account for how these disturbances affect rewards across a sequence of decisions. The paper identifies drawbacks in methods that assess correlated steps separately or jointly train a policy and a separate reinforcement learning attacker.

WocaR-RL directly estimates and optimizes a policy’s worst-case reward under attacks constrained by an l_p perturbation budget. This puts the long-term reward under bounded disturbances at the center of training. It also avoids requiring extra samples to learn an attacker, addressing a source of computational and sampling overhead.

Experiments across multiple environments report state-of-the-art performance against various strong attacks and substantially better training efficiency than prior leading robust training methods. These findings support the practical value of optimizing estimated worst-case reward directly. The attack model remains explicitly bounded, and the reported experimental robustness concerns the strong attacks evaluated in those environments.
summary.tldr: WocaR-RL improves robustness and training efficiency by optimizing estimated worst-case reward without learning a separate attacker.

title: Efficient Adversarial Training without Attacking: Worst-Case-Aware Robust Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Obtaining the human-like perception ability of abstracting visual concepts from concrete pixels has always been a fundamental and important target in machine learning research fields such as disentangled representation learning and scene decomposition. Towards this goal, we propose an unsupervised transformer-based Visual Concepts Tokenization framework, dubbed VCT, to perceive an image into a set of disentangled visual concept tokens, with each concept token responding to one type of independent visual concept. Particularly, to obtain these concept tokens, we only use cross-attention to extract visual information from the image tokens layer by layer without self-attention between concept tokens, preventing information leakage across concept tokens. We further propose a Concept Disentangling Loss to facilitate that different concept tokens represent independent visual concepts. The cross-attention and disentangling loss play the role of induction and mutual exclusion for the concept tokens, respectively. Extensive experiments on several popular datasets verify the effectiveness of VCT on the tasks of disentangled representation learning and scene decomposition. VCT achieves the state of the art results by a large margin.

paragraphs: Visual Concepts Tokenization aims to turn an image into a set of representations that each capture an independent visual concept. The method is unsupervised and transformer-based, addressing both disentangled representation learning and scene decomposition. Its goal is to separate meaningful visual factors instead of allowing every representation to mix information about the entire image.

Concept tokens gather information from image tokens through cross-attention at successive layers. The architecture excludes self-attention between concept tokens to prevent information from passing directly among them. A separate Concept Disentangling Loss encourages different tokens to represent independent concepts. These components respectively help tokens acquire visual information and discourage overlap in what they represent.

Experiments across several datasets evaluate both disentangled representations and scene decomposition. The authors report state-of-the-art results by a large margin on the evaluated tasks. The findings support combining restrictions on information flow with a loss that encourages separation: the architecture controls how concepts are formed, while the objective pushes their representations toward distinct visual content.
summary.tldr: VCT combines isolated cross-attention pathways and a disentangling loss to learn separate visual concept tokens without supervision.

title: Visual Concepts Tokenization

abstract: Deep learning models such as the Transformer are often constructed by heuristics and experience. To provide a complementary foundation, in this work we study the following problem: Is it possible to find an energy function underlying the Transformer model, such that descent steps along this energy correspond with the Transformer forward pass? By finding such a function, we can reinterpret Transformers as the unfolding of an interpretable optimization process. This unfolding perspective has been frequently adopted in the past to elucidate more straightforward deep models such as MLPs and CNNs; however, it has thus far remained elusive obtaining a similar equivalence for more complex models with self-attention mechanisms like the Transformer. To this end, we first outline several major obstacles before providing companion techniques to at least partially address them, demonstrating for the first time a close association between energy function minimization and deep layers with self-attention. This interpretation contributes to our intuition and understanding of Transformers, while potentially laying the ground-work for new model designs.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether a Transformer's forward computation can be understood as steps that reduce an underlying energy function. Such an interpretation would connect the architecture to an explicit optimization process. The motivation is to provide a mathematical perspective complementary to the heuristics and experience commonly used in model design.

The authors investigate obstacles to extending this perspective to self-attention. Related interpretations exist for simpler architectures, but the complexity of attention makes the correspondence harder to establish. They outline the main difficulties and introduce techniques that address them at least partially.

The result is a close association between energy minimization and deep layers containing self-attention. The abstract presents this as progress toward an optimization interpretation, rather than a complete resolution of every obstacle for Transformers. Its significance is explanatory: viewing successive computations as an unfolding optimization process can sharpen intuition about the model. The authors also identify possible value for future architectures, without claiming that new designs are already established by this analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes a close connection between self-attention layers and energy minimization while partially addressing obstacles to an optimization interpretation of Transformers.

title: Transformers from an Optimization Perspective

abstract: In this paper, we empirically study how to make the most of low-resolution frames for efficient video recognition. Existing methods mainly focus on developing compact networks or alleviating temporal redundancy of video inputs to increase efficiency, whereas compressing frame resolution has rarely been considered a promising solution. A major concern is the poor recognition accuracy on low-resolution frames. We thus start by analyzing the underlying causes of performance degradation on low-resolution frames. Our key finding is that the major cause of degradation is not information loss in the down-sampling process, but rather the mismatch between network architecture and input scale. Motivated by the success of knowledge distillation (KD), we propose to bridge the gap between network and input size via cross-resolution KD (ResKD). Our work shows that ResKD is a simple but effective method to boost recognition accuracy on low-resolution frames. Without bells and whistles, ResKD considerably surpasses all competitive methods in terms of efficiency and accuracy on four large-scale benchmark datasets, i.e., ActivityNet, FCVID, Mini-Kinetics, Something-Something V2. In addition, we extensively demonstrate its effectiveness over state-of-the-art architectures, i.e., 3D-CNNs and Video Transformers, and scalability towards super low-resolution frames. The results suggest ResKD can serve as a general inference acceleration method for state-of-the-art video recognition. Our code will be available at https://github.com/CVMI-Lab/ResKD.

paragraphs: Reducing video-frame resolution offers a route to cheaper recognition, but low-resolution inputs often produce poor accuracy. This paper investigates why that degradation occurs. Its central empirical finding is that the mismatch between network architecture and input scale is the main cause in the studied setting, rather than information lost during downsampling.

The authors introduce cross-resolution knowledge distillation, called ResKD, to bridge that mismatch. Knowledge transfer across resolutions helps the network recognize videos from smaller frames. This targets spatial input cost alongside more familiar efficiency strategies involving compact networks or reduced temporal redundancy.

ResKD reportedly surpasses competitive methods in both efficiency and accuracy on ActivityNet, FCVID, Mini-Kinetics, and Something-Something V2. The authors also demonstrate its effectiveness with 3D convolutional networks and video transformers, including very low-resolution inputs. These experiments support its potential as a broadly useful inference acceleration method. The explanation for accuracy loss remains an empirical finding from the paper’s study, rather than a claim that downsampling can never remove essential information.
summary.tldr: Cross-resolution distillation improves low-resolution video recognition by addressing the observed mismatch between networks and input scale.

title: Rethinking Resolution in the Context of Efficient Video Recognition

abstract: We present the first diffusion-based framework that can learn an unknown distribution using only highly-corrupted samples. This problem arises in scientific applications where access to uncorrupted samples is impossible or expensive to acquire. Another benefit of our approach is the ability to train generative models that are less likely to memorize any individual training sample, since they never observe clean training data. Our main idea is to introduce additional measurement distortion during the diffusion process and require the model to predict the original corrupted image from the further corrupted image. We prove that our method leads to models that learn the conditional expectation of the full uncorrupted image given this additional measurement corruption. This holds for any corruption process that satisfies some technical conditions (and in particular includes inpainting and compressed sensing). We train models on standard benchmarks (CelebA, CIFAR-10 and AFHQ) and show that we can learn the distribution even when all the training samples have 90\% of their pixels missing. We also show that we can finetune foundation models on small corrupted datasets (e.g. MRI scans with block corruptions) and learn the clean distribution without memorizing the training set.

paragraphs: Ambient Diffusion addresses generative learning when every available training example is already heavily corrupted. This situation arises in scientific applications where clean measurements are expensive or impossible to obtain. The objective is to learn the underlying clean distribution, even though the model never directly observes a clean training image.

The method adds further measurement distortion during diffusion training and asks the model to predict the original corrupted observation. Under technical conditions on the corruption process, the authors prove that this procedure learns the conditional expectation of the full clean image given the additional corruption. The supported processes include inpainting and compressed sensing, so the theoretical claim is broader than one particular missing-pixel pattern.

Experiments on CelebA, CIFAR-10, and AFHQ show distribution learning even when every training image lacks 90% of its pixels. The authors also demonstrate fine-tuning foundation models on small corrupted datasets, including MRI scans with block corruption, without memorizing the training set in those experiments. Avoiding exposure to clean examples offers a potential reduction in memorization, rather than a blanket privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: Ambient Diffusion learns clean data distributions from corrupted observations by training with an additional layer of measurement corruption.

title: Ambient Diffusion: Learning Clean Distributions from Corrupted Data

abstract: Massive web datasets play a key role in the success of large vision-language models like CLIP and Flamingo. However, the raw web data is noisy, and existing filtering methods to reduce noise often come at the expense of data diversity. Our work focuses on caption quality as one major source of noise, and studies how generated captions can increase the utility of web-scraped datapoints with nondescript text. Through exploring different mixing strategies for raw and generated captions, we outperform the best filtering method proposed by the DataComp benchmark by 2% on ImageNet and 4% on average across 38 tasks, given a candidate pool of 128M image-text pairs. Our best approach is also 2x better at Flickr and MS-COCO retrieval. We then analyze what makes synthetic captions an effective source of text supervision. In experimenting with different image captioning models, we also demonstrate that the performance of a model on standard image captioning benchmarks (e.g., NoCaps CIDEr) is not a reliable indicator of the utility of the captions it generates for multimodal training. Finally, our experiments with using generated captions at DataComp's large scale (1.28B image-text pairs) offer insights into the limitations of synthetic text, as well as the importance of image curation with increasing training data quantity. The synthetic captions used in our experiments are now available on HuggingFace.

paragraphs: Web image-text datasets contain many images paired with vague or uninformative text. Filtering can remove noise, but can also reduce diversity. This paper investigates whether generated image captions can make those examples more useful, studying different ways of mixing original web text with synthetic descriptions for multimodal training.

With a candidate pool of 128 million image-text pairs, the best strategy exceeds the strongest DataComp filtering method by a reported 2% on ImageNet and 4% on average across 38 tasks. Experiments at the 1.28-billion-pair scale also reveal limits of synthetic text and emphasize the growing importance of image curation. The practical lesson is to judge generated captions by their training utility, while recognizing that better text does not remove the need to curate images.
summary.tldr: Mixing generated captions with web text improves multimodal training, although captioning benchmark scores do not reliably predict that benefit.

title: Improving multimodal datasets with image captioning

abstract: Text-conditional diffusion models are able to generate high-fidelity images with diverse contents.However, linguistic representations frequently exhibit ambiguous descriptions of the envisioned objective imagery, requiring the incorporation of additional control signals to bolster the efficacy of text-guided diffusion models. In this work, we propose Cocktail, a pipeline to mix various modalities into one embedding, amalgamated with a generalized ControlNet (gControlNet), a controllable normalisation (ControlNorm), and a spatial guidance sampling method, to actualize multi-modal and spatially-refined control for text-conditional diffusion models. Specifically, we introduce a hyper-network gControlNet, dedicated to the alignment and infusion of the control signals from disparate modalities into the pre-trained diffusion model. gControlNet is capable of accepting flexible modality signals, encompassing the simultaneous reception of any combination of modality signals, or the supplementary fusion of multiple modality signals. The control signals are then fused and injected into the backbone model according to our proposed ControlNorm.Furthermore, our advanced spatial guidance sampling methodology proficiently incorporates the control signal into the designated region, thereby circumventing the manifestation of undesired objects within the generated image.We demonstrate the results of our method in controlling various modalities, proving high-quality synthesis and fidelity to multiple external signals.

paragraphs: Text prompts can leave important aspects of an intended image ambiguous. Cocktail addresses this by adding multiple kinds of external control to text-conditioned diffusion generation. Its purpose is to combine those signals while also controlling where they influence the image, giving the generation process more specific direction than language alone provides.

The pipeline uses a generalized ControlNet, called gControlNet, to align signals from different modalities and introduce them into a pretrained diffusion model. This hypernetwork can receive combinations of modality signals simultaneously or incorporate additional signals through supplementary fusion. A controllable normalization mechanism, ControlNorm, combines the signals and injects them into the image-generation backbone.

Cocktail also introduces spatial guidance during sampling so that a control signal affects its designated region, addressing unwanted objects in the generated image. The reported demonstrations show high-quality synthesis that follows multiple external signals. Together, the components address two related requirements: combining different kinds of guidance and applying that guidance to the intended spatial locations.
summary.tldr: Cocktail combines multiple control modalities and spatial guidance to steer text-conditioned diffusion images toward several external signals.

title: Cocktail: Mixing Multi-Modality Control for Text-Conditional Image Generation

abstract: Recently, the anchor acceleration, an acceleration mechanism distinct from Nesterov's, has been discovered for minimax optimization and fixed-point problems, but its mechanism is not understood well, much less so than Nesterov acceleration. In this work, we analyze continuous-time models of anchor acceleration. We provide tight, unified analyses for characterizing the convergence rate as a function of the anchor coefficient $\beta(t)$, thereby providing insight into the anchor acceleration mechanism and its accelerated $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$-convergence rate. Finally, we present an adaptive method inspired by the continuous-time analyses and establish its effectiveness through theoretical analyses and experiments.

paragraphs: Anchor acceleration is a mechanism for speeding up algorithms for minimax optimization and fixed-point problems. Although it has achieved accelerated convergence, the reasons for its effectiveness have been less well understood than those of Nesterov acceleration. This paper studies the mechanism by analyzing continuous-time models, which describe the evolution of the optimization process through time.

The analysis centers on the anchor coefficient, beta(t), and how its behavior determines convergence speed. The authors provide tight, unified characterizations of the convergence rate as a function of that coefficient. This connects a controllable part of the method to its mathematical performance and gives insight into the accelerated O(1/k^2) rate associated with anchor acceleration.

The paper then uses these continuous-time insights to develop an adaptive method, moving from explanation toward algorithm design. Its effectiveness is supported by both theoretical analysis and experiments. The contribution is therefore twofold: a more systematic account of how the anchor coefficient affects acceleration, and an adaptive approach motivated by that account.
summary.tldr: Continuous-time analysis explains how the anchor coefficient controls acceleration and motivates an adaptive optimization method.

title: Continuous-time Analysis of Anchor Acceleration

abstract: We revisit the classical problem of designing Budget-Feasible Mechanisms (BFMs) for submodular valuation functions, which has been extensively studied since the seminal paper of Singer [FOCS’10] due to its wide applications in crowdsourcing and social marketing. We propose TripleEagle, a novel algorithmic framework for designing BFMs, based on which we present several simple yet effective BFMs thatachieve better approximation ratios than the state-of-the-art work for both monotone and non-monotone submodular valuation functions. Moreover, our BFMs are the first in the literature to achieve linear complexities while ensuring obvious strategyproofness, making them more practical than the previous BFMs. We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the empirical performance of our BFMs, and the experimental results strongly demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Budget-feasible mechanisms aim to obtain valuable outcomes while respecting a spending limit and accounting for participants’ incentives. This paper revisits their design for submodular valuation functions, a setting relevant to crowdsourcing and social marketing. It introduces TripleEagle, a framework for constructing mechanisms that combine solution quality with computational and strategic simplicity.

The resulting mechanisms improve approximation ratios over the state of the art for both monotone and non-monotone submodular valuations. These ratios describe how closely a mechanism’s outcome can approximate the optimal value. Covering both cases addresses settings where adding more selected participants or items can only help, as well as settings where it need not.

The authors also report the first mechanisms in this literature that combine linear computational complexity with obvious strategyproofness. This pairs efficient computation with a strong incentive property intended to make truthful participation straightforward. Extensive experiments support the mechanisms’ efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution therefore addresses several requirements for practical use together, rather than measuring progress solely through approximation quality.
summary.tldr: TripleEagle improves approximation guarantees for budget-feasible mechanisms while combining linear complexity with obvious strategyproofness.

title: Triple Eagle: Simple, Fast and Practical Budget-Feasible Mechanisms

abstract: We propose a novel multimodal video benchmark - the Perception Test - to evaluate the perception and reasoning skills of pre-trained multimodal models (e.g. Flamingo, BEiT-3, or GPT-4). Compared to existing benchmarks that focus on computational tasks (e.g. classification, detection or tracking), the Perception Test focuses on skills (Memory, Abstraction, Physics, Semantics) and types of reasoning (descriptive, explanatory, predictive, counterfactual) across video, audio, and text modalities, to provide a comprehensive and efficient evaluation tool. The benchmark probes pre-trained models for their transfer capabilities, in a zero-shot / few-shot or limited finetuning regime. For these purposes, the Perception Test introduces 11.6k real-world videos, 23s average length, designed to show perceptually interesting situations, filmed by around 100 participants worldwide. The videos are densely annotated with six types of labels (multiple-choice and grounded video question-answers, object and point tracks, temporal action and sound segments), enabling both language and non-language evaluations. The fine-tuning and validation splits of the benchmark are publicly available (CC-BY license), in addition to a challenge server with a held-out test split. Human baseline results compared to state-of-the-art video QA models show a significant gap in performance (91.4% vs 45.8%), suggesting that there is significant room for improvement in multimodal video understanding.Dataset, baselines code, and challenge server are available at https://github.com/deepmind/perception_test

paragraphs: The Perception Test evaluates what pretrained multimodal models understand about events in videos. It organises evaluation around memory, abstraction, physics, and semantics, together with descriptive, explanatory, predictive, and counterfactual reasoning. This skill-oriented design aims to reveal abilities that broad task labels such as classification or tracking may not describe precisely.

The benchmark contains 11,600 real-world videos averaging 23 seconds, filmed by roughly 100 participants worldwide. Six kinds of annotation support both language and non-language evaluation, including questions and answers, object and point tracks, and timed action and sound segments. Evaluations probe transfer with no examples, a few examples, or limited fine-tuning across video, audio, and text.

The reported comparison finds a substantial performance gap between humans and leading video question-answering models: 91.4% versus 45.8%. This indicates considerable room for improvement on the benchmark's perceptual and reasoning demands. Public fine-tuning and validation data, together with a held-out test server, provide infrastructure for examining those capabilities consistently.
summary.tldr: The Perception Test probes multimodal video understanding through explicit skills and reasoning types, revealing a large reported gap between models and humans.

title: Perception Test: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Video Models

abstract: While 3D human body modeling has received much attention in computer vision, modeling the acoustic equivalent, i.e. modeling 3D spatial audio produced by body motion and speech, has fallen short in the community. To close this gap, we present a model that can generate accurate 3D spatial audio for full human bodies. The system consumes, as input, audio signals from headset microphones and body pose, and produces, as output, a 3D sound field surrounding the transmitter's body, from which spatial audio can be rendered at any arbitrary position in the 3D space. We collect a first-of-its-kind multimodal dataset of human bodies, recorded with multiple cameras and a spherical array of 345 microphones. In an empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that our model can produce accurate body-induced sound fields when trained with a suitable loss. Dataset and code are available online.

paragraphs: A three-dimensional model of a person can describe their visible body while leaving out how their speech and movements sound from different locations. This paper addresses that acoustic counterpart. It presents a model for generating the three-dimensional sound field produced by a full human body.

The system takes headset-microphone audio and body pose as inputs. Its output is a sound field surrounding the person, from which spatial audio can be rendered at an arbitrary position in three-dimensional space. This connects a relatively localized audio recording with information about the body's configuration to model sound throughout the surrounding space.

To support this task, the authors collect a multimodal dataset using multiple cameras and a spherical array of 345 microphones. Their empirical evaluation shows that the model can accurately reproduce body-induced sound fields when trained with a suitable loss. The dataset and model together support studying human spatial audio, with the reported accuracy explicitly tied to the training objective used.
summary.tldr: The model combines headset audio and body pose to generate human sound fields that support spatial audio rendering at arbitrary locations.

title: Sounding Bodies: Modeling 3D Spatial Sound of Humans Using Body Pose and Audio

abstract: Designing effective policies for the online 3D bin packing problem (3D-BPP) has been a long-standing challenge, primarily due to the unpredictable nature of incoming box sequences and stringent physical constraints. While current deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods for online 3D-BPP have shown promising results in optimizing average performance over an underlying box sequence distribution, they often fail in real-world settings where some worst-case scenarios can materialize. Standard robust DRL algorithms tend to overly prioritize optimizing the worst-case performance at the expense of performance under normal problem instance distribution. To address these issues, we first introduce a permutation-based attacker to investigate the practical robustness of both DRL-based and heuristic methods proposed for solving online 3D-BPP. Then, we propose an adjustable robust reinforcement learning (AR2L) framework that allows efficient adjustment of robustness weights to achieve the desired balance of the policy's performance in average and worst-case environments. Specifically, we formulate the objective function as a weighted sum of expected and worst-case returns, and derive the lower performance bound by relating to the return under a mixture dynamics. To realize this lower bound, we adopt an iterative procedure that searches for the associated mixture dynamics and improves the corresponding policy. We integrate this procedure into two popular robust adversarial algorithms to develop the exact and approximate AR2L algorithms. Experiments demonstrate that AR2L is versatile in the sense that it improves policy robustness while maintaining an acceptable level of performance for the nominal case.

paragraphs: Online three-dimensional bin packing requires placing arriving boxes while respecting physical constraints and facing uncertainty about future arrivals. A policy that performs well on typical sequences can struggle on unfavorable ones. Conversely, optimizing primarily for the worst case can sacrifice too much performance under normal conditions.

The paper introduces a permutation-based attacker to examine the robustness of learned and heuristic packing methods. It then proposes adjustable robust reinforcement learning, or AR2L. Its objective combines expected return and worst-case return with adjustable weights, making the desired balance explicit. The analysis derives a lower performance bound by relating this objective to returns under a mixture of dynamics.

The learning procedure alternates between finding the relevant mixture dynamics and improving the policy. Incorporating this procedure into two robust adversarial algorithms yields exact and approximate versions of AR2L. Experiments show improved robustness while retaining acceptable nominal performance. The result supports adjustable tradeoffs between ordinary and difficult packing sequences, rather than a single fixed emphasis on worst-case behavior.
summary.tldr: AR2L makes the tradeoff between average and worst-case packing performance adjustable and empirically improves robustness while retaining acceptable nominal performance.

title: Adjustable Robust Reinforcement Learning for Online 3D Bin Packing

abstract: We present HUME, a simple model-agnostic framework for inferring human labeling of a given dataset without any external supervision. The key insight behind our approach is that classes defined by many human labelings are linearly separable regardless of the representation space used to represent a dataset. HUME utilizes this insight to guide the search over all possible labelings of a dataset to discover an underlying human labeling. We show that the proposed optimization objective is strikingly well-correlated with the ground truth labeling of the dataset. In effect, we only train linear classifiers on top of pretrained representations that remain fixed during training, making our framework compatible with any large pretrained and self-supervised model. Despite its simplicity, HUME outperforms a supervised linear classifier on top of self-supervised representations on the STL-10 dataset by a large margin and achieves comparable performance on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Compared to the existing unsupervised baselines, HUME achieves state-of-the-art performance on four benchmark image classification datasets including the large-scale ImageNet-1000 dataset. Altogether, our work provides a fundamentally new view to tackle unsupervised learning by searching for consistent labelings between different representation spaces.

paragraphs: HUME approaches unsupervised learning as a search for labels that agree across different representations of the same dataset. Its motivating observation is that many human-defined categories can be separated by linear classifiers in different representation spaces. A candidate labeling that remains easy to separate across spaces can therefore provide evidence of an underlying human labeling.

The framework keeps pretrained representations fixed and trains only linear classifiers on top of them. Its objective guides the search over candidate labelings without external supervision for that search. The authors find that the objective correlates strongly with the dataset's ground-truth labeling. Because it operates on fixed representations, the framework is compatible with large pretrained and self-supervised models.

It also reports state-of-the-art unsupervised results on four image classification benchmarks, including ImageNet-1000. These findings support consistency across representation spaces as a useful signal for discovering categories, with the reported supervised comparisons tied to their particular datasets and classifier setup.
summary.tldr: HUME discovers labels without external supervision by searching for labelings that linear classifiers can consistently recover across fixed representation spaces.

title: The Pursuit of Human Labeling: A New Perspective on Unsupervised Learning

abstract: Machine learning (ML) models are only as good as the data they are trained on. But recent studies have found datasets widely used to train and evaluate ML models, e.g. _ImageNet_, to have pervasive labeling errors. Erroneous labels on the train set hurt ML models' ability to generalize, and they impact evaluation and model selection using the test set. Consequently, learning in the presence of labeling errors is an active area of research, yet this field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate these methods. Most of these methods are evaluated on a few computer vision datasets with significant variance in the experimental protocols. With such a large pool of methods and inconsistent evaluation, it is also unclear how ML practitioners can choose the right models to assess label quality in their data. To this end, we propose a benchmarking environment _AQuA_ to rigorously evaluate methods that enable machine learning in the presence of label noise. We also introduce a design space to delineate concrete design choices of label error detection models. We hope that our proposed design space and benchmark enable practitioners to choose the right tools to improve their label quality and that our benchmark enables objective and rigorous evaluation of machine learning tools facing mislabeled data.

paragraphs: Incorrect labels create two distinct problems for machine learning: they can impair learning from training data, and they can distort evaluation and model selection when they appear in test data. The paper responds to evidence that labeling errors are widespread even in commonly used datasets. Its focus is how to evaluate tools that detect or otherwise handle those errors.

The authors introduce AQuA, a benchmarking environment for methods used in the presence of label noise. The motivation is that existing evaluations often cover only a few computer vision datasets and use substantially different experimental protocols. Those differences make it difficult to tell whether apparent advantages reflect the methods themselves or the circumstances under which they were tested.

Alongside the benchmark, the paper proposes a design space that identifies concrete choices in label error detection models. Together, these contributions aim to make comparisons more rigorous and help practitioners select suitable tools. The abstract presents those benefits as intended outcomes; it does not establish a universally best label assessment method.
summary.tldr: AQuA provides a benchmark and design framework intended to make label quality assessment methods easier to compare and select.

title: AQuA: A Benchmarking Tool for Label Quality Assessment

abstract: Accurate environment dynamics modeling is crucial for obtaining effective state representations in visual reinforcement learning (RL) applications. However, when facing multiple input modalities, existing dynamics modeling methods (e.g., DeepMDP) usually stumble in addressing the complex and volatile relationship between different modalities. In this paper, we study the problem of efficient dynamics modeling for multi-modal visual RL. We find that under the existence of modality heterogeneity, modality-correlated and distinct features are equally important but play different roles in reflecting the evolution of environmental dynamics. Motivated by this fact, we propose Dissected Dynamics Modeling (DDM), a novel multi-modal dynamics modeling method for visual RL. Unlike existing methods, DDM explicitly distinguishes consistent and inconsistent information across modalities and treats them separately with a divide-and-conquer strategy. This is done by dispatching the features carrying different information into distinct dynamics modeling pathways, which naturally form a series of implicit regularizations along the learning trajectories. In addition, a reward predictive function is further introduced to filter task-irrelevant information in both modality-consistent and inconsistent features, ensuring information integrity while avoiding potential distractions. Extensive experiments show that DDM consistently achieves competitive performance in challenging multi-modal visual environments.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning needs representations that capture how an environment changes. When an agent receives multiple input modalities, those inputs can contain both shared information and meaningful differences. The paper finds that, when modalities are heterogeneous, correlated and distinct features are equally important but play different roles in describing environmental dynamics.

Dissected Dynamics Modeling, or DDM, explicitly separates information that is consistent across modalities from information that is inconsistent. It routes these features through different dynamics-modeling pathways instead of treating their relationships uniformly. This separation introduces implicit regularization during learning. A reward-prediction function further filters out task-irrelevant information from both categories of features, preserving useful distinctions while reducing distractions.

Experiments in challenging multimodal visual environments show consistently competitive performance. The contribution is a way to organize representation learning around the different roles of shared and modality-specific information. Its findings support retaining meaningful differences between inputs while also modeling their common content, with task relevance assessed through reward prediction rather than through cross-modal agreement alone.
summary.tldr: DDM separates shared and differing multimodal features into dynamics pathways and uses reward prediction to retain task-relevant information.

title: Seek Commonality but Preserve Differences: Dissected Dynamics Modeling for Multi-modal Visual RL

abstract: Mathematical reasoning is an important capability of large language models~(LLMs) for real-world applications.To enhance this capability, existing work either collects large-scale math-related texts for pre-training, or relies on stronger LLMs (\eg GPT-4) to synthesize massive math problems. Both types of work generally lead to large costs in training or synthesis.To reduce the cost, based on open-source available texts, we propose an efficient way that trains a small LLM for math problem synthesis, to efficiently generate sufficient high-quality pre-training data.To achieve it, we create a dataset using GPT-4 to distill its data synthesis capability into the small LLM.Concretely, we craft a set of prompts based on human education stages to guide GPT-4, to synthesize problems covering diverse math knowledge and difficulty levels.Besides, we adopt the gradient-based influence estimation method to select the most valuable math-related texts.The both are fed into GPT-4 for creating the knowledge distillation dataset to train the small LLM.We leverage it to synthesize 6 million math problems for pre-training our JiuZhang3.0 model. The whole process only needs to invoke GPT-4 API 9.3k times and use 4.6B data for training.Experimental results have shown that JiuZhang3.0 achieves state-of-the-art performance on several mathematical reasoning datasets, under both natural language reasoning and tool manipulation settings.Our code and data will be publicly released in \url{https://github.com/RUCAIBox/JiuZhang3.0}.

paragraphs: JiuZhang3.0 tackles the expense of obtaining large amounts of mathematical training material. Existing approaches can require extensive pretraining text or large-scale problem generation by a stronger language model. This paper trains a smaller language model to synthesize mathematical problems, using a limited amount of GPT-4-generated supervision to transfer the data-generation capability.

The supervision combines prompts organized around human educational stages with selected mathematical texts. The prompts encourage coverage of varied knowledge and difficulty levels, while gradient-based influence estimation identifies valuable source texts. GPT-4 uses these inputs to create a distillation dataset for the smaller synthesis model. That model then generates six million problems for pretraining JiuZhang3.0.

The reported process uses 9.3 thousand GPT-4 API calls and 4.6B of training data. JiuZhang3.0 achieves state-of-the-art results on several mathematical reasoning datasets in both natural-language reasoning and tool-manipulation settings. The findings support concentrating stronger-model assistance on training a reusable data generator, allowing the smaller model to carry out the subsequent large-scale synthesis.
summary.tldr: JiuZhang3.0 transfers mathematical problem synthesis from GPT-4 to a smaller model to generate large-scale training data efficiently.

title: JiuZhang3.0: Efficiently Improving Mathematical Reasoning by Training Small Data Synthesis Models

abstract: Rubinfeld \& Vasilyan recently introduced the framework of *testable learning* as an extension of the classical agnostic model. It relaxes distributional assumptions which are difficult to verify by conditions that can be checked efficiently by a *tester*. The tester has to accept whenever the data truly satisfies the original assumptions, and the learner has to succeed whenever the tester accepts. We focus on the setting where the tester has to accept standard Gaussian data. There, it is known that basic concept classes such as halfspaces can be learned testably with the same time complexity as in the (distribution-specific) agnostic model. In this work, we ask whether there is a price to pay for testably learning more complex concept classes. In particular, we consider polynomial threshold functions (PTFs), which naturally generalize halfspaces. We show that PTFs of arbitrary constant degree can be testably learned up to excess error $\varepsilon > 0$ in time $n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$. This qualitatively matches the best known guarantees in the agnostic model. Our results build on a connection between testable learning and *fooling*. In particular, we show that distributions that approximately match at least $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ moments of the standard Gaussian fool constant-degree PTFs (up to error $\varepsilon$). As a secondary result, we prove that a direct approach to show testable learning (without fooling), which was successfully used for halfspaces, cannot work for PTFs.

The tester must accept data satisfying the original assumptions, and learning must succeed whenever it accepts. This paper studies testers that must accept standard Gaussian data, focusing on polynomial threshold functions of arbitrary constant degree.

The authors show that these functions can be learned testably to excess error epsilon in time n raised to a polynomial in 1/epsilon. This qualitatively matches the best known guarantees in the distribution-specific agnostic setting. The result extends the reach of testable learning beyond simpler classes such as halfspaces without introducing a qualitatively worse runtime guarantee.

The proof uses a connection to fooling: distributions that approximately match sufficiently many Gaussian moments behave similarly to the Gaussian when evaluated by constant-degree polynomial threshold functions. The required moment count is polynomial in 1/epsilon. The authors also establish that a direct proof approach previously successful for halfspaces cannot work for these functions, clarifying why their alternative route through fooling is useful.
summary.tldr: Constant-degree polynomial threshold functions admit testable learning guarantees that qualitatively match known agnostic learning runtimes.

title: Testably Learning Polynomial Threshold Functions

abstract: We consider the problem of online multiclass U-calibration, where a forecaster aims to make sequential distributional predictions over $K$ classes with low U-calibration error, that is, low regret with respect to all bounded proper losses simultaneously. Kleinberg et al. (2023) developed an algorithm with U-calibration error $\mathcal{O}(K\sqrt{T})$ after $T$ rounds and raised the open question of what the optimal bound is. We resolve this question by showing that the optimal U-calibration error is $\Theta(\sqrt{KT})$ --- we start with a simple observation that the Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader algorithm of Daskalakis and Syrgkanis (2016) achieves this upper bound, followed by a matching lower bound constructed with a specific proper loss (which, as a side result, also proves the optimality of the algorithm of Daskalakis and Syrgkanis (2016) in the context of online learning against an adversary with finite choices). We also strengthen our results under natural assumptions on the loss functions, including $\Theta(\log T)$ U-calibration error for Lipschitz proper losses, $\mathcal{O}(\log T)$ U-calibration error for a certain class of decomposable proper losses, U-calibration error bounds for proper losses with a low covering number, and others.

We resolve this question by showing that the optimal U-calibration error is $\Theta(\sqrt{KT})$ --- we start with a simple observation that the Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader algorithm of Daskalakis and Syrgkanis (2016) achieves this upper bound, followed by a matching lower bound constructed with a specific proper loss (which, as a side result, also proves the optimality of the algorithm of Daskalakis and Syrgkanis (2016) in the context of online learning against an adversary with finite choices). paragraphs: An online forecaster repeatedly predicts probabilities over K possible classes. U-calibration asks whether those predictions have low regret across all bounded proper losses simultaneously, rather than under just one scoring rule. This paper determines the optimal growth rate of that error over T prediction rounds.

Earlier work provided a bound of order K times the square root of T. The authors show that Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader achieves the smaller order square root of KT. A matching lower bound, built using a particular proper loss, establishes that this dependence is optimal. The lower-bound construction also proves optimality of the algorithm in a related online-learning setting with an adversary having finitely many choices.

Additional assumptions on the loss functions allow stronger guarantees. For Lipschitz proper losses, the paper establishes an optimal logarithmic dependence on T; it also gives a logarithmic upper bound for a specified class of decomposable proper losses. Further bounds use low covering numbers. These results distinguish the general worst-case rate from improvements available when the loss family has additional structure.
summary.tldr: The paper proves the optimal multiclass U-calibration rate is proportional to √(KT), with stronger bounds for structured loss families.

title: Optimal Multiclass U-Calibration Error and Beyond

abstract: Latent-based image generative models, such as Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) and Mask Image Models (MIMs), have achieved notable success in image generation tasks. These models typically leverage reconstructive autoencoders like VQGAN or VAE to encode pixels into a more compact latent space and learn the data distribution in the latent space instead of directly from pixels. However, this practice raises a pertinent question: Is it truly the optimal choice? In response, we begin with an intriguing observation: despite sharing the same latent space, autoregressive models significantly lag behind LDMs and MIMs in image generation. This finding contrasts sharply with the field of NLP, where the autoregressive model GPT has established a commanding presence. To address this discrepancy, we introduce a unified perspective on the relationship between latent space and generative models, emphasizing the stability of latent space in image generative modeling. Furthermore, we propose a simple but effective discrete image tokenizer to stabilize the latent space for image generative modeling by applying K-Means on the latent features of self-supervised learning models. Experimental results show that image autoregressive modeling with our tokenizer (DiGIT) benefits both image understanding and image generation with the next token prediction principle, which is inherently straightforward for GPT models but challenging for other generative models. Remarkably, for the first time, a GPT-style autoregressive model for images outperforms LDMs, which also exhibits substantial improvement akin to GPT when scaling up model size. Our findings underscore the potential of an optimized latent space and the integration of discrete tokenization in advancing the capabilities of image generative models. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/DAMO-NLP-SG/DiGIT}.

paragraphs: Image generators often work in a compact latent space produced by an autoencoder instead of directly modeling pixels. Its starting observation is that autoregressive models trail diffusion and masked-image models even when they use the same latent space.

The authors propose a unified view emphasizing latent-space stability. Their tokenizer, DiGIT, applies K-Means clustering to features from self-supervised learning models, producing discrete image tokens. This offers a different representation for learning images through next-token prediction, the basic training principle used by GPT-style models.

Experiments show benefits for both image understanding and generation using this approach. The authors report a GPT-style image autoregressive model that outperforms latent diffusion models in their evaluation and improves substantially as model size increases. These findings support the potential of better latent representations and discrete tokenization to strengthen autoregressive image modeling. The contribution links the choice of representation to the effectiveness of the generative training method.
summary.tldr: DiGIT clusters self-supervised image features into discrete tokens, improving autoregressive image understanding and generation through a more stable latent representation.

title: Stabilize the Latent Space for Image Autoregressive Modeling: A Unified Perspective

abstract: Recent work has shown the immense potential of synthetically generated datasets for training large language models (LLMs), especially for acquiring targeted skills. Current large-scale math instruction tuning datasets such as MetaMathQA (Yu et al., 2024) and MAmmoTH (Yue et al., 2024) are constructed using outputs from closed-source LLMs with commercially restrictive licenses. A key reason limiting the use of open-source LLMs in these data generation pipelines has been the wide gap between the mathematical skills of the best closed-source LLMs, such as GPT-4, and the best open-source LLMs. Building on the recent progress in open-source LLMs, our proposed prompting novelty, and some brute-force scaling, we construct OpenMathInstruct-1, a math instruction tuning dataset with 1.8M problem-solution pairs. The dataset is constructed by synthesizing code-interpreter solutions for GSM8K and MATH, two popular math reasoning benchmarks, using the recently released and permissively licensed Mixtral model. Our best model, OpenMath-CodeLlama-70B, trained on a subset of OpenMathInstruct-1, achieves a score of 84.6% on GSM8K and 50.7% on MATH, which is competitive with the best gpt-distilled models. We will release our code, models, and the OpenMathInstruct-1 dataset under a commercially permissive license.

OpenMathInstruct-1 explores an alternative built with a permissively licensed model. The challenge is producing useful mathematical supervision despite the skill gap between leading closed and open models described in the paper.

The authors combine prompting innovations with large-scale generation using Mixtral. They synthesize solutions involving a code interpreter for problems from GSM8K and MATH, producing 1.8 million problem–solution pairs. This creates a substantial instruction-tuning resource through an open-model generation pipeline and makes the resulting mathematical solutions available as training material.

Their strongest reported model, OpenMath-CodeLlama-70B, is trained on a subset of the dataset and scores 84.6% on GSM8K and 50.7% on MATH. These results are competitive with the best GPT-distilled models in the paper's comparison. The authors state that code, models, and data will be released under a commercially permissive license, connecting the performance contribution with broader reuse of the training pipeline and its outputs.
summary.tldr: OpenMathInstruct-1 uses Mixtral to create 1.8 million math training pairs, supporting models competitive with leading GPT-distilled alternatives.

title: OpenMathInstruct-1: A 1.8 Million Math Instruction Tuning Dataset

abstract: This paper advances temporal reasoning within dynamically changing high-dimensional noisy observations, focusing on a latent space that characterizes the nonlinear dynamics of objects in their environment. We introduce the *Gated Inference Network* (GIN), an efficient approximate Bayesian inference algorithm for state space models (SSMs) with nonlinear state transitions and emissions. GIN disentangles two latent representations: one representing the object derived from a nonlinear mapping model, and another representing the latent state describing its dynamics. This disentanglement enables direct state estimation and missing data imputation as the world evolves. To infer the latent state, we utilize a deep extended Kalman filter (EKF) approach that integrates a novel compact RNN structure to compute both the Kalman Gain (KG) and smoothing gain (SG), completing the data flow. This design results in a computational cost per step that is linearly faster than EKF but introduces issues such as the exploding gradient problem. To mitigate the exploding gradients caused by the compact RNN structure in our model, we propose a specialized learning method that ensures stable training and inference. The model is then trained end-to-end on videos depicting a diverse range of simulated and real-world physical systems, and outperforms its ounterparts —RNNs, autoregressive models, and variational approaches— in state estimation and missing data imputation tasks.
