The findings identify a gap in their ability to connect fine-grained structure with molecular properties. The authors propose the dataset construction methodology as a foundation for further question–answer generation, with the potential to support more interpretable, structure-aware models for chemistry.
summary.tldr: FGBench provides 625,000 functional-group reasoning problems and finds that current language models struggle with fine-grained molecular property reasoning.

title: FGBench: A Dataset and Benchmark for Molecular Property Reasoning at Functional Group-Level in Large Language Models

abstract: Graph-based learned simulators have emerged as a promising approach for simulating physical systems on unstructured meshes, offering speed and generalization across diverse geometries. However, they often struggle with capturing global phenomena, such as bending or long-range correlations usually occurring in solid mechanics, and suffer from error accumulation over long rollouts due to their reliance on local message passing and direct next-step prediction. We address these limitations by introducing the Rolling Diffusion-Batched Inference Network (ROBIN), a novel learned simulator that integrates two key innovations: (i) Rolling Diffusion-Batched Inference (ROBI), a parallelized inference scheme that amortizes the cost of diffusion-based refinement across physical time steps by overlapping denoising steps across a temporal window. (ii) A Hierarchical Graph Neural Network built on algebraic multigrid coarsening, enabling multiscale message passing across different mesh resolutions. This architecture, implemented via Algebraic-hierarchical Message Passing Networks, captures both fine-scale local dynamics and global structural effects critical for phenomena like beam bending or multi-body contact. We validate ROBIN on challenging 2D and 3D solid mechanics benchmarks involving geometric, material, and contact nonlinearities. ROBIN achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on all tasks, substantially outperforming existing next-step learned simulators while reducing inference time by up to an order of magnitude compared to standard diffusion simulators.

paragraphs: Learned simulators operating on mesh graphs can struggle with effects that span a whole structure, such as bending. Local message passing makes these relationships difficult to capture, while repeated next-step predictions can accumulate errors. ROBIN addresses these problems by combining a hierarchical graph network with diffusion-based refinement.

Its graph hierarchy uses algebraic multigrid coarsening to pass information across multiple mesh resolutions. This lets the model represent both local dynamics and broader structural effects, including those involved in bending and contact. These findings support combining multiscale information exchange with temporally overlapping refinement for accurate, more efficient learned simulation.
summary.tldr: ROBIN combines multiscale graph processing with overlapping diffusion refinement to improve nonlinear solid simulation accuracy and inference speed.

title: Diffusion-Based Hierarchical Graph Neural Networks for Simulating Nonlinear Solid Mechanics

abstract: Despite their proficiency in various language tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with combinatorial problems like Satisfiability, Traveling Salesman Problem, or even basic arithmetic. We address this gap through a novel approach for solving problems in the class NP. We focus on the paradigmatic task of Sudoku and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy (99\%) compared to prior neuro-symbolic approaches. Unlike prior work that used custom architectures, our method employs a vanilla decoder-only Transformer (GPT-2) without external tools or function calling. Our method integrates imitation learning of simple Sudoku rules with an explicit Depth-First Search (DFS) exploration strategy involving informed guessing and backtracking. Moving beyond imitation learning, we seek to minimize the number of guesses until reaching a solution. We provide a rigorous analysis of this setup by formalizing its connection to a contextual variant of $\textit{Min-Sum Set Cover}$, a well-studied problem in algorithms and stochastic optimization.

Sudoku serves as the main task, allowing the authors to combine simple logical rules with explicit search. Their model is a vanilla decoder-only GPT-2, operating without external tools, function calls, or a custom problem-specific architecture.

Training combines imitation of basic Sudoku rules with depth-first search. The search process includes informed guesses and backtracking, so a failed choice can be revisited instead of forcing the model to continue down an unproductive path. The authors also move beyond imitating demonstrations by targeting the number of guesses required to reach a solution.

The method achieves 99% accuracy, which the paper reports as state of the art relative to prior neuro-symbolic approaches. For theoretical analysis, the authors connect the guess-minimization objective to a contextual version of Min-Sum Set Cover. This gives a formal framework for studying search efficiency. Although the broader motivation concerns problems in NP, the stated experimental achievement is specifically demonstrated through Sudoku.
summary.tldr: A standard GPT-2 learns Sudoku rules, guessing, and backtracking, reaching 99% accuracy while targeting more efficient search.

title: Teaching Transformers to Solve Combinatorial Problems through Efficient Trial & Error

abstract: The increasing use of generative ML foundation models for image restoration tasks such as super-resolution calls for robust and interpretable uncertainty quantification methods. We address this need by presenting a novel approach based on conformal prediction techniques to create a `confidence mask' capable of reliably and intuitively communicating where the generated image can be trusted. Our method is adaptable to any black-box generative model, including those locked behind an opaque API, requires only easily attainable data for calibration, and is highly customizable via the choice of a local image similarity metric. We prove strong theoretical guarantees for our method that span fidelity error control (according to our local image similarity metric), reconstruction quality, and robustness in the face of data leakage. Finally, we empirically evaluate these results and establish our method's solid performance.

paragraphs: This paper addresses uncertainty in image super-resolution produced by generative models. Its proposed output is a confidence mask that communicates where the restored image can be trusted. The aim is to make uncertainty local and interpretable, so confidence is tied to particular image regions rather than treated only as an overall property.

The method uses conformal prediction and calibration data to construct the mask. It can work with any black-box generative model, including one accessible only through an opaque API. Users can customize it through a local image similarity metric, which determines how fidelity is assessed. This makes the meaning of the mask depend explicitly on the chosen comparison criterion.

The authors prove guarantees covering fidelity error control under that metric, reconstruction quality, and robustness to data leakage. They also evaluate the method empirically and report solid performance. The contribution is a way to attach theoretically supported uncertainty information to generated restorations without needing access to the underlying model’s internal implementation.
summary.tldr: Conformal prediction produces local confidence masks for black-box super-resolution models, with guarantees tied to a chosen image similarity metric.

title: Image Super-Resolution with Guarantees via Conformalized Generative Models

abstract: We propose **GAM-Agent**, a game-theoretic multi-agent framework for enhancing vision-language reasoning. Unlike prior single-agent or monolithic models, GAM-Agent formulates the reasoning process as a non-zero-sum game between base agents—each specializing in visual perception subtasks—and a critical agent that verifies logic consistency and factual correctness. Agents communicate via structured claims, evidence, and uncertainty estimates. The framework introduces an uncertainty-aware controller to dynamically adjust agent collaboration, triggering multi-round debates when disagreement or ambiguity is detected. This process yields more robust and interpretable predictions. Experiments on four challenging benchmarks—MMMU, MMBench, MVBench, and V*Bench—demonstrate that GAM-Agent significantly improves performance across various VLM backbones. Notably, GAM-Agent boosts the accuracy of small-to-mid scale models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-14B) by 5–6\%, and still enhances strong models like GPT-4o by up to 2–3\%. Our approach is modular, scalable, and generalizable, offering a path toward reliable and explainable multi-agent multimodal reasoning.

paragraphs: GAM-Agent tackles visual reasoning by coordinating several specialized agents. The framework describes their interaction as a non-zero-sum game, allowing the reasoning process to combine different contributions rather than relying on one model's uninterrupted judgment.

An uncertainty-aware controller adjusts the collaboration and initiates additional debate rounds when agents disagree or the evidence is ambiguous. This makes disagreement an explicit signal for further reasoning. The structured exchanges also make the route to a prediction more interpretable.

title: GAM-Agent: Game-Theoretic and Uncertainty-Aware Collaboration for Complex Visual Reasoning

abstract: Training Reinforcement Learning (RL) controllers in simulation offers cost-efficiency and safety advantages. However, the resultant policies often suffer significant performance degradation during real-world deployment due to the reality gap. Previous works like System Identification (Sys-Id) have attempted to bridge this discrepancy by improving simulator fidelity, but encounter challenges including the collapse of high-dimensional parameter identification, low identification accuracy, and unstable convergence dynamics. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Sys-Id framework that combines Diffusion Evolution with Adversarial Learning (DEAL) to iteratively infer physical parameters with limited real-world data, which makes the state transitions between simulation and reality as similar as possible. Specifically, our method iteratively refines physical parameters through a dual mechanism: a discriminator network evaluates the similarity of state transitions between parameterized simulations and target environment as fitness guidance, while diffusion evolution adaptively modulates noise prediction and denoising processes to optimize parameter distributions. We validate DEAL in both simulated and real-world environments. Compared to baseline methods, DEAL demonstrates state-of-the-art stability and identification accuracy in high-dimensional parameter identification tasks, and significantly enhances sim-to-real transfer performance while requiring minimal real-world data.

paragraphs: Controllers trained with reinforcement learning in simulation can lose substantial performance when deployed in the real world. DEAL addresses this reality gap through system identification: estimating physical parameters so that the simulator better matches the target environment. The paper focuses on difficulties that arise when many parameters must be identified, including inaccurate estimates and unstable convergence.

DEAL combines two mechanisms in an iterative process using limited real-world data. A discriminator evaluates how similar simulated state transitions are to transitions in the target environment, supplying fitness guidance. Diffusion evolution then adjusts noise prediction and denoising to improve the distribution of candidate physical parameters. These components jointly pursue closer agreement between simulated and target dynamics.

The authors evaluate the framework in both simulated and real-world environments. The stated findings connect better parameter estimation with better controller deployment while emphasizing that the method requires only a small amount of real-world data.
summary.tldr: DEAL combines adversarial feedback with diffusion evolution to estimate simulator parameters from limited real data and improve sim-to-real controller transfer.

title: DEAL: Diffusion Evolution Adversarial Learning for Sim-to-Real Transfer

abstract: The explosive growth of generative video models has amplified the demand for reliable copyright preservation of AI-generated content. Despite its popularity in image synthesis, invisible generative watermarking remains largely underexplored in video generation. To address this gap, we propose Safe-Sora, the first framework to embed graphical watermarks directly into the video generation process. Motivated by the observation that watermarking performance is closely tied to the visual similarity between the watermark and cover content, we introduce a hierarchical coarse-to-fine adaptive matching mechanism. Specifically, the watermark image is divided into patches, each assigned to the most visually similar video frame, and further localized to the optimal spatial region for seamless embedding. To enable spatiotemporal fusion of watermark patches across video frames, we develop a 3D wavelet transform-enhanced Mamba architecture with a novel scanning strategy, effectively modeling long-range dependencies during watermark embedding and retrieval. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to apply state space models to watermarking, opening new avenues for efficient and robust watermark protection. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Safe-Sora achieves state-of-the- art performance in terms of video quality, watermark fidelity, and robustness, which is largely attributed to our proposals. Code and additional supporting materials are provided in the supplementary.

title: Safe-Sora: Safe Text-to-Video Generation via Graphical Watermarking

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated broad applications but suffer from issues like hallucinations, erroneous outputs and outdated knowledge. Model editing emerges as an effective solution to refine knowledge in LLMs, yet existing methods typically depend on structured knowledge representations. However, real-world knowledge is primarily embedded within complex, unstructured text. Existing structured knowledge editing approaches face significant challenges when handling the entangled and intricate knowledge present in unstructured text, resulting in issues such as representation ambiguity and editing conflicts. To address these challenges, we propose a Conflict-Aware Knowledge Editing in the Wild (CAKE) framework, the first framework explicitly designed for editing knowledge extracted from wild unstructured text. CAKE comprises two core components: a Semantic-augmented Graph Representation module and a Conflict-aware Knowledge Editing strategy. The Semantic-augmented Graph Representation module enhances knowledge encoding through structural disambiguation, relational enrichment, and semantic diversification. Meanwhile, the Conflict-aware Knowledge Editing strategy utilizes a graph-theoretic coloring algorithm to disentangle conflicted edits by allocating them to orthogonal parameter subspaces, thereby effectively mitigating editing conflicts. Experimental results on the AKEW benchmark demonstrate that CAKE significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a 15.43\% improvement in accuracy on llama3 editing tasks. Our framework successfully bridges the gap between unstructured textual knowledge and reliable model editing, enabling more robust and scalable updates for practical LLM applications.

Meanwhile, the Conflict-aware Knowledge Editing strategy utilizes a graph-theoretic coloring algorithm to disentangle conflicted edits by allocating them to orthogonal parameter subspaces, thereby effectively mitigating editing conflicts. Experimental results on the AKEW benchmark demonstrate that CAKE significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a 15.43\% improvement in accuracy on llama3 editing tasks. Our framework successfully bridges the gap between unstructured textual knowledge and reliable model editing, enabling more robust and scalable updates for practical LLM applications.

paragraphs: Updating a language model’s knowledge becomes difficult when the new information arrives as ordinary text containing intertwined relationships. Methods designed around structured facts can represent that information ambiguously, and multiple edits can interfere with one another. CAKE addresses these connected problems by pairing a richer knowledge representation with a strategy for separating conflicting updates.

Its representation module converts knowledge into a semantically augmented graph. Structural disambiguation clarifies how information is organized, relational enrichment adds connections, and semantic diversification broadens the encoding. The editing component then uses graph coloring to organize conflicting edits and assigns them to orthogonal parameter subspaces, separating the parts of the model used for those updates.

On the AKEW benchmark, CAKE outperforms existing methods and reports a 15.43% improvement in accuracy for llama3 editing tasks. The result supports treating knowledge extraction and edit interference as a joint problem. The framework’s practical contribution is a route from complex unstructured text to model updates that better preserve the intended knowledge relationships while reducing conflicts between edits.
summary.tldr: CAKE represents unstructured knowledge as an enriched graph and separates conflicting edits to improve language-model knowledge updates.

title: Conflict-Aware Knowledge Editing in the Wild: Semantic-Augmented Graph Representation for Unstructured Text

abstract: 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) aims to localize target objects within a 3D scene based on natural language queries. To alleviate the reliance on costly 3D training data, recent studies have explored zero-shot 3DVG by leveraging the extensive knowledge and powerful reasoning capabilities of pre-trained LLMs and VLMs. However, existing paradigms tend to emphasize either spatial (3D-based) or semantic (2D-based) understanding, limiting their effectiveness in complex real-world applications. In this work, we introduce SPAZER — a VLM-driven agent that combines both modalities in a progressive reasoning framework. It first holistically analyzes the scene and produces a 3D rendering from the optimal viewpoint. Based on this, anchor-guided candidate screening is conducted to perform a coarse-level localization of potential objects. Furthermore, leveraging retrieved relevant 2D camera images, 3D-2D joint decision-making is efficiently performed to determine the best-matching object. By bridging spatial and semantic reasoning neural streams, SPAZER achieves robust zero-shot grounding without training on 3D-labeled data. Extensive experiments on ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that SPAZER significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art zero-shot methods, achieving notable gains of $\mathbf{9.0\}$% and $\mathbf{10.9\}$% in accuracy.

The agent combines those sources through a progressive process driven by a vision-language model. It first analyzes the scene as a whole and creates a 3D rendering from a selected viewpoint. Anchor-guided screening then narrows the possible objects. Finally, relevant retrieved camera images contribute 2D evidence to a joint 3D–2D decision about the best match.

The findings support combining spatial and semantic reasoning for this task, with zero-shot referring to the absence of training on 3D-labeled grounding data.
summary.tldr: SPAZER progressively combines 3D scene structure and 2D imagery to improve object grounding without training on 3D-labeled data.

title: SPAZER: Spatial-Semantic Progressive Reasoning Agent for Zero-shot 3D Visual Grounding

abstract: We present and analyze a theoretical model designed to understand and explain the effectiveness of ontologies for learning multiple related tasks from primarily unlabeled data. We present both information-theoretic results as well as efficient algorithms. We show in this model that an ontology, which specifies the relationships between multiple outputs, in some cases is sufficient to completely learn a classification using a large unlabeled data source.
originalAbstract: We present and analyze a theoretical model designed to understand and explain the effectiveness of ontologies for learning multiple related tasks from primarily unlabeled data. We present both information-theoretic results as well as efficient algorithms. We show in this model that an ontology, which specifies the relationships between multiple outputs, in some cases is sufficient to completely learn a classification using a large unlabeled data source.

paragraphs: An ontology specifies relationships among multiple outputs. This paper asks how such relationships can help learn several related classification tasks when the available data are primarily unlabeled. The motivation is that learning tasks together may provide information through their connections, even when direct examples of the correct outputs are scarce.

The authors introduce a theoretical model for studying this effect. Their analysis includes information-theoretic results and efficient algorithms, addressing both what information can support learning and how that information can be used computationally. In this setting, the ontology supplies structure that a large unlabeled data source can help make useful.

The strongest stated result is conditional: in some cases within the model, the ontology and a large unlabeled source are sufficient to learn a classification completely. This gives a precise sense in which relationships among outputs can carry substantial learning information. The result explains a possible source of ontologies' effectiveness without asserting that every ontology makes labeled data unnecessary.
summary.tldr: A theoretical model shows that, in some cases, output relationships and abundant unlabeled data suffice to learn a classification completely.

title: Exploiting Ontology Structures and Unlabeled Data for Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel scheme for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) retrieval based on dictionary learning and sparse coding. Our key innovation is to build compact codes, dubbed SpANN codes, using the active set of sparse coded data. These codes are then used to index an inverted file table for fast retrieval. The active sets are often found to be sensitive to small differences among data points, resulting in only near duplicate retrieval. We show that this sensitivity is related to the coherence of the dictionary; small coherence resulting in better retrieval. To this end, we propose a novel dictionary learning formulation with incoherence constraints and an efficient method to solve it. Experiments are conducted on two state-of-the-art computer vision datasets with 1M data points and show an order of magnitude improvement in retrieval accuracy without sacrificing memory and query time compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: This paper develops approximate nearest neighbor retrieval using dictionary learning and sparse coding. Its compact SpANN codes are built from the active set of a sparse representation: the dictionary elements used to represent a point. These codes index an inverted file table, providing a mechanism for fast retrieval.

A problem with active-set codes is that small differences between points can change the active set, making retrieval effective mainly for near duplicates. The authors connect this sensitivity to dictionary coherence and show that lower coherence produces better retrieval. They therefore introduce a dictionary-learning formulation with incoherence constraints and an efficient method for solving it.

Experiments on two computer vision datasets with one million data points report an order-of-magnitude improvement in retrieval accuracy over the compared state-of-the-art methods, without sacrificing memory or query time. The central insight is that the dictionary must support useful retrieval codes, so controlling its coherence is part of designing the search representation.
summary.tldr: SpANN builds compact retrieval codes from sparse active sets and learns low-coherence dictionaries to improve retrieval accuracy without reported memory or query-time costs.

title: Nearest Neighbors Using Compact Sparse Codes

abstract: We introduce a new structured kernel interpolation (SKI) framework, which generalises and unifies inducing point methods for scalable Gaussian processes (GPs). SKI methods produce kernel approximations for fast computations through kernel interpolation. The SKI framework clarifies how the quality of an inducing point approach depends on the number of inducing (aka interpolation) points, interpolation strategy, and GP covariance kernel. SKI also provides a mechanism to create new scalable kernel methods, through choosing different kernel interpolation strategies. Using SKI, with local cubic kernel interpolation, we introduce KISS-GP, which is 1) more scalable than inducing point alternatives, 2) naturally enables Kronecker and Toeplitz algebra for substantial additional gains in scalability, without requiring any grid data, and 3) can be used for fast and expressive kernel learning. KISS-GP costs O(n) time and storage for GP inference. We evaluate KISS-GP for kernel matrix approximation, kernel learning, and natural sound modelling.

SKI methods produce kernel approximations for fast computations through kernel interpolation. SKI also provides a mechanism to create new scalable kernel methods, through choosing different kernel interpolation strategies. Using SKI, with local cubic kernel interpolation, we introduce KISS-GP, which is 1) more scalable than inducing point alternatives, 2) naturally enables Kronecker and Toeplitz algebra for substantial additional gains in scalability, without requiring any grid data, and 3) can be used for fast and expressive kernel learning. KISS-GP costs O(n) time and storage for GP inference. We evaluate KISS-GP for kernel matrix approximation, kernel learning, and natural sound modelling.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process methods need efficient kernel computations to scale to large datasets. This paper introduces structured kernel interpolation, or SKI, as a framework that unifies and generalizes inducing-point approaches. It constructs kernel approximations through interpolation, providing a common way to understand existing methods and create new ones.

The framework makes explicit three influences on approximation quality: the number of interpolation points, the interpolation strategy, and the covariance kernel. Choosing local cubic interpolation yields KISS-GP. This method also enables structured Kronecker and Toeplitz computations for additional scalability gains without requiring the observed data themselves to lie on a grid.

The paper states that KISS-GP requires time and storage linear in the number of observations for Gaussian-process inference and is more scalable than inducing-point alternatives. It also supports fast, expressive kernel learning. Evaluations examine kernel-matrix approximation, kernel learning, and natural-sound modeling, connecting the computational framework to both approximation quality and learning useful covariance structure.
summary.tldr: KISS-GP uses structured kernel interpolation for linear-time, linear-storage Gaussian-process inference without requiring grid-structured observations.

title: Kernel Interpolation for Scalable Structured Gaussian Processes (KISS-GP)

abstract: Boolean matrix factorization and Boolean matrix completion from noisy observations are desirable unsupervised data-analysis methods due to their interpretability, but hard to perform due to their NP-hardness. We treat these problems as maximum a posteriori inference problems in a graphical model and present a message passing approach that scales linearly with the number of observations and factors. Our empirical study demonstrates that message passing is able to recover low-rank Boolean matrices, in the boundaries of theoretically possible recovery and compares favorably with state-of-the-art in real-world applications, such collaborative filtering with large-scale Boolean data.
originalAbstract: Boolean matrix factorization and Boolean matrix completion from noisy observations are desirable unsupervised data-analysis methods due to their interpretability, but hard to perform due to their NP-hardness. We treat these problems as maximum a posteriori inference problems in a graphical model and present a message passing approach that scales linearly with the number of observations and factors. Our empirical study demonstrates that message passing is able to recover low-rank Boolean matrices, in the boundaries of theoretically possible recovery and compares favorably with state-of-the-art in real-world applications, such collaborative filtering with large-scale Boolean data.

paragraphs: Boolean matrix factorization seeks an interpretable factor representation of binary data, while Boolean completion seeks to reconstruct a matrix from incomplete, potentially noisy observations. Both are attractive for unsupervised analysis, but their NP-hardness makes general-purpose exact solution difficult. The paper develops a shared inference approach for these two related tasks.

The authors formulate the problems as maximum a posteriori inference in a graphical model. In this formulation, the goal is to find the explanation of the observations favored by the model and its prior assumptions. They then use message passing to perform inference. The reported computational scaling is linear in the number of observations and factors, supporting applications with large amounts of Boolean data.

The empirical study reports recovery of low-rank Boolean matrices near the boundaries where recovery is theoretically possible. It also finds favorable comparisons with leading methods in real-world applications, including collaborative filtering. These findings demonstrate empirical effectiveness in the studied settings; they do not turn the underlying NP-hard problems into universally tractable exact computations.
summary.tldr: A graphical-model message-passing method tackles noisy Boolean matrix factorization and completion with favorable empirical recovery and scaling.

title: Boolean Matrix Factorization and Noisy Completion via Message Passing

abstract: Non-negative matrix factorization is a basic tool for decomposing data into the feature and weight matrices under non-negativity constraints, and in practice is often solved in the alternating minimization framework. However, it is unclear whether such algorithms can recover the ground-truth feature matrix when the weights for different features are highly correlated, which is common in applications. This paper proposes a simple and natural alternating gradient descent based algorithm, and shows that with a mild initialization it provably recovers the ground-truth in the presence of strong correlations. In most interesting cases, the correlation can be in the same order as the highest possible. Our analysis also reveals its several favorable features including robustness to noise. We complement our theoretical results with empirical studies on semi-synthetic datasets, demonstrating its advantage over several popular methods in recovering the ground-truth.

paragraphs: Non-negative matrix factorization separates data into feature and weight matrices whose entries are nonnegative. A difficult question is whether alternating optimization can recover the true features when their weights are strongly correlated. This paper addresses that question, motivated by the prevalence of such correlations in applications.

The authors propose an alternating gradient-descent algorithm and prove recovery of the ground-truth feature matrix with a mild initialization requirement, even in the presence of strong correlations. In many cases of interest, the permitted correlation is of the same order as the highest possible. The guarantee therefore addresses a challenging correlation regime while retaining an explicit initialization condition.

The theoretical analysis also establishes favorable properties including robustness to noise. Experiments on semi-synthetic datasets complement the theory and show advantages over several popular methods in recovering the ground truth. Together, these results support alternating gradient descent as a recovery method in the analyzed setting, beyond merely finding a nonnegative factorization that fits the observations.
summary.tldr: With mild initialization, an alternating gradient method provably recovers nonnegative features despite strong weight correlations.

title: Provable Alternating Gradient Descent for Non-negative Matrix Factorization with Strong Correlations

abstract: We consider estimating the parametric component of single index models in high dimensions. Compared with existing work, we do not require the covariate to be normally distributed. Utilizing Stein’s Lemma, we propose estimators based on the score function of the covariate. Moreover, to handle score function and response variables that are heavy-tailed, our estimators are constructed via carefully thresholding their empirical counterparts. Under a bounded fourth moment condition, we establish optimal statistical rates of convergence for the proposed estimators. Extensive numerical experiments are provided to back up our theory.
originalAbstract: We consider estimating the parametric component of single index models in high dimensions. Compared with existing work, we do not require the covariate to be normally distributed. Utilizing Stein’s Lemma, we propose estimators based on the score function of the covariate. Moreover, to handle score function and response variables that are heavy-tailed, our estimators are constructed via carefully thresholding their empirical counterparts. Under a bounded fourth moment condition, we establish optimal statistical rates of convergence for the proposed estimators. Extensive numerical experiments are provided to back up our theory.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimation of the parametric part of a single-index model when the number of input dimensions is high. A central aim is to move beyond methods that require normally distributed covariates. The proposed approach allows non-Gaussian inputs while still providing a theoretical account of estimation accuracy.

Using Stein's Lemma, the authors construct estimators from the covariate distribution's score function. They also address heavy-tailed score functions and responses by carefully thresholding the empirical quantities used in estimation. Thresholding is the mechanism used to handle these potentially extreme observations, making tail behavior an explicit part of the estimator's design.

Under a bounded fourth-moment condition, the authors establish optimal statistical convergence rates. That assumption is part of the guarantee: allowing non-Gaussian and heavy-tailed variables does not mean removing all distributional requirements. Extensive numerical experiments support the theory. The contribution is therefore a combination of broader input distributions, a method for handling heavy tails, and strong statistical guarantees under a stated moment condition.
summary.tldr: Thresholded score-function estimators achieve optimal rates for high-dimensional non-Gaussian single-index models under a bounded fourth-moment condition.

title: High-dimensional Non-Gaussian Single Index Models via Thresholded Score Function Estimation

abstract: Training of discrete latent variable models remains challenging because passing gradient information through discrete units is difficult. We propose a new class of smoothing transformations based on a mixture of two overlapping distributions, and show that the proposed transformation can be used for training binary latent models with either directed or undirected priors. We derive a new variational bound to efficiently train with Boltzmann machine priors. Using this bound, we develop DVAE++, a generative model with a global discrete prior and a hierarchy of convolutional continuous variables. Experiments on several benchmarks show that overlapping transformations outperform other recent continuous relaxations of discrete latent variables including Gumbel-Softmax (Maddison et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2016), and discrete variational autoencoders (Rolfe 2016).
originalAbstract: Training of discrete latent variable models remains challenging because passing gradient information through discrete units is difficult. We propose a new class of smoothing transformations based on a mixture of two overlapping distributions, and show that the proposed transformation can be used for training binary latent models with either directed or undirected priors. We derive a new variational bound to efficiently train with Boltzmann machine priors. Using this bound, we develop DVAE++, a generative model with a global discrete prior and a hierarchy of convolutional continuous variables. Experiments on several benchmarks show that overlapping transformations outperform other recent continuous relaxations of discrete latent variables including Gumbel-Softmax (Maddison et al., 2016; Jang et al., 2016), and discrete variational autoencoders (Rolfe 2016).

paragraphs: Discrete latent variables are difficult to train with gradient-based methods because gradient information does not pass easily through discrete choices. This paper introduces smoothing transformations built from two overlapping distributions. The transformations provide a mechanism for training models with binary latent variables while accommodating either directed or undirected prior distributions.

The authors also derive a new variational bound for efficient training with Boltzmann machine priors. They use that bound to construct DVAE++, a generative model combining a global discrete prior with a hierarchy of convolutional continuous variables. The method therefore connects a new smoothing mechanism with an objective suited to the chosen prior structure.

Experiments on several benchmarks show that overlapping transformations outperform the compared continuous relaxations, including Gumbel-Softmax and earlier discrete variational autoencoders. The results support the proposed transformation as a useful way to handle discrete variables during training. Together, the transformation and bound enable the particular combination of discrete global structure and continuous hierarchical variables used in DVAE++.
summary.tldr: DVAE++ uses overlapping smoothing distributions and a new variational bound to train generative models with discrete latent structure.

title: DVAE++: Discrete Variational Autoencoders with Overlapping Transformations

abstract: We propose a stochastic variance-reduced cubic regularized Newton method (SVRC) for non-convex optimization. At the core of our algorithm is a novel semi-stochastic gradient along with a semi-stochastic Hessian, which are specifically designed for cubic regularization method. We show that our algorithm is guaranteed to converge to an $(\epsilon,\sqrt{\epsilon})$-approximate local minimum within $\tilde{O}(n^{4/5}/\epsilon^{3/2})$ second-order oracle calls, which outperforms the state-of-the-art cubic regularization algorithms including subsampled cubic regularization. Our work also sheds light on the application of variance reduction technique to high-order non-convex optimization methods. Thorough experiments on various non-convex optimization problems support our theory.
originalAbstract: We propose a stochastic variance-reduced cubic regularized Newton method (SVRC) for non-convex optimization. At the core of our algorithm is a novel semi-stochastic gradient along with a semi-stochastic Hessian, which are specifically designed for cubic regularization method. We show that our algorithm is guaranteed to converge to an $(\epsilon,\sqrt{\epsilon})$-approximate local minimum within $\tilde{O}(n^{4/5}/\epsilon^{3/2})$ second-order oracle calls, which outperforms the state-of-the-art cubic regularization algorithms including subsampled cubic regularization. Our work also sheds light on the application of variance reduction technique to high-order non-convex optimization methods. Thorough experiments on various non-convex optimization problems support our theory.

paragraphs: The paper develops SVRC, a stochastic variance-reduced Newton method for non-convex optimization. Its target is an approximate local minimum, making both gradient information and curvature relevant. The method combines variance reduction with cubic regularization, extending the use of variance reduction beyond methods centered only on first derivatives.

At its core are a semi-stochastic gradient and a semi-stochastic Hessian designed specifically for the cubic-regularization setting. These two estimates provide the first- and second-order information used by the algorithm. Designing them together is central to the proposed method and to the resulting bound on its computational requirements.

The authors prove convergence to an (epsilon, square-root-of-epsilon) approximate local minimum within a second-order oracle complexity of order n^(4/5)/epsilon^(3/2), up to logarithmic factors. They report that this improves on existing cubic-regularization algorithms, including subsampled cubic regularization. Experiments across non-convex optimization problems support the theory. The result demonstrates a concrete role for variance reduction in reducing the analyzed cost of higher-order optimization.
summary.tldr: SVRC reduces the second-order oracle complexity of finding approximate local minima by combining variance reduction with cubic-regularized Newton updates.

title: Stochastic Variance-Reduced Cubic Regularized Newton Methods

abstract: This study addresses an issue of co-adaptation between a feature extractor and a classifier in a neural network. A naive joint optimization of a feature extractor and a classifier often brings situations in which an excessively complex feature distribution adapted to a very specific classifier degrades the test performance. We introduce a method called Feature-extractor Optimization through Classifier Anonymization (FOCA), which is designed to avoid an explicit co-adaptation between a feature extractor and a particular classifier by using many randomly-generated, weak classifiers during optimization. We put forth a mathematical proposition that states the FOCA features form a point-like distribution within the same class in a class-separable fashion under special conditions. Real-data experiments under more general conditions provide supportive evidences.
originalAbstract: This study addresses an issue of co-adaptation between a feature extractor and a classifier in a neural network. A naive joint optimization of a feature extractor and a classifier often brings situations in which an excessively complex feature distribution adapted to a very specific classifier degrades the test performance. We introduce a method called Feature-extractor Optimization through Classifier Anonymization (FOCA), which is designed to avoid an explicit co-adaptation between a feature extractor and a particular classifier by using many randomly-generated, weak classifiers during optimization. We put forth a mathematical proposition that states the FOCA features form a point-like distribution within the same class in a class-separable fashion under special conditions. Real-data experiments under more general conditions provide supportive evidences.

paragraphs: A neural network's feature extractor and classifier are often optimized together. The paper identifies a possible consequence: the extractor can produce an unnecessarily complex feature distribution tailored to one particular classifier, degrading test performance. This dependence between the two components motivates a training method that reduces explicit co-adaptation.

Feature-extractor Optimization through Classifier Anonymization, or FOCA, trains the extractor using many randomly generated weak classifiers. The method therefore exposes the learned features to multiple classifiers during optimization. Its purpose is to avoid organizing the representation around the specific requirements of a single classifier, addressing the relationship between network components directly.

Under special conditions, a mathematical proposition shows that FOCA features collapse toward a point-like distribution within each class while keeping classes separable. This describes a particularly simple class structure, but the conditions are part of the result. Experiments on real data under more general conditions provide supporting evidence. Together, the theory and experiments suggest that changing how the extractor interacts with classifiers can encourage useful feature organization.
summary.tldr: FOCA trains feature extractors with many random weak classifiers to reduce co-adaptation, with conditional theory and supporting real-data experiments.

title: Breaking Inter-Layer Co-Adaptation by Classifier Anonymization

abstract: We investigate the feasibility of learning from both fully-labeled supervised data and contextual bandit data. We specifically consider settings in which the underlying learning signal may be different between these two data sources. Theoretically, we state and prove no-regret algorithms for learning that is robust to divergences between the two sources. Empirically, we evaluate some of these algorithms on a large selection of datasets, showing that our approaches are feasible, and helpful in practice.
originalAbstract: We investigate the feasibility of learning from both fully-labeled supervised data and contextual bandit data. We specifically consider settings in which the underlying learning signal may be different between these two data sources. Theoretically, we state and prove no-regret algorithms for learning that is robust to divergences between the two sources. Empirically, we evaluate some of these algorithms on a large selection of datasets, showing that our approaches are feasible, and helpful in practice.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a learner can use both fully labeled supervised data and contextual bandit feedback. The motivation is to benefit from an existing source of supervision while also learning from bandit data. A central complication is that the underlying learning signals in the two sources may differ, so their combination must account for possible disagreement.

The authors develop and prove no-regret algorithms that are robust to divergences between those signals. Robustness to the mismatch is part of the theoretical objective, rather than assuming that the two sources provide interchangeable information. The resulting framework addresses whether supervised information can help initialize or support bandit learning even when the sources do not align.

The paper evaluates some of its algorithms on a large collection of datasets and finds the approaches feasible and helpful in practice. The theoretical and empirical contributions play complementary roles: the guarantees address divergence between sources, while the experiments support the practical usefulness of combining the two forms of feedback.
summary.tldr: No-regret algorithms combine supervised and contextual bandit data while remaining robust to differences in their learning signals.

title: Warm-starting Contextual Bandits: Robustly Combining Supervised and Bandit Feedback

abstract: Although it is widely known that Gaussian processes can be conditioned on observations of the gradient, this functionality is of limited use due to the prohibitive computational cost of $\mathcal{O}(N^3 D^3)$ in data points $N$ and dimension $D$. The dilemma of gradient observations is that a single one of them comes at the same cost as $D$ independent function evaluations, so the latter are often preferred. Careful scrutiny reveals, however, that derivative observations give rise to highly structured kernel Gram matrices for very general classes of kernels (inter alia, stationary kernels). We show that in the \emph{low-data} regime $N < D$, the Gram matrix can be decomposed in a manner that reduces the cost of inference to $\mathcal{O}(N^2D + (N^2)^3)$ (i.e., linear in the number of dimensions) and, in special cases, to $\mathcal{O}(N^2D + N^3)$. This reduction in complexity opens up new use-cases for inference with gradients especially in the high-dimensional regime, where the information-to-cost ratio of gradient observations significantly increases. We demonstrate this potential in a variety of tasks relevant for machine learning, such as optimization and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with predictive gradients.
originalAbstract: Although it is widely known that Gaussian processes can be conditioned on observations of the gradient, this functionality is of limited use due to the prohibitive computational cost of $\mathcal{O}(N^3 D^3)$ in data points $N$ and dimension $D$. The dilemma of gradient observations is that a single one of them comes at the same cost as $D$ independent function evaluations, so the latter are often preferred. Careful scrutiny reveals, however, that derivative observations give rise to highly structured kernel Gram matrices for very general classes of kernels (inter alia, stationary kernels). We show that in the \emph{low-data} regime $N < D$, the Gram matrix can be decomposed in a manner that reduces the cost of inference to $\mathcal{O}(N^2D + (N^2)^3)$ (i.e., linear in the number of dimensions) and, in special cases, to $\mathcal{O}(N^2D + N^3)$. This reduction in complexity opens up new use-cases for inference with gradients especially in the high-dimensional regime, where the information-to-cost ratio of gradient observations significantly increases. We demonstrate this potential in a variety of tasks relevant for machine learning, such as optimization and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with predictive gradients.

paragraphs: Gradient observations can tell a Gaussian process how a function changes in every input direction. Yet incorporating them is expensive: with N observation points and D dimensions, the standard computational cost grows as N cubed times D cubed. This cost can make separate function observations more attractive despite the information gradients contain.

The paper identifies exploitable structure in the kernel Gram matrices created by derivative observations. This structure occurs for broad kernel classes, including stationary kernels. When N is smaller than D, the authors derive a decomposition reducing inference cost to O(N²D + N⁶). In special cases, the cost falls further to O(N²D + N³). For fixed N, both expressions are linear in dimension.

The low-data condition is central to the claimed advantage. It makes gradient information more computationally attractive in high-dimensional problems. Demonstrations include optimization and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with predictive gradients, illustrating applications where the reduced cost can make derivative-conditioned Gaussian processes useful.
summary.tldr: Structured kernel decompositions make Gaussian-process inference with gradients linear in dimension when the number of observations is smaller than dimension.

title: High-Dimensional Gaussian Process Inference with Derivatives

abstract: Variational representations of $f$-divergences are central to many machine learning algorithms, with Lipschitz constrained variants recently gaining attention. Inspired by this, we define the Moreau-Yosida approximation of $f$-divergences with respect to the Wasserstein-$1$ metric. The corresponding variational formulas provide a generalization of a number of recent results, novel special cases of interest and a relaxation of the hard Lipschitz constraint. Additionally, we prove that the so-called tight variational representation of $f$-divergences can be to be taken over the quotient space of Lipschitz functions, and give a characterization of functions achieving the supremum in the variational representation. On the practical side, we propose an algorithm to calculate the tight convex conjugate of $f$-divergences compatible with automatic differentiation frameworks. As an application of our results, we propose the Moreau-Yosida $f$-GAN, providing an implementation of the variational formulas for the Kullback-Leibler, reverse Kullback-Leibler, $\chi^2$, reverse $\chi^2$, squared Hellinger, Jensen-Shannon, Jeffreys, triangular discrimination and total variation divergences as GANs trained on CIFAR-10, leading to competitive results and a simple solution to the problem of uniqueness of the optimal critic.

The corresponding variational formulas provide a generalization of a number of recent results, novel special cases of interest and a relaxation of the hard Lipschitz constraint. Additionally, we prove that the so-called tight variational representation of $f$-divergences can be to be taken over the quotient space of Lipschitz functions, and give a characterization of functions achieving the supremum in the variational representation. paragraphs: Many learning algorithms use variational formulas to express differences between probability distributions through optimization over functions. This paper develops Moreau-Yosida approximations of f-divergences using the Wasserstein-1 metric. The resulting formulas unify several recent results, introduce additional special cases, and relax a hard Lipschitz constraint on the functions used in the optimization.

The theoretical work also examines the tight variational representation of f-divergences. The authors show that it can be formulated over a quotient space of Lipschitz functions and characterize functions that achieve its supremum. These results address the structure of the optimizing functions, alongside the broader question of how distributional discrepancies can be represented.

It then introduces Moreau-Yosida f-GANs, implementing a range of divergences, including Kullback-Leibler, Jensen-Shannon, and total variation. CIFAR-10 experiments produce competitive results. The framework also provides a simple treatment of the optimal critic’s uniqueness, connecting the mathematical characterization to a practical generative-model application.
summary.tldr: Moreau-Yosida approximations unify and extend variational f-divergences, relax Lipschitz constraints, and support practical GAN implementations.

title: Moreau-Yosida $f$-divergences

abstract: The variance-stabilizing transformation (VST) problem is to transform heteroscedastic data to homoscedastic data so that they are more tractable for subsequent analysis. However, most of the existing approaches focus on finding an analytical solution for a certain parametric distribution, which severely limits the applications, because simple distributions cannot faithfully describe the real data while more complicated distributions cannot be analytically solved. In this paper, we converted the VST problem into a convex optimization problem, which can always be efficiently solved, identified the specific structure of the convex problem, which further improved the efficiency of the proposed algorithm, and showed that any finite discrete distributions and the discretized version of any continuous distributions from real data can be variance-stabilized in an easy and nonparametric way. We demonstrated the new approach on bioimaging data and achieved superior performance compared to peer algorithms in terms of not only the variance homoscedasticity but also the impact on subsequent analysis such as denoising. Source codes are available at https://github.com/yu-lab-vt/ConvexVST.

paragraphs: Variance stabilization transforms data whose variability changes across observations into data with more uniform variability. This can make later analysis easier. Many existing approaches derive a transformation for a chosen parametric distribution, creating a tradeoff: simple distributions may poorly describe real measurements, while more realistic distributions may resist an analytical solution.

ConvexVST replaces the search for an analytical formula with a convex optimization problem. The authors identify additional structure within that problem to improve computational efficiency. Their method is nonparametric, and they show that it can stabilize variance for any finite discrete distribution, as well as discretized versions of continuous distributions obtained from real data.

The bioimaging experiments assess both the transformed data and their usefulness downstream. ConvexVST outperforms peer algorithms in making variance more uniform and in its effect on subsequent analysis, including denoising. The findings connect a broader optimization-based formulation with practical benefits: stabilization can be evaluated by whether it improves the analysis that follows, as well as by how evenly it distributes variability.
summary.tldr: ConvexVST uses convex optimization to stabilize variance nonparametrically and improves bioimaging results, including downstream denoising.

title: ConvexVST: A Convex Optimization Approach to Variance-stabilizing Transformation

abstract: Neural networks are increasingly being used to solve partial differential equations (PDEs), replacing slower numerical solvers. However, a critical issue is that neural PDE solvers require high-quality ground truth data, which usually must come from the very solvers they are designed to replace. Thus, we are presented with a proverbial chicken-and-egg problem. In this paper, we present a method, which can partially alleviate this problem, by improving neural PDE solver sample complexity—Lie point symmetry data augmentation (LPSDA). In the context of PDEs, it turns out we are able to quantitatively derive an exhaustive list of data transformations, based on the Lie point symmetry group of the PDEs in question, something not possible in other application areas. We present this framework and demonstrate how it can easily be deployed to improve neural PDE solver sample complexity by an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Neural solvers for partial differential equations depend on high-quality training solutions, which usually come from the numerical solvers they aim to replace. Generating that training data therefore remains a bottleneck. This paper addresses part of the problem by improving how efficiently neural solvers learn from the available examples.

The proposed method, Lie point symmetry data augmentation, derives transformations from the symmetry group of the equation being solved. These symmetries provide a principled basis for transforming training data. In this setting, the authors can derive an exhaustive collection of transformations associated with the PDE’s Lie point symmetries, giving augmentation a mathematical connection to the governing equation.

The authors present the framework and demonstrate an order-of-magnitude improvement in neural solver sample complexity. The significance is that equation-derived transformations can make existing solution data substantially more useful for learning. The method partially alleviates dependence on expensive ground-truth generation; its stated contribution is improved data efficiency, rather than eliminating the need for training solutions.
summary.tldr: Data augmentation derived from PDE symmetries demonstrates an order-of-magnitude improvement in neural solver sample complexity.

title: Lie Point Symmetry Data Augmentation for Neural PDE Solvers

abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework for problems with continuous action spaces: Action Quantization from Demonstrations (AQuaDem). The proposed approach consists in learning a discretization of continuous action spaces from human demonstrations. This discretization returns a set of plausible actions (in light of the demonstrations) for each input state, thus capturing the priors of the demonstrator and their multimodal behavior. By discretizing the action space, any discrete action deep RL technique can be readily applied to the continuous control problem. Experiments show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods such as SAC in the RL setup, and GAIL in the Imitation Learning setup. We provide a website with interactive videos: https://google-research.github.io/aquadem/ and make the code available: https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/aquadem.

We provide a website with interactive videos: https://google-research.github.io/aquadem/ and make the code available: https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/aquadem.

paragraphs: Continuous control involves choosing actions from a continuous range, whereas many deep reinforcement learning methods operate on discrete alternatives. Action Quantization from Demonstrations, or AQuaDem, connects these settings by learning a discrete set of action choices from human demonstrations.

The learned discretization depends on the current state. For each input state, it supplies several actions that are plausible in light of the demonstrations. This lets the available choices reflect the demonstrator’s preferences and multimodal behavior: there can be multiple plausible ways to act in the same situation. The discretization therefore carries information about demonstrated behavior into the control problem.

Once actions are represented this way, discrete-action deep reinforcement learning techniques can be applied to the continuous task. The authors report experimental improvements over SAC in reinforcement learning and GAIL in imitation learning. These results support demonstration-based action discretization as a useful interface between continuous environments and discrete learning algorithms, with demonstrations shaping the choices available to the learner.
summary.tldr: AQuaDem learns state-dependent discrete action choices from demonstrations so discrete reinforcement learning methods can tackle continuous control.

title: Continuous Control with Action Quantization from Demonstrations

abstract: In generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL), the agent aims to learn a policy from an expert demonstration so that its performance cannot be discriminated from the expert policy on a certain predefined reward set. In this paper, we study GAIL in both online and offline settings with linear function approximation, where both the transition and reward function are linear in the feature maps. Besides the expert demonstration, in the online setting the agent can interact with the environment, while in the offline setting the agent only accesses an additional dataset collected by a prior. For online GAIL, we propose an optimistic generative adversarial policy imitation algorithm (OGAPI) and prove that OGAPI achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{H^4d^3K}+\sqrt{H^3d^2K^2/N_1})$ regret. Here $N_1$ represents the number of trajectories of the expert demonstration, $d$ is the feature dimension, and $K$ is the number of episodes. For offline GAIL, we propose a pessimistic generative adversarial policy imitation algorithm (PGAPI). We also obtain the optimality gap of PGAPI, achieving the minimax lower bound in the utilization of the additional dataset. Assuming sufficient coverage on the additional dataset, we show that PGAPI achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{H^4d^2/K}+\sqrt{H^4d^3/N_2}+\sqrt{H^3d^2/N_1})$ optimality gap. Here $N_2$ represents the number of trajectories of the additional dataset with sufficient coverage.

Assuming sufficient coverage on the additional dataset, we show that PGAPI achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{H^4d^2/K}+\sqrt{H^4d^3/N_2}+\sqrt{H^3d^2/N_1})$ optimality gap. paragraphs: Generative adversarial imitation learning seeks a policy whose performance cannot be distinguished from an expert's using a predefined reward family. This paper analyzes that objective when both transition and reward functions are linear in specified features. It considers online learning with environment interaction and offline learning with an additional dataset collected by a prior policy.

For the online setting, the authors introduce OGAPI, an optimistic policy-imitation algorithm, and prove a regret bound. The bound accounts for the feature dimension, the number of learning episodes, the horizon, and the amount of expert demonstration data. This makes the role of limited demonstrations explicit alongside the cost of learning through interaction.

For offline learning, PGAPI uses a pessimistic approach and receives an optimality-gap guarantee. Its use of the additional dataset matches a minimax lower bound. Under sufficient coverage in that dataset, the authors provide a bound separating contributions from optimization episodes, additional trajectories, and expert trajectories. The guarantees therefore depend on the linear model structure and, for the stated coverage-based result, adequate offline data coverage.
summary.tldr: Optimistic and pessimistic imitation algorithms receive online and offline guarantees under linear transition and reward models.

title: Learning from Demonstration: Provably Efficient Adversarial Policy Imitation with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Model selection in contextual bandits is an important complementary problem to regret minimization with respect to a fixed model class. We consider the simplest non-trivial instance of model-selection: distinguishing a simple multi-armed bandit problem from a linear contextual bandit problem. Even in this instance, current state-of-the-art methods explore in a suboptimal manner and require strong "feature-diversity" conditions. In this paper, we introduce new algorithms that a) explore in a data-adaptive manner, and b) provide model selection guarantees of the form O(d^{\alpha} T^{1 - \alpha}) with no feature diversity conditions whatsoever, where d denotes the dimension of the linear model and T denotes the total number of rounds. The first algorithm enjoys a "best-of-both-worlds" property, recovering two prior results that hold under distinct distributional assumptions, simultaneously. The second removes distributional assumptions altogether, expanding the scope for tractable model selection. Our approach extends to model selection among nested linear contextual bandits under some additional assumptions.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit learner may need to determine whether contextual information is useful at all. This paper studies that basic model-selection problem: distinguishing a simple multi-armed bandit from a linear contextual bandit. Even this choice can require exploration that differs from what is needed to optimize decisions within a fixed model.

The authors introduce algorithms that adapt exploration to the data and provide model-selection guarantees without feature-diversity conditions. Their bounds take the form of a power of the feature dimension multiplied by a complementary power of the number of rounds. The first algorithm simultaneously recovers two earlier results that were established under different distributional assumptions.

The second algorithm removes distributional assumptions altogether for the studied selection problem, extending where tractable model selection is available. The approach also extends to selection among nested linear contextual models, although that extension needs additional assumptions. Together, the results show how adapting exploration can reduce dependence on restrictive assumptions about the features while retaining formal guarantees for choosing the model.
summary.tldr: Data-adaptive exploration enables bandit model selection without feature-diversity conditions, with one algorithm also removing distributional assumptions.

title: Universal and data-adaptive algorithms for model selection in linear contextual bandits

abstract: This paper aims to theoretically analyze the complexity of feature transformations encoded in piecewise linear DNNs with ReLU layers. We propose metrics to measure three types of complexities of transformations based on the information theory. We further discover and prove the strong correlation between the complexity and the disentanglement of transformations. Based on the proposed metrics, we analyze two typical phenomena of the change of the transformation complexity during the training process, and explore the ceiling of a DNN’s complexity. The proposed metrics can also be used as a loss to learn a DNN with the minimum complexity, which also controls the over-fitting level of the DNN and influences adversarial robustness, adversarial transferability, and knowledge consistency. Comprehensive comparative studies have provided new perspectives to understand the DNN. The code is released at https://github.com/sjtu-XAI-lab/transformation-complexity.

We further discover and prove the strong correlation between the complexity and the disentanglement of transformations. Based on the proposed metrics, we analyze two typical phenomena of the change of the transformation complexity during the training process, and explore the ceiling of a DNN’s complexity. The proposed metrics can also be used as a loss to learn a DNN with the minimum complexity, which also controls the over-fitting level of the DNN and influences adversarial robustness, adversarial transferability, and knowledge consistency. paragraphs: A neural network transforms its inputs into internal features, but describing the complexity of those transformations requires a suitable measure. This paper develops information-theoretic metrics for three types of transformation complexity in piecewise linear networks with ReLU layers. The goal is to analyze what the network encodes through its transformations.

The authors establish a strong correlation between transformation complexity and disentanglement. They use the metrics to analyze two characteristic patterns of complexity change during training and to investigate the ceiling of a network’s complexity. This makes the proposed quantities tools for studying both how learning unfolds and how complex the learned transformations can become.

The metrics can also serve as a training loss aimed at minimizing complexity. The authors report that this controls the level of overfitting and affects adversarial robustness, adversarial transferability, and knowledge consistency. Comparative studies provide additional perspectives on network behavior. These claims establish that the metrics relate to several properties of learning, without implying that reducing complexity improves every one of those properties in every setting.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic metrics quantify ReLU networks’ transformation complexity, connect it with disentanglement, and provide an objective for controlling complexity during training.

title: Towards Theoretical Analysis of Transformation Complexity of ReLU DNNs

abstract: We propose LESS-VFL, a communication-efficient feature selection method for distributed systems with vertically partitioned data. We consider a system of a server and several parties with local datasets that share a sample ID space but have different feature sets. The parties wish to collaboratively train a model for a prediction task. As part of the training, the parties wish to remove unimportant features in the system to improve generalization, efficiency, and explainability. In LESS-VFL, after a short pre-training period, the server optimizes its part of the global model to determine the relevant outputs from party models. This information is shared with the parties to then allow local feature selection without communication. We analytically prove that LESS-VFL removes spurious features from model training. We provide extensive empirical evidence that LESS-VFL can achieve high accuracy and remove spurious features at a fraction of the communication cost of other feature selection approaches.

paragraphs: In vertical federated learning, several parties hold different features for samples drawn from a shared ID space. They collaborate with a server to train a prediction model. Removing unimportant features can support generalization, efficiency, and explainability, but coordinating feature selection across the distributed system introduces communication costs.

LESS-VFL separates the coordination step from local feature selection. After a short pretraining stage, the server optimizes its portion of the global model to identify which outputs from the parties' models are relevant. It communicates that information to the parties, which then use it to select their own features without further communication during that local selection step.

The authors analytically establish that LESS-VFL removes spurious features from training. Their experiments also show that the method can retain high accuracy while removing such features at a fraction of the communication cost of other selection approaches. The contribution is a way to make local decisions informed by the global prediction task while reducing the communication needed for feature selection.
summary.tldr: LESS-VFL uses server guidance followed by local feature selection to remove spurious features with substantially less communication.

title: LESS-VFL: Communication-Efficient Feature Selection for Vertical Federated Learning

abstract: Explaining predictions based on multivariate time series data carries the additional difficulty of handling not only multiple features, but also time dependencies. It matters not only what happened, but also when, and the same feature could have a very different impact on a prediction depending on this time information. Previous work has used perturbation-based saliency methods to tackle this issue, perturbing an input using a trainable mask to discover which features at which times are driving the predictions. However these methods introduce fixed perturbations, inspired from similar methods on static data, while there seems to be little motivation to do so on temporal data. In this work, we aim to explain predictions by learning not only masks, but also associated perturbations. We empirically show that learning these perturbations significantly improves the quality of these explanations on time series data.

It matters not only what happened, but also when, and the same feature could have a very different impact on a prediction depending on this time information. Previous work has used perturbation-based saliency methods to tackle this issue, perturbing an input using a trainable mask to discover which features at which times are driving the predictions. However these methods introduce fixed perturbations, inspired from similar methods on static data, while there seems to be little motivation to do so on temporal data. In this work, we aim to explain predictions by learning not only masks, but also associated perturbations. We empirically show that learning these perturbations significantly improves the quality of these explanations on time series data.

paragraphs: Explaining a prediction from multivariate time series requires identifying both the relevant features and the moments when they matter. A feature's influence can change with its position in time, so an explanation must account for temporal dependence as well as the presence of particular observations.

Perturbation-based saliency methods approach this by altering the input and learning a mask that identifies influential feature-time locations. Earlier methods learn the mask while keeping the perturbation rule fixed. The paper questions that choice because those fixed alterations were inspired by methods for static data, whose structure differs from temporal data.

The proposed approach learns the perturbations together with the masks. This lets the explanation procedure adapt both where it changes a time series and how it changes those locations. Empirical results show a significant improvement in explanation quality on time-series data. The finding makes the perturbation itself an important part of explanation design: the changes used to probe a prediction can affect how well the resulting saliency identifies relevant temporal information.
summary.tldr: Learning input perturbations alongside saliency masks significantly improves time-series explanation quality in the paper's experiments.

title: Learning Perturbations to Explain Time Series Predictions

abstract: The ability to plan actions on multiple levels of abstraction enables intelligent agents to solve complex tasks effectively. However, learning the models for both low and high-level planning from demonstrations has proven challenging, especially with higher-dimensional inputs. To address this issue, we propose to use reinforcement learning to identify subgoals in expert trajectories by associating the magnitude of the rewards with the predictability of low-level actions given the state and the chosen subgoal. We build a vector-quantized generative model for the identified subgoals to perform subgoal-level planning. In experiments, the algorithm excels at solving complex, long-horizon decision-making problems outperforming state-of-the-art. Because of its ability to plan, our algorithm can find better trajectories than the ones in the training set.
