paragraphs: Different neural network minima can often be connected by parameter-space curves along which training and test losses change little. This phenomenon, called mode connectivity, is useful for merging and fine-tuning models, but its theoretical explanation remains incomplete. The paper investigates it through parameter symmetries: transformations that relate equivalent network representations.

The authors connect the topology of symmetry groups with the topology of network minima. For linear networks, they derive the number of connected components and show that skip connections reduce that number. They also examine conditions under which curved-path connectivity and straight-line connectivity hold or fail, using symmetries that account for a significant portion of the minimum.

The work gives explicit formulas for connecting curves within minima that arise from symmetry. Analyzing their curvature then yields conditions under which straight-line connections approximately preserve the relevant low-loss behavior. These results provide a geometric explanation for part of the observed connectivity, highlighting continuous symmetries while keeping the linear-network results and conditional statements distinct from universal claims about all neural networks.
summary.tldr: Parameter-space symmetries explain aspects of connected neural network minima and yield conditions for approximate straight-line connectivity.

title: Understanding Mode Connectivity via Parameter Space Symmetry

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on various medical benchmarks, but their capabilities across different cognitive levels remain underexplored. Inspired by Bloom’s Taxonomy, we propose a multi-cognitive-level evaluation framework for assessing LLMs in the medical domain in this study. The framework integrates existing medical datasets and introduces tasks targeting three cognitive levels: preliminary knowledge grasp, comprehensive knowledge application, and scenario-based problem solving. Using this framework, we systematically evaluate state-of-the-art general and medical LLMs from six prominent families: Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Phi, GPT, and DeepSeek. Our findings reveal a significant performance decline as cognitive complexity increases across evaluated models, with model size playing a more critical role in performance at higher cognitive levels. Our study highlights the need to enhance LLMs’ medical capabilities at higher cognitive levels and provides insights for developing LLMs suited to real-world medical applications.

paragraphs: Strong scores on medical benchmarks leave an important question about what a language model can do with its knowledge. This paper evaluates capabilities at different cognitive levels, distinguishing basic understanding from applying knowledge and solving contextual problems. The framework is inspired by Bloom's Taxonomy and is designed to make those differences visible within medical evaluation.

The authors combine existing medical datasets with tasks organized around three levels: preliminary knowledge grasp, comprehensive knowledge application, and scenario-based problem solving. They evaluate both general-purpose and medical language models from the Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Phi, GPT, and DeepSeek families. This organization allows performance to be examined as the intellectual demands of the tasks increase.

Across the evaluated models, performance declines significantly at higher cognitive complexity. Model size also plays a more critical role at those higher levels. These findings identify applying medical knowledge in complex scenarios as a development priority and show why evaluation should distinguish levels of capability. The framework offers a more differentiated view of progress toward models suited to real-world medical applications.
summary.tldr: A three-level medical evaluation finds that LLM performance falls as cognitive demands increase, with model size becoming more consequential.

title: Evaluating LLMs Across Multi-Cognitive Levels: From Medical Knowledge Mastery to Scenario-Based Problem Solving

abstract: Machine learning has demonstrated transformative potential for database operations, such as query optimization and in-database data analytics. However, dynamic database environments, characterized by frequent updates and evolving data distributions, introduce concept drift, which leads to performance degradation for learned models and limits their practical applicability. Addressing this challenge requires efficient frameworks capable of adapting to shifting concepts while minimizing the overhead of retraining or fine-tuning. In this paper, we propose FLAIR, an online adaptation framework that introduces a new paradigm called in-context adaptation for learned database operations. FLAIR leverages the inherent property of data systems, i.e., immediate availability of execution results for predictions, to enable dynamic context construction. By formalizing adaptation as $f:(\mathbf{x} | \mathcal{C}_t) \to \mathbf{y}$, with $\mathcal{C}_t$ representing a dynamic context memory, FLAIR delivers predictions aligned with the current concept, eliminating the need for runtime parameter optimization. To achieve this, FLAIR integrates two key modules: a Task Featurization Module for encoding task-specific features into standardized representations, and a Dynamic Decision Engine, pre-trained via Bayesian meta-training, to adapt seamlessly using contextual information at runtime. Extensive experiments across key database tasks demonstrate that FLAIR outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to $5.2\times$ faster adaptation and reducing error by 22.5% for cardinality estimation.

However, dynamic database environments, characterized by frequent updates and evolving data distributions, introduce concept drift, which leads to performance degradation for learned models and limits their practical applicability. Addressing this challenge requires efficient frameworks capable of adapting to shifting concepts while minimizing the overhead of retraining or fine-tuning. In this paper, we propose FLAIR, an online adaptation framework that introduces a new paradigm called in-context adaptation for learned database operations. FLAIR leverages the inherent property of data systems, i.e., immediate availability of execution results for predictions, to enable dynamic context construction. By formalizing adaptation as $f:(\mathbf{x} | \mathcal{C}_t) \to \mathbf{y}$, with $\mathcal{C}_t$ representing a dynamic context memory, FLAIR delivers predictions aligned with the current concept, eliminating the need for runtime parameter optimization. To achieve this, FLAIR integrates two key modules: a Task Featurization Module for encoding task-specific features into standardized representations, and a Dynamic Decision Engine, pre-trained via Bayesian meta-training, to adapt seamlessly using contextual information at runtime. Extensive experiments across key database tasks demonstrate that FLAIR outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to $5.2\times$ faster adaptation and reducing error by 22.5% for cardinality estimation.

paragraphs: Models used for database operations can lose accuracy as updates change the data and the relationships they learned. Repeated retraining or fine-tuning adds overhead. FLAIR addresses this concept drift by changing the context supplied to a prediction model at runtime, allowing adaptation without optimizing the model’s parameters during operation.

The framework uses a useful feature of database systems: execution results become available immediately after predictions are acted on. These results support a dynamic context memory that informs subsequent predictions. A Task Featurization Module converts task-specific information into standardized representations, while a Dynamic Decision Engine, pretrained through Bayesian meta-training, uses the changing context to adapt its decisions.

Experiments across database tasks report stronger results than state-of-the-art baselines, including adaptation that is up to 5.2 times faster and a 22.5% error reduction for cardinality estimation. The findings support using current execution feedback as an adaptation mechanism. The reported speed advantage concerns the tested settings, while the underlying design avoids runtime parameter optimization.
summary.tldr: FLAIR adapts learned database operations to changing data through execution-informed context, without updating model parameters at runtime.

title: In-Context Adaptation to Concept Drift for Learned Database Operations

abstract: We address the problem of reward hacking, where maximising a proxy reward does not necessarily increase the true reward. This is a key concern for Large Language Models (LLMs), as they are often fine-tuned on human preferences that may not accurately reflect a true objective. Existing work uses various tricks such as regularisation, tweaks to the reward model, and reward hacking detectors, to limit the influence that such proxy preferences have on a model. Luckily, in many contexts such as medicine, education, and law, a sparse amount of expert data is often available. In these cases, it is often unclear whether the addition of proxy data can improve policy learning. We outline a set of sufficient conditions on proxy feedback that, if satisfied, indicate that proxy data can provably improve the sample complexity of learning the ground truth policy. These conditions can inform the data collection process for specific tasks. The result implies a parameterisation for LLMs that achieves this improved sample complexity. We detail how one can adapt existing architectures to yield this improved sample complexity.

paragraphs: Preference feedback can serve as a proxy for what a model should actually achieve, but optimizing that proxy may fail to improve the true objective. This paper asks when proxy feedback can still help if a small amount of expert data is available. The focus is on learning the ground-truth policy more efficiently.

The authors give sufficient conditions on proxy feedback under which adding proxy data provably improves sample complexity, meaning the amount of data needed for learning. These conditions describe a route to a benefit; they are not presented as necessary conditions that all useful proxies must satisfy. They can also inform how feedback is collected for particular tasks.

The theoretical result implies a language-model parameterization that achieves the improved sample complexity, and the paper explains how existing architectures can be adapted accordingly. Its contribution is a conditional account of when imperfect feedback helps, linking assumptions about that feedback to a learning design with a provable data-efficiency advantage.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions under which proxy preferences, combined with sparse expert data, provably reduce the data needed to learn the true policy.

title: When Can Proxies Improve the Sample Complexity of Preference Learning?

abstract: In this position paper, we promote the study of function spaces parameterized by machine learning models through the lens of algebraic geometry. To this end, we focus on algebraic models, such as neural networks with polynomial activations, whose associated function spaces are semi-algebraic varieties. We outline a dictionary between algebro-geometric invariants of these varieties, such as dimension, degree, and singularities, and fundamental aspects of machine learning, such as sample complexity, expressivity, training dynamics, and implicit bias. Along the way, we review the literature and discuss ideas beyond the algebraic domain. This work lays the foundations of a research direction bridging algebraic geometry and deep learning, that we refer to as neuroalgebraic geometry.

The authors name this research direction neuroalgebraic geometry and present it as a bridge between mathematical geometry and deep learning.

Their main setting is algebraic models, including neural networks whose activation functions are polynomials. The associated function spaces form mathematical objects called semi-algebraic varieties. The paper outlines a dictionary connecting geometric properties, including dimension, degree, and singularities, with machine learning questions about representational power, data requirements, training behavior, and implicit bias.

This perspective matters because it organizes several learning questions around properties of the same underlying function space. The authors review existing literature and also discuss ideas extending beyond the algebraic setting. The contribution is a foundation and research agenda for developing these connections, with algebraic models providing the central setting in which the proposed geometric language applies.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes algebraic geometry as a framework for connecting neural-network function spaces with fundamental learning behavior.

title: Position: Algebra Unveils Deep Learning - An Invitation to Neuroalgebraic Geometry

abstract: Generative video diffusion models have shown strong robustness to large motion and occlusions for video frame interpolation (VFI). However, their inference efficiency lags significantly behind learning-based methods due to the structural redundancy of pairwise inference and the procedural latency of multi-step iterative denoising. To address these limitations, we propose SpeedVFI, a task-specific one-step diffusion formulation that recasts generative VFI as unified sequence interpolation. SpeedVFI achieves dual efficiency improvements by interpolating the entire video sequence in a single forward pass to eliminate pairwise overhead, and by distilling the generation trajectory into a one-step denoising process to bypass iterative latency. To make this formulation effective for VFI, we introduce temporal RoPE alignment for temporally consistent conditioning and noise-centric partial attention to reduce computational overhead while preserving global context. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SpeedVFI accelerates diffusion-based VFI by orders of magnitude while maintaining competitive quantitative and visual quality.

paragraphs: Video frame interpolation generates intermediate frames between observed ones. SpeedVFI addresses both sources of overhead by reformulating interpolation as a unified operation over a video sequence.

These components adapt the one-step formulation specifically to frame interpolation.

Experiments report speed improvements of orders of magnitude over diffusion-based frame interpolation while maintaining competitive numerical and visual quality. The findings support combining a change in processing scope with a change in denoising procedure: sequence-wide inference removes repeated work, and one-step generation removes iterative latency. Together, they make the evaluated diffusion-based interpolation process substantially more efficient.
summary.tldr: SpeedVFI combines sequence-wide interpolation with one-step diffusion, accelerating diffusion-based frame interpolation by orders of magnitude.

title: SpeedVFI: One-step Diffusion for Efficient Video Frame Interpolation

abstract: Each layer of a Transformer refines the hidden state toward a prediction, an iterative process resembling fixed-point iteration. Yet when should this iteration terminate? Existing early exit methods rely on output confidence as a proxy for internal convergence. We take a more direct approach by examining the geometry of the hidden state trajectory. We find that layer-wise updates exhibit a two-phase structure: large, volatile updates in early layers, followed by small, aligned updates as the model propagates an already-formed representation. The transition is remarkably sharp. This yields a simple criterion: exit when step size vanishes and direction stabilizes. We track the normalized update norm and cosine similarity between consecutive updates, exiting when both indicate convergence. The overhead is $O(d)$ per layer, independent of vocabulary size, requiring no learned components or architectural modifications. On LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B across question answering and commonsense reasoning tasks, this geometric criterion reduces FLOPs by 30–35% while retaining over 98% of full-depth accuracy.

paragraphs: A Transformer repeatedly updates its hidden representation as information passes through its layers. The paper asks whether this process sometimes settles before the final layer, making further computation less useful. Instead of using confidence in the output as an indirect stopping signal, the authors examine how the internal representation changes from one layer to the next.

They find two phases: early updates are large and variable, while later updates are small and point in similar directions. The transition between these phases is sharp in their observations. Their early-exit rule tracks the normalized size of each update and the cosine similarity of consecutive updates, stopping when both indicate that the representation has stabilized.

The checks require work proportional to hidden-state dimension per layer, independently of vocabulary size, and need no learned components or architectural changes. On LLaMA-2-7B and LLaMA-2-13B across question answering and commonsense reasoning tasks, the method reduces FLOPs by 30–35% while retaining over 98% of full-depth accuracy. These results support internal convergence geometry as a practical signal for reducing inference computation in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: Tracking when hidden-state updates become small and aligned enables early exits that save 30–35% of FLOPs while retaining over 98% of full-depth accuracy in the reported tests.

title: Detecting the Semantic Fixed Point: A Geometric Framework for Efficient Inference

abstract: Can a diffusion model trained on bedrooms recover human faces? Diffusion models are widely used as priors for inverse problems, but standard approaches usually assume a high-fidelity model trained on data that closely match the unknown signal. In practice, one often must use a mismatched or low-fidelity diffusion prior. Surprisingly, these weak priors often perform nearly as well as full-strength, in-domain baselines. We study when and why inverse solvers are robust to weak diffusion priors. Through extensive experiments, we find that weak priors succeed when measurements are highly informative (e.g., many observed pixels), and we identify regimes where they fail. To explain this behavior, we combine Bayesian-consistency theory with local-correlation analysis: the theory gives conditions under which high-dimensional measurements make the posterior concentrate near the true signal, while the correlation analysis shows that weak and stronger natural-image priors can share similar local spatial structure. These results provide a principled justification on when weak diffusion priors can be used reliably. Code is available at https://github.com/jjia131/weak-diffusion-priors-inverse-problem.

paragraphs: This paper studies why diffusion models can help recover signals even when their training data differ from the target or their generative quality is limited. Such models serve as weak priors in inverse problems. The authors investigate the surprising observation that these priors can sometimes perform nearly as well as stronger models trained on matching data.

Experiments find that weak priors succeed when measurements are highly informative, such as when many pixels are observed, and also identify regimes where they fail. The explanation combines Bayesian-consistency theory with analysis of local spatial correlations. The theory gives conditions under which high-dimensional measurements concentrate the posterior near the true signal, while the correlation analysis shows that weak and strong natural-image priors can share useful local structure.

The contribution is a conditional account of robustness to prior mismatch. Informative measurements and shared spatial structure can make a weak diffusion prior useful despite its shortcomings. This supports using such priors in suitable regimes while preserving the paper’s finding that their reliability does not extend to every inverse problem.
summary.tldr: Weak diffusion priors can support strong signal recovery when measurements are informative, with theory and local-correlation analysis explaining this conditional robustness.

title: Weak Diffusion Priors Can Still Achieve Strong Inverse-Problem Performance

abstract: Foundation models (FMs) pretrained on large-scale sequence data have emerged as a promising paradigm for RNA biology, yet the mechanisms underlying their transferability remain unclear. In this work, we conduct a systematic investigation of transfer learning in RNA FMs across diverse structural and functional tasks. Our results demonstrate that frozen representations from pretrained RNA FMs are not universally transferable, and that the hierarchical feature reuse paradigm prevalent in computer vision does not generally extend to RNA FMs. Instead, pretraining primarily benefits downstream tasks by providing a favorable optimization initialization when pretraining and downstream objectives are well aligned, which accelerates convergence toward flatter minima associated with improved generalization. Overall, our findings characterize pretraining as an optimization prior whose effectiveness is governed by task alignment and model capacity, offering principled guidance for future RNA FMs.

paragraphs: RNA foundation models learn from large collections of sequences, but why that pretraining helps later biological tasks remains unclear. This paper systematically examines transfer across structural and functional tasks. It asks whether pretrained models mainly supply reusable features or help downstream training in another way.

The findings show that frozen representations do not transfer universally. The familiar computer-vision picture of reusing a hierarchy of pretrained features also does not generally carry over to these RNA models. Instead, when pretraining and downstream objectives align well, pretraining primarily supplies a favorable starting point for optimization. This starting point accelerates convergence toward flatter minima associated with improved generalization.

The paper therefore characterizes pretraining as an optimization prior whose value depends on task alignment and model capacity. That is a conditional account of transfer: usefulness is shaped by what the model learned and what the downstream task requires. The study provides guidance for understanding RNA foundation models by separating the benefit of fixed representations from the benefit of initializing subsequent learning in a favorable region.
summary.tldr: RNA pretraining primarily helps optimization when objectives align, while frozen features are not universally transferable across downstream tasks.

title: Understanding Transfer Learning of RNA Foundation Models on Downstream Tasks

abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to replace a full training set with a tiny synthetic one, yet current theories neither explain why heterogeneous matching objectives (gradient, distribution, trajectory) work nor provide a quantitative boundary for robustness under configuration changes (optimizer, architecture, augmentation). We propose configuration-dynamics-error (CDE) analysis for a broad class of matching-based DD methods, a unified generalization framework that treats a training configuration as an update operator inducing optimization dynamics and measures distillation robustness by the test-risk gap between models trained on distilled versus full data. Within this framework, gradient, distribution, and trajectory matching reduce the same dynamics-induced risk gap, explaining why these heterogeneous objectives can all support dataset distillation. CDE yields two predictive laws: within a fixed configuration, the gap decays as $\mathcal{O}(k^{-1/2})$ with the distilled set size $k$ until a configuration-dependent floor, explaining IPC saturation and indicating when reducing the floor is more valuable than enlarging $k$. Across configurations, an order-tight coverage law formalizes the utility boundary: the required $k$ grows linearly with the configuration diversity captured by covering-number complexity. Experiments with representative DD methods and configuration changes exhibit predictive behavior consistent with both laws.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation replaces a large training set with a small synthetic one. This paper asks why different matching objectives can achieve that goal and how far a distilled set remains useful when training configurations change. Its configuration-dynamics-error framework measures the test-risk gap between models trained on distilled data and those trained on the full dataset.

The framework represents a training configuration as an update operator that determines optimization dynamics. Gradient, distribution, and trajectory matching are then understood as reducing the same dynamics-induced risk gap. Within a fixed configuration, the analysis predicts that the gap decreases at order k to the power of minus one-half as the distilled set size k grows, until reaching a configuration-dependent floor.

Across configurations, an order-tight coverage law says the required set size grows linearly with configuration diversity measured through covering-number complexity. This formalizes a boundary on how broadly a small distilled dataset can serve different training setups. Experiments with representative methods and configuration changes behave consistently with both laws, supporting guidance on when enlarging the synthetic set helps and when reducing the error floor matters more.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies dataset-distillation objectives and derives laws linking their usefulness to synthetic-set size and training-configuration diversity.

title: Utility Boundary of Dataset Distillation: Scaling and Coverage Laws

abstract: Extensive research has highlighted the severe threats posed by backdoor attacks to deep reinforcement learning (DRL). However, prior studies primarily focus on vanilla scenarios, while plasticity interventions have emerged as indispensable built-in components of modern DRL agents. Despite their effectiveness in mitigating plasticity loss, the impact of these interventions on DRL backdoor vulnerabilities remains underexplored, and this lack of systematic investigation poses risks in practical DRL deployments. To bridge this gap, we empirically study 14,664 cases integrating representative interventions and attack scenarios. We find that only one intervention (i.e., SAM) exacerbates backdoor threats, while other interventions mitigate them. Pathological analysis identifies that the exacerbation is attributed to backdoor gradient amplification, while the mitigation stems from activation pathway disruption and representation space compression. From these findings, we derive two novel insights: (1) a conceptual framework SCC for robust backdoor injection that deconstructs the mechanistic interplay between interventions and backdoors in DRL, and (2) abnormal loss landscape sharpness as a key indicator for DRL backdoor detection.

paragraphs: Modern deep reinforcement learning agents use plasticity interventions to preserve their capacity to keep learning. This paper asks how those interventions affect backdoor vulnerabilities, a security question that studies of agents without such interventions leave unresolved. An intervention that improves learning behavior may also change how malicious behavior is retained.

The authors examine 14,664 cases combining representative interventions and attack scenarios. Among the interventions studied, only SAM worsens backdoor threats; the others reduce them. Their mechanistic analysis attributes the worsening to amplification of gradients associated with the backdoor. Mitigation is linked to disruption of activation pathways and compression of the model’s representation space.

These findings lead to two further contributions. SCC is a conceptual framework for understanding how backdoor injection interacts with plasticity interventions and how injection can remain robust. The authors also identify unusual sharpness in the loss landscape as an indicator for backdoor detection. Together, the results show that the tested interventions have materially different security effects, making their interaction with attacks relevant to evaluating modern reinforcement learning agents.
summary.tldr: A study of 14,664 cases finds that most tested plasticity interventions mitigate reinforcement learning backdoors, while SAM exacerbates them.

title: Angel or Demon: Investigating the Plasticity Interventions’ Impact on Backdoor Threats in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This work studies the convergence of two-timescale stochastic approximations (SA), a class of iterative algorithms that update two sets of parameters in fast and slow timescales respectively. Notable examples of two-timescale SA in reinforcement learning (RL) include temporal difference learning with gradient correction (TDC) and actor-critic methods. Previously, the stability (i.e., boundedness) and convergence of two-timescale SA were only established under i.i.d. noise. This work instead establishes the stability and convergence of two-timescale SA under Markovian noise, a setup that is more realistic in RL. Notably, we do not need to use any projection operator and the noise does not need to live in a compact space. Our key technical novelty is to control the fast timescale parameter with the running max of the slow timescale parameter, instead of with the current slow timescale parameter, as most prior works do. As a key application, we establish the first almost sure convergence of TDC with eligibility traces under off-policy learning with linear function approximation.

paragraphs: Some learning algorithms update two interacting sets of parameters at different speeds. Establishing that these updates remain bounded and eventually converge becomes more difficult when successive observations are dependent. This paper studies that situation using Markovian noise, a setting relevant to reinforcement learning because observations arrive through an evolving process.

The analysis establishes stability and convergence for two-timescale stochastic approximation under this noise model. It does not require a projection operator to force parameters back into a bounded region, and the noise need not occupy a compact space. The paper establishes its first almost sure convergence result for off-policy learning with linear function approximation. This connects the general mathematical argument to a concrete reinforcement learning method, extending convergence analysis to dependent observations without the stated projection or compact-noise requirements.
summary.tldr: A new stability argument establishes two-timescale convergence under Markovian noise and yields an off-policy TDC convergence result.

title: Convergence of Two-Timescale Markovian Stochastic Approximations with Applications in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Backdoor attacks can introduce deceptive behaviors into large language models, causing them to execute prohibited actions only when specific secret triggers appear in the input. Existing safety training methods largely fail to address this vulnerability, due to the inherent difficulty of uncovering hidden triggers embedded within the model. Motivated by recent findings on LLMs’ situational awareness, we propose a novel post-training framework that cultivates backdoor self-awareness, enabling a poisoned LLM to precisely articulate its own implanted triggers. At its core, our approach introduces an inversion-inspired reinforcement learning framework that encourages models to introspectively reason about their behaviors and gradually reverse-engineer the triggers responsible for misaligned outputs. Building upon precise trigger articulation, we further present two complementary defense strategies for mitigating and detecting backdoor threats. Experiments on five backdoor attacks, compared against six baseline methods, demonstrate that our approach has strong potential to improve the robustness of LLMs against backdoor risks.

paragraphs: A backdoored language model can behave acceptably on ordinary inputs while taking prohibited actions when a secret trigger appears. The abstract identifies discovering those triggers as a major obstacle for existing safety training. This paper explores whether a poisoned model can be trained to describe the triggers implanted in it.

The proposed post-training framework uses reinforcement learning inspired by inversion: working backward from undesirable behavior toward the input condition responsible for it. Training encourages the model to reason about its behavior and progressively reconstruct its hidden triggers. Here, backdoor self-awareness refers to the operational ability to articulate those triggers precisely.

Once triggers can be described, the authors introduce two complementary defenses addressing mitigation and detection. Experiments cover five backdoor attacks and compare against six baseline methods, with results indicating strong potential to improve robustness. The contribution is a way to make hidden triggering conditions explicit and usable for defense. The stated findings support this approach as promising without establishing that every implanted backdoor can be exposed or removed.
summary.tldr: The framework trains poisoned language models to articulate hidden backdoor triggers and uses that information for detection and mitigation.

title: From Poisoned to Aware: Fostering Backdoor Self-Awareness in LLMs

abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) provides the gold standard for sleep assessment but suffers from substantial heterogeneity across recording devices and cohorts. There have been growing efforts to build general-purpose foundation models (FMs) for sleep physiology, but lack an in-depth understanding of the pre-training process and scaling patterns that lead to more generalizable sleep FMs. To fill this gap, we curate a massive corpus of 166,500 hours of sleep recordings from nine public sources and establish SleepBench, a comprehensive, fully open-source benchmark. Leveraging SleepBench, we systematically evaluate four families of self-supervised pre-training objectives and uncover three critical findings: (1) existing FMs fail to generalize to missing channels at inference; (2) channel-invariant feature learning is essential for pre-training; and (3) scaling sample size, model capacity, and multi-source data mixture consistently improves downstream performance. With an enhanced pre-training and scaling recipe, we introduce OSF, a family of sleep FMs that achieves state-of-the-art performance across nine datasets on diverse sleep and disease prediction tasks. Further analysis of OSF also reveals intriguing properties in sample efficiency, hierarchical aggregation, and cross-dataset scaling. Codes are available at: https://github.com/yang-ai-lab/OSF-Open-Sleep-FM.
originalAbstract: Polysomnography (PSG) provides the gold standard for sleep assessment but suffers from substantial heterogeneity across recording devices and cohorts. There have been growing efforts to build general-purpose foundation models (FMs) for sleep physiology, but lack an in-depth understanding of the pre-training process and scaling patterns that lead to more generalizable sleep FMs. To fill this gap, we curate a massive corpus of 166,500 hours of sleep recordings from nine public sources and establish SleepBench, a comprehensive, fully open-source benchmark. Leveraging SleepBench, we systematically evaluate four families of self-supervised pre-training objectives and uncover three critical findings: (1) existing FMs fail to generalize to missing channels at inference; (2) channel-invariant feature learning is essential for pre-training; and (3) scaling sample size, model capacity, and multi-source data mixture consistently improves downstream performance. With an enhanced pre-training and scaling recipe, we introduce OSF, a family of sleep FMs that achieves state-of-the-art performance across nine datasets on diverse sleep and disease prediction tasks. Further analysis of OSF also reveals intriguing properties in sample efficiency, hierarchical aggregation, and cross-dataset scaling. Codes are available at: https://github.com/yang-ai-lab/OSF-Open-Sleep-FM.

paragraphs: OSF studies how to pretrain sleep foundation models that generalize across differences in recording equipment and patient cohorts. The authors assemble 166,500 hours of sleep recordings from nine public sources and introduce the open-source SleepBench benchmark. This provides a common setting for examining training objectives and the effects of increasing data and model scale.

The study compares four families of self-supervised objectives. It finds that existing foundation models struggle when recording channels are missing at inference, and identifies channel-invariant feature learning as essential to pretraining. It also reports consistent downstream gains from increasing the number of samples, model capacity, and the mixture of data sources.

Using an improved pretraining and scaling recipe, the authors develop the OSF model family, which achieves state-of-the-art results across nine datasets covering sleep and disease prediction tasks. Further analyses examine sample efficiency, hierarchical aggregation, and cross-dataset scaling. The contribution connects model performance to concrete pretraining choices, especially how representations handle channel variation and benefit from diverse recording sources.
summary.tldr: OSF uses a large open sleep benchmark to identify pretraining and scaling choices that improve generalization across recording sources.

title: OSF: On Pre-training and Scaling of Sleep Foundation Models

abstract: We study first-order methods for solving monotone variational inequalities arising in min-max optimization. Classical approaches such as the extragradient method rely on two gradient queries per iteration, which limits their analysis and applicability in the online and stochastic settings. We propose a family of Generalized Optimistic Methods with Anchoring (GOMA), which combine two-time-scale optimistic updates with an anchoring term inspired by Halpern iteration. In the deterministic setting, GOMA achieves the optimal accelerated last-iterate rate $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ on the squared gradient norm for monotone Lipschitz operators. In the stochastic setting with unbounded variance, a simplified single-call variant of GOMA achieves a last-iterate convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{k})$ on the squared gradient norm. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first such guarantee for stochastic monotone Lipschitz variational inequalities in the unconstrained setting without variance reduction or growing batches.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems in which progress means finding an equilibrium, as in min-max optimization. It focuses on monotone variational inequalities, a mathematical formulation for these problems. Classical extragradient methods request gradient information twice per iteration, which complicates their use and analysis when updates must happen online or gradients contain noise.

The authors introduce Generalized Optimistic Methods with Anchoring, or GOMA. These methods combine optimistic updates operating on two time scales with an anchoring term inspired by Halpern iteration. The analysis concerns the last iterate: the actual point reached after a given number of updates, rather than an average of earlier points.

For deterministic monotone Lipschitz operators, GOMA achieves an optimal O(1/k²) rate for the squared gradient norm. With stochastic gradients and unbounded variance, a simplified variant using one call per iteration achieves O(1/√k) on that same quantity. The authors identify the latter as, to their knowledge, the first such unconstrained guarantee without variance reduction or growing batches. These assumptions define the settings in which the convergence claims apply.
summary.tldr: GOMA combines optimistic updates with anchoring to obtain accelerated deterministic convergence and a single-call stochastic convergence guarantee for monotone variational inequalities.

title: Accelerated and Stable Convergence with Anchored Generalized Optimistic Method

abstract: Histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) are routinely acquired in clinical practice and contain rich tissue morphology but lack direct molecular architecture and functional programs defining pathological states, whereas RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) provides genome-wide transcriptional profiles at substantial cost, thereby motivating WSI-based genome-wide transcriptomic prediction. Existing approaches for predicting gene expression from WSIs predominantly rely on deterministic regression with one-to-one mapping, limiting their ability to capture biological heterogeneity and predictive uncertainty. We propose RNA-FM, a flow-matching generative framework for genome-wide bulk RNA-seq prediction from WSIs. RNA-FM formulates transcriptomic prediction as a continuous-time conditional transport problem, learning a velocity field that maps a simple prior to the target gene expression distribution conditioned on morphologies. By integrating pathway-level structure, RNA-FM enables scalable and biologically interpretable genome-wide gene expression imputation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RNA-FM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches while maintaining biological meaningfulness. Code is available at https://github.com/YXSong000/RNA-FM.

paragraphs: RNA-FM predicts genome-wide bulk RNA-sequencing profiles from histopathology whole-slide images. These images provide rich information about tissue appearance, while RNA sequencing measures transcriptional activity at substantial cost. Existing prediction methods commonly assign one fixed expression profile to each image, limiting their ability to represent biological variation and predictive uncertainty.

The proposed framework instead learns a conditional distribution of gene expression using flow matching. It learns a velocity field that continuously transforms a simple starting distribution into the target expression distribution, conditioned on tissue morphology. This makes transcriptomic prediction a generative transport problem rather than a deterministic one-to-one regression task.

RNA-FM also incorporates pathway-level structure to make genome-wide imputation scalable and biologically interpretable. This connects the broad prediction task with organized biological information rather than treating its outputs only as an undifferentiated collection of values. Extensive experiments show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art approaches while retaining biological meaningfulness, supporting distribution-based modeling for recovering transcriptomic information from tissue images.
summary.tldr: RNA-FM uses morphology-conditioned flow matching and pathway structure to predict distributions of genome-wide gene expression from tissue images.

title: RNA-FM: Flow-Matching Generative Model for Genome-wide RNA-Seq Prediction

abstract: We develop horizon-aware anytime-valid tests and confidence sequences for bounded means under a strict deadline $N$. Using the betting/e-process framework, we cast horizon-aware betting as a finite-horizon optimal control problem with state space $(t, \log W_t)$, where $t$ is the time and $W_t$ is the test martingale value. We first show that in certain interior regions of the state space, policies that deviate significantly from Kelly betting are provably suboptimal, while Kelly betting reaches the threshold with high probability. We then identify sufficient conditions showing that outside this region, more aggressive betting than Kelly can be better if the bettor is behind schedule, and less aggressive can be better if the bettor is ahead. Taken together these results suggest a simple phase diagram in the $(t, \log W_t)$ plane, delineating regions where Kelly, fractional Kelly, and aggressive betting may be preferable. Guided by this phase diagram, we introduce a Deep Reinforcement Learning approach based on a universal Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent that learns a single policy from synthetic experience and maps simple statistics of past observations to bets across horizons and null values. In limited-horizon experiments, the learned DQN policy yields state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Anytime-valid statistical tests allow evidence to be checked as observations arrive, but a strict deadline changes which evidence-gathering strategy is useful. This paper studies tests and confidence sequences for bounded means when no more than N observations are available. It frames the choice of statistical bets as a finite-horizon control problem.

The state records elapsed time and the logarithm of the test’s accumulated wealth. In certain interior regions, the authors prove that substantial deviations from Kelly betting are suboptimal and that Kelly betting reaches the decision threshold with high probability. Elsewhere, sufficient conditions favor more aggressive bets when behind schedule and less aggressive bets when ahead.

These conditional results motivate a phase diagram rather than a universally best betting rule. Guided by it, the authors train one Deep Q-Network policy using synthetic experience. The policy maps simple summaries of past observations to bets across different deadlines and null values. Limited-horizon experiments report state-of-the-art results, supporting the value of adapting betting behavior to both accumulated evidence and remaining time.
summary.tldr: A learned betting policy adapts anytime-valid tests to deadlines using theoretical guidance on when to bet more or less aggressively.

title: Learning to Bet for Horizon-Aware Anytime-Valid Testing

abstract: Learning causal relationships between variables from data is a fundamental research area with many applications across disciplines. Most of the existing causal discovery algorithms rely on the assumptions that (i) the underlying system is acyclic, (ii) the exogenous noise variables are Gaussian, and (iii) that the intervention targets for the data generating experiments are known. While these assumptions simplify the analysis, they are violated in real-life systems. Most existing methods that address these issues either assume the underlying model is linear or are constrained to operate in limited interventional settings. To that end, we propose SCOUT, a novel causal discovery framework to learn nonlinear causal cyclic relationships from soft interventional data with unknown targets. Our main approach maximizes the data log-likelihood to recover the graph structure, using two normalizing-flow architectures—contractive residual flows and neural spline flows. By conducting experiments on synthetic and real-world data, we show that SCOUT outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both causal graph and unknown target recovery across various interventional and noise settings.

paragraphs: Causal discovery methods often simplify their task by excluding feedback loops, assuming Gaussian noise, or requiring knowledge of which variables an experiment changed. SCOUT addresses a setting where nonlinear relationships may form cycles and the targets of soft interventions are unknown. This brings several difficulties together within one causal-learning problem.

The framework maximizes the likelihood of observed data to recover the graph structure. It uses two normalizing-flow architectures: contractive residual flows and neural spline flows. These provide the modeling machinery for learning nonlinear cyclic relationships from interventional observations, while the method also seeks to recover the unknown intervention targets.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that SCOUT outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both graph recovery and target recovery across varied intervention and noise settings. The findings support tackling feedback, nonlinearity, and unidentified interventions jointly rather than requiring those aspects to be simplified away beforehand. The contribution is a framework and empirical evidence for causal discovery under this more flexible combination of conditions, with evaluation covering both the causal structure and the interventions that help reveal it.
summary.tldr: SCOUT learns nonlinear causal graphs with feedback loops and unknown soft-intervention targets using normalizing flows.

title: SCOUT: Cyclic Causal Discovery Under Soft Interventions with Unknown Targets

abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) has emerged as a key solution to accelerate the inference of autoregressive models. However, in the field of image generation, it faces the challenge of low acceptance rates, and directly relaxing its criteria leads to degradation in image quality. In this paper, we propose a novel content-aware speculative decoding algorithm, termed CSD, which integrates an entropy-based probability relaxation mechanism with an optimal resampling strategy to enhance the inference efficiency for autoregressive image generation. By leveraging the informational uncertainty inherent in different regions of an image, CSD dynamically adjusts the acceptance probability of candidate tokens, increasing the acceptance rate in low-detail areas to accelerate generation. Moreover, a distribution alignment filter is introduced to ensure the output distribution to be aligned with the target model, which significantly improves the generative quality. Experiments conducted on Lumina-mGPT and Janus-Pro demonstrate that the superiority of the proposed CSD. Our source code is available at https://github.com/aderfebr/CSD.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by proposing candidate tokens that a target model can accept. For image generation, low acceptance rates limit the benefit, while simply loosening acceptance rules can damage image quality. CSD addresses this tension by making acceptance depend on the content being generated, rather than applying the same relaxation everywhere.

Its acceptance mechanism uses entropy to account for differences in informational uncertainty across image regions. It raises acceptance rates in areas with little detail, where the method seeks opportunities to generate faster. An optimal resampling strategy accompanies this probability relaxation, making candidate handling part of the overall decoding design rather than an isolated change to the acceptance threshold.

CSD also includes a distribution alignment filter to keep generated outputs aligned with the target model’s distribution and improve quality. Experiments on Lumina-mGPT and Janus-Pro report advantages for the approach. The central idea is to coordinate regional acceptance flexibility with distribution alignment, addressing the quality problems that arise from relaxing speculative decoding criteria directly.
summary.tldr: CSD adapts speculative token acceptance to image content and adds distribution alignment to improve generation efficiency and quality.

title: CSD: Content-aware Speculative Decoding for Efficient Image Generation

abstract: Structured scientific spectra encode rich physical information while obeying hard constraints, such as conservation laws and characteristic spectral geometry. Accurate prediction of these spectra is central to materials discovery, yet existing methods often treat them as unconstrained sequences and therefore fail to enforce the underlying physical structure. Taking electronic density of states (eDOS) as the prototypical example, we introduce DeepSciReasoner, a general paradigm for predicting scientific spectra under physical constraints. The framework combines structure-aware spectrum decoding with constraint-preserving physical reasoning, allowing predictions to capture rich spectral structure while respecting the underlying physics. We evaluate DeepSciReasoner on eDOS, phonon density of states (phDOS), X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), and Raman spectra, where it substantially improves prediction accuracy while maintaining physical consistency. These results establish DeepSciReasoner as a reusable blueprint for structured scientific spectrum prediction under hard physical constraints.

paragraphs: Scientific spectra contain structured physical information, and their predictions must respect constraints such as conservation laws and characteristic spectral geometry. The paper argues that treating spectra as unconstrained sequences overlooks this structure. That matters for materials discovery, where an accurate prediction should also remain compatible with the physics represented by the spectrum.

DeepSciReasoner combines two parts: a decoder designed around spectral structure and a physical reasoning process that preserves constraints. Electronic density of states serves as the main motivating example. The approach aims to retain detailed spectral information while enforcing the physical conditions that govern it, making those conditions part of prediction rather than a separate consideration.

The authors evaluate the framework on electronic and phonon density of states, X-ray absorption near-edge structure, and Raman spectra. They report substantial gains in predictive accuracy while maintaining physical consistency across these tasks. The findings support the framework’s proposed reuse across different scientific spectra: structure-aware decoding and constraint-preserving reasoning can work together within a shared prediction paradigm.
summary.tldr: DeepSciReasoner improves scientific spectrum prediction by combining structure-aware decoding with reasoning that preserves physical constraints.

title: Deep Scientific Reasoning under Physical Constraints: Structure-Aware Spectrum Prediction

abstract: Predicting 3D geometric trajectory requires capturing complex spatiotemporal dependencies while preserving physical symmetries. While flow matching offers a powerful generative paradigm, extending it to SE(3)-equivariant dynamics is challenging due to the inherent gap between deterministic history and stochastic evolving flows. To address this, we introduce GSE-Flow, an SE(3)-equivariant flow matching framework. We first propose a Coherent Sequence Encoding and Time-Modulated Embedding strategy that unifies historical and evolving streams, incorporating velocity and flow time via equivariant affine transformations to guide continuous evolution. We further design a Geometry-Feature Tensorization mechanism that projects node states into a tensor product space, enabling Context-Flow Fusion to guide trajectory evolution with historical context. GSE-Flow guarantees theoretical SE(3)-equivariance and achieves SOTA accuracy on MD17, MD22, and CMU MoCap benchmarks for geometric trajectory prediction, while demonstrating generality by enhancing deterministic baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/aegine/GSE-Flow.

paragraphs: Predicting future movement in three dimensions requires a model to connect past motion with possible future trajectories. It should also respect physical symmetries: rotating or translating the input should transform the prediction consistently. This paper develops GSE-Flow, a flow-matching framework that guarantees this rotation-and-translation behavior, known as SE(3) equivariance.

A central challenge is combining a fixed observed history with a stochastic trajectory that changes during generation. GSE-Flow addresses this through coherent sequence encoding and time-modulated embeddings. These incorporate velocity and flow time using transformations that preserve equivariance, allowing historical information and the evolving prediction to participate in the same process.

The framework also maps geometric and feature information into a tensor-product space, where historical context can guide trajectory evolution. The authors establish equivariance theoretically and report state-of-the-art prediction accuracy on MD17, MD22, and CMU MoCap. They additionally demonstrate improvements to deterministic baselines. Together, these results connect a mathematical symmetry guarantee with empirical gains across the tested geometric trajectory tasks.
summary.tldr: GSE-Flow combines motion history with generative flow matching while guaranteeing consistent predictions under 3D rotations and translations.

title: Flow for Future: Geometric SE(3)-Equivariant Flow Matching for 3D Trajectory Prediction

abstract: Synthesizing physics-grounded 3D assets is a critical bottleneck for interactive virtual worlds and embodied AI. Existing methods predominantly focus on static geometry, overlooking the functional properties essential for interaction. We propose that interactive asset generation must be rooted in functional logic and hierarchical physics. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysForge, a decoupled two-stage framework supported by PhysDB, a large-scale dataset of 150,000 assets with four-tier physical annotations. First, a VLM acts as a physical architect to plan a Hierarchical Physical Blueprint defining material, functional, and kinematic constraints. Second, a physics-grounded diffusion model realizes this blueprint by synthesizing high-fidelity geometry alongside precise kinematic parameters via a novel KineVoxel Injection (KVI) mechanism. Experiments demonstrate that PhysForge produces functionally plausible, simulation-ready assets, providing a robust data engine for interactive 3D content and embodied agents.

paragraphs: Interactive virtual worlds need objects with functional and physical properties, as well as convincing geometry. PhysForge addresses asset generation by making those properties part of the design process. The framework separates planning how an object should function from generating its geometry and motion parameters.

In the first stage, a vision-language model produces a hierarchical physical blueprint specifying material, functional, and kinematic constraints. In the second, a physics-grounded diffusion model turns that plan into detailed geometry together with kinematic parameters. A mechanism called KineVoxel Injection supports this joint generation, connecting the planned physical behavior to the resulting asset.

The framework is supported by PhysDB, a dataset of 150,000 assets with four tiers of physical annotations. Experiments show that PhysForge produces functionally plausible assets ready for simulation. These findings support organizing generation around functional logic and hierarchical physics. The resulting assets are intended to provide content for interactive environments and embodied agents, linking visual construction with the information needed for interaction.
summary.tldr: PhysForge plans physical and functional constraints before generating 3D geometry and motion parameters, producing simulation-ready interactive assets.

title: PhysForge: Generating Physics-Grounded 3D Assets for Interactive Virtual World

abstract: The increasing impact of climate change and extreme weather events has spurred growing interest in deep learning for weather research. However, existing studies often rely on weather data in pixel space, which presents several challenges such as smooth outputs in model outputs, limited applicability to a single pressure-variable subset (PVS), and high data storage and computational costs. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Weather Latent Autoencoder (WLA) that transforms weather data from pixel space to latent space, enabling efficient data representation. By decoupling weather reconstruction from downstream tasks, WLA improves the accuracy and sharpness of weather task model results. The incorporated Pressure-Variable Unified Module transforms multiple PVS into a unified representation, enhancing the adaptability of the model in multiple weather scenarios. Furthermore, weather tasks can be performed in a low-storage latent space of WLA rather than a high-storage pixel space, thus significantly reducing data storage and computational costs. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate its superior compression and reconstruction performance, enabling the creation of the ERA5-Latent dataset with unified representations of multiple PVS from ERA5 data. The compressed full PVS in the ERA5-Latent dataset reduces the original 244.34 TB of data to 0.43 TB. The downstream task further demonstrates that task models can apply to multiple PVS with low data costs in latent space and achieve superior performance compared to models in pixel space.

The Weather Latent Autoencoder addresses these issues by converting weather fields into compact latent representations. It separates weather reconstruction from downstream tasks so that task models can operate in the compressed space.

A Pressure-Variable Unified Module brings multiple pressure-variable subsets into a common representation. This supports using task models across different weather scenarios while retaining a reconstruction mechanism for returning to weather fields. The authors report improved accuracy and sharpness alongside reduced storage and computational costs from working in latent space.

Experiments demonstrate superior compression and reconstruction performance, and downstream evaluation shows task models handling multiple subsets at low data cost while outperforming pixel-space models. The findings connect representation compression with improved task results rather than treating storage reduction as the only objective.
summary.tldr: WLA unifies and compresses weather data into latent space, reducing ERA5 storage substantially while improving evaluated downstream results.

title: Transforming Weather Data from Pixel to Latent Space

abstract: Despite significant recent progress of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), current MLLMs are challenged by "spatio-temporal" prompts, i.e., prompts that refer to 1) the entirety of an environment encoded in a point cloud that the MLLM should consider; and simultaneously also refer to 2) actions that happened in part of the environment and are encoded in a short ego-centric video clip. However, such a holistic spatio-temporal understanding is important for agents operating in the real world. To address this challenge, we first develop a framework to collect a large-scale dataset. Using the collected "Reasoning about Environments and Actions" (REA) dataset, we show that recent MLLMs indeed struggle to correctly answer "spatio-temporal" prompts. Building on this dataset, we study two spatio-temporal LLM (STLLM) baselines: 1) STLLM-3D, which directly fuses point cloud, video, and text representations as inputs to the LLM; and 2) STLLM-Aligner, which aligns spatial context with video and text before LLM decoding. Both baselines aim to enhance spatial understanding of environments and temporal grounding of egocentric observations. On REA, the STLLM baselines outperform existing models, demonstrating the effectiveness of our designs.

paragraphs: Understanding an action can require both a view of what happened locally and knowledge of the surrounding environment. This paper studies prompts that combine a point cloud of an entire environment with a short first-person video of actions occurring within it. The task requires models to relate spatial context to observations unfolding over time.

The authors develop a collection framework and build the Reasoning about Environments and Actions dataset, or REA. They use it to demonstrate that recent multimodal language models struggle with these combined prompts. They then introduce two baselines: STLLM-3D directly fuses point-cloud, video, and text representations, while STLLM-Aligner aligns spatial context with video and text before language-model decoding.

Both designs outperform existing models on REA. The results support explicitly incorporating environmental geometry when reasoning about localized first-person actions, and show that the proposed fusion and alignment approaches are effective on this dataset. The contribution combines a way to evaluate holistic spatial-temporal understanding with model designs intended to improve that capability.
summary.tldr: REA and two STLLM baselines address reasoning that connects whole-environment point clouds with actions shown in first-person video.

title: Spatio-Temporal LLM: Reasoning about Environments and Actions
Second Tier for Decision Trees
Identifying Predictive Structures in Relational Data Using Multiple Instance Learning

abstract: In this study we introduce a novel algorithm for learning a polyhedron to describe the target class. The proposed approach takes advantage of the limited subclass information made available for the negative samples and jointly optimizes multiple hyperplane classifiers each of which is designed to classify positive samples from a subclass of the negative samples. The flat faces of the polyhedron provides robustness whereas multiple faces contributes to the flexibility required to deal with complex datasets. Apart from improving the prediction accuracy of the system, the proposed polyhedral classifier also provides run-time speedups as a by-product when executed in a cascaded framework in real-time. We introduce the Computer Aided Detection for Colon Cancer as a case study and evaluate the performance of the proposed technique on a real-world Colon dataset both in terms of prediction accuracy and online execution speed. We also compare the proposed technique against some benchmark classifiers.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a classifier that represents the target class with a polyhedron, a shape bounded by multiple flat faces. Its training procedure uses limited information about subclasses among the negative examples. Each hyperplane classifier is designed to distinguish positive examples from one of those negative subclasses.

The hyperplanes are optimized jointly so that they collectively describe the target class. The authors attribute robustness to the flat faces and flexibility to having multiple faces. This combines simple individual boundaries into a shape able to accommodate more complex data. The available negative subclass information gives the separate boundaries distinct classification roles.

The proposed classifier is evaluated on a real-world colon dataset in a computer-aided detection case study. The authors report improved prediction accuracy and runtime speedups when the model operates within a real-time cascade. They also compare it with benchmark classifiers. The contribution connects a structured geometric representation to both prediction and execution efficiency, with the stated evidence coming from this target-detection application.
summary.tldr: Jointly learned polyhedral boundaries use negative subclasses to improve target detection and accelerate cascaded execution.

title: Polyhedral classifier for target detection: a case study: colorectal cancer

abstract: In this work we address the question of finding symmetries of a given MDP. We show that the problem is Isomorphism Complete , that is, the problem is polynomially equivalent to verifying whether two graphs are isomorphic. Apart from the theoretical importance of this result it has an important practical application. The reduction presented can be used together with any off-the-shelf Graph Isomorphism solver, which performs well in the average case, to find symmetries of an MDP. In fact, we present results of using NAutY (the best Graph Isomorphism solver currently available), to find symmetries of MDPs.

paragraphs: The paper investigates the computational difficulty of finding symmetries in a given Markov decision process. It shows that this problem is isomorphism complete: it is polynomially equivalent to determining whether two graphs are isomorphic. This characterizes the symmetry-finding problem through its relationship to a well-established computational problem.

The equivalence also supplies a practical method. The reduction can be paired with an off-the-shelf graph isomorphism solver to find MDP symmetries. Thus the theoretical construction does more than classify difficulty; it makes existing graph-processing tools available for a problem originally expressed in the language of decision processes.

The authors report results using the NAutY graph isomorphism solver for this purpose. The practical motivation relies on graph isomorphism solvers performing well in the average case, rather than on a claim of uniformly easy computation. The contribution is both a complexity result and a usable reduction, connecting MDP symmetry discovery to established algorithms for detecting equivalence in graphs.
summary.tldr: Finding MDP symmetries is polynomially equivalent to graph isomorphism, and the reduction enables practical use of graph isomorphism solvers.

title: On the hardness of finding symmetries in Markov decision processes

abstract: This paper presents a theoretical framework for ranking, and demonstrates how to perform generalization analysis of listwise ranking algorithms using the framework. Many learning-to-rank algorithms have been proposed in recent years. Among them, the listwise approach has shown higher empirical ranking performance when compared to the other approaches. However, there is no theoretical study on the listwise approach as far as we know. In this paper, we propose a theoretical framework for ranking, which can naturally describe various listwise learning- to-rank algorithms. With this framework, we prove a theorem which gives a generalization bound of a listwise ranking algorithm, on the basis of Rademacher Average of the class of compound functions. The compound functions take listwise loss functions as outer functions and ranking models as inner functions. We then compute the Rademacher Averages for existing listwise algorithms of ListMLE, ListNet, and RankCosine. We also discuss the tightness of the bounds in different situations with regard to the list length and transformation function.

We also discuss the tightness of the bounds in different situations with regard to the list length and transformation function.

paragraphs: Listwise ranking methods learn by evaluating ranked lists as a whole. Although these methods had shown strong empirical performance, the authors identify a lack of corresponding theoretical analysis. This paper develops a framework that describes different listwise algorithms and supports reasoning about how their learned rankings may generalize beyond the training data.

The main theorem bounds generalization using the Rademacher average of a class of compound functions. Each compound function combines a ranking model with a listwise loss: the model produces ranking information, and the loss evaluates it. Analyzing this combination makes the bound sensitive to both the prediction family and the way ranking errors are measured.

The authors calculate these complexity quantities for ListMLE, ListNet, and RankCosine. They also examine how tight the bounds are under different list lengths and transformation functions. The contribution is a common theoretical language for assessing these algorithms, including how design choices affect the resulting guarantees. It does not turn prior empirical superiority into a universal ranking-performance claim.
summary.tldr: A shared theoretical framework provides Rademacher-based generalization bounds for listwise ranking methods, including ListMLE, ListNet, and RankCosine.

title: Generalization analysis of listwise learning-to-rank algorithms

abstract: Information theoretic based measures form a fundamental class of similarity measures for comparing clusterings, beside the class of pair-counting based and set-matching based measures. In this paper, we discuss the necessity of correction for chance for information theoretic based measures for clusterings comparison. We observe that the baseline for such measures, i.e. average value under random partitioning of a data set, does not take on a constant value, and tends to have larger variation when the ratio between the number of data points and the number of clusters is small. This effect is similar in some other non-information theoretic based measures such as the well-known Rand Index. Assuming a hypergeometric model of randomness, we derive the analytical formula for the expected mutual information value between a pair of clusterings, and then propose the adjusted version for several popular information theoretic based measures. Some examples are given to demonstrate the need and usefulness of the adjusted measures.

Some examples are given to demonstrate the need and usefulness of the adjusted measures.

paragraphs: Comparing two clusterings requires a measure of how similarly they group the same data. This paper examines information-theoretic similarity measures and asks how much of their score can arise by chance. The authors observe that the average score under random partitioning is not constant, complicating the interpretation of an unadjusted similarity value.

This baseline varies more when the number of data points is small relative to the number of clusters. The issue also occurs in some measures outside the information-theoretic family, including the Rand Index. A score can therefore reflect features of the partitioning setup as well as meaningful agreement between the clusterings.

Assuming a hypergeometric model of randomness, the authors derive an analytical expression for expected mutual information. They use it to construct adjusted versions of several popular information-theoretic measures and provide examples showing their usefulness. The correction gives similarity scores a chance-based reference under the specified random model, helping separate observed agreement from the agreement that model would already predict.
summary.tldr: Chance agreement can distort clustering similarity scores, motivating adjusted information-theoretic measures based on expected mutual information.

title: Information theoretic measures for clusterings comparison: is a correction for chance necessary?

abstract: Training principles for unsupervised learning are often derived from motivations that appear to be independent of supervised learning, causing a proliferation of semisupervised training methods. In this paper we present a simple unification of several supervised and unsupervised training principles through the concept of optimal reverse prediction: predict the inputs from the target labels, optimizing both over model parameters and any missing labels. In particular, we show how supervised least squares, principal components analysis, k-means clustering and normalized graph-cut clustering can all be expressed as instances of the same training principle, differing only in constraints made on the target labels. Natural forms of semi-supervised regression and classification are then automatically derived, yielding semi-supervised learning algorithms for regression and classification that, surprisingly, are novel and refine the state of the art. These algorithms can all be combined with standard regularizers and made non-linear via kernels.

In this paper we present a simple unification of several supervised and unsupervised training principles through the concept of optimal reverse prediction: predict the inputs from the target labels, optimizing both over model parameters and any missing labels. In particular, we show how supervised least squares, principal components analysis, k-means clustering and normalized graph-cut clustering can all be expressed as instances of the same training principle, differing only in constraints made on the target labels. Natural forms of semi-supervised regression and classification are then automatically derived, yielding semi-supervised learning algorithms for regression and classification that, surprisingly, are novel and refine the state of the art. These algorithms can all be combined with standard regularizers and made non-linear via kernels.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a shared training principle for several supervised and unsupervised methods. Called optimal reverse prediction, it predicts inputs from target labels while optimizing both model parameters and labels that are missing. This reverses the familiar direction of predicting a target from an input and makes missing labels part of the optimization.

Under this principle, supervised least squares, principal components analysis, k-means, and normalized graph-cut clustering become instances of one framework. Their differences are expressed through constraints on the target labels. This connection explains how methods that appear to have separate motivations can arise from related optimization problems.

The same construction yields semi-supervised regression and classification algorithms by allowing some labels to be known and others to be optimized. The authors describe these algorithms as novel refinements of the state of the art. They can also incorporate standard regularizers and use kernels to become nonlinear. The contribution therefore includes both a conceptual unification and new learning procedures derived from that common principle.
summary.tldr: Predicting inputs from labels unifies several established learning methods and yields new semi-supervised regression and classification algorithms.

title: Optimal reverse prediction: a unified perspective on supervised, unsupervised and semi-supervised learning

abstract: Bayesian treatments of Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) -type latent variable models have been recently proposed for coping with overfitting in small sample sizes, as well as for producing factorizations of the data sources into correlated and non-shared effects. However, all of the current implementations of Bayesian CCA and its extensions are computationally inefficient for high-dimensional data and, as shown in this paper, break down completely for high-dimensional sources with low sample count. Furthermore, they cannot reliably separate the correlated effects from non-shared ones. We propose a new Bayesian CCA variant that is computationally efficient and works for high-dimensional data, while also learning the factorization more accurately. The improvements are gained by introducing a group sparsity assumption and an improved variational approximation. The method is demonstrated to work well on multi-label prediction tasks and in analyzing brain correlates of naturalistic audio stimulation.

The method is demonstrated to work well on multi-label prediction tasks and in analyzing brain correlates of naturalistic audio stimulation.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis concerns relationships between data sources. Bayesian versions of related latent-variable models aim to handle small samples and separate effects shared across sources from effects specific to one source. The paper identifies a serious practical problem: the existing implementations it considers are computationally inefficient for high-dimensional data and fail when high dimensionality is combined with few samples.

The proposed Bayesian CCA variant changes both the modeling assumption and the approximation used for inference. It introduces group sparsity together with an improved variational approximation. These changes are intended to make computation manageable while improving the separation between correlated effects and non-shared effects, a distinction the earlier methods do not reliably recover.

The authors report that the method works efficiently with high-dimensional data and learns the factorization more accurately. Demonstrations include multi-label prediction and analysis of brain responses associated with naturalistic audio stimulation. The contribution therefore concerns both computational practicality and the meaning of the extracted factors: identifying which variation connects sources and which remains specific to each.
summary.tldr: Group sparsity and improved variational inference make Bayesian CCA more practical and accurate for separating shared and source-specific effects in high-dimensional data.

title: Bayesian CCA via Group Sparsity
Domain-specific Learning and the Subset Principle
